articles.title: I get £4,062 a year and am trying my best - here's what I want from the Budget
articles.standfirst: People on a range of incomes from £4,062 to £150,000 a year tell the BBC what they want to see in this year's Budget.
paragraphs: Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the Budget
Chancellor John Healey is set to unveil his first Budget on Wednesday.

Unlike in previous years there have been very few leaks about what will be in it, though Healey's tax and spending plans will be under close scrutiny at a time when government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".
BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and what they would like to see in the Budget.
If there are issues you would like to see covered, you can get in touch via BBC Your Voice.
Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college.
The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers.
"I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."

She wants the government to provide more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government's Jobs Guarantee scheme extended.

The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.
She is living with her parents but wants to move out eventually. "My parents want me to get a job first. They are not putting pressure on me to go yet."
Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.
He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.
He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."
The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.
"The best thing they could do at the Budget is drastically remove or reduce fuel duty for a period of time."

The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, and the BBC understands it will be frozen again, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."
Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.
Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.
"Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."
Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax.
He wants the chancellor to cut fuel duty and income tax, or increase the personal allowance - the amount of income you do not have to pay tax on - to about £16,000, up from £12,570 currently.

He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announced a scheme to help first-time buyers in England who have a deposit of 2.5%, but Robert says: "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment."
Chloe Chin-Saad's husband passed away four years ago and her biggest worry is the cost of living.

She's very grateful that the rent she pays on her south London maisonette is set below the market rate as it is housing association accommodation, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."
She lives with her 16-year-old son, and says her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity.
"We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."
Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.

But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, the £250 a month she pays on car finance, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.

Two mobile phone bills, and food and pet insurance for her dog also add to her costs. She says the amount she has left over at the end of each month varies, and sometimes she is left with as little as £50.
Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families.
"I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."

Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.
His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year.

"I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."

More generally, Jonathan, 52, would welcome taxes being put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution". He would also like to see a one-off wealth tax for people with assets worth over £10m and new taxes on the oil and gas and banking sectors.
"If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax."
Christine Morris, from Worksop, has been retired for eight years and lives on a state pension combined with a small private pension her late husband left her.
"It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."

Although the prime minister has asked ministers to look at removing standing charges from gas bills, Christine thinks there should be some relief for people who live alone when it comes to standing charges on electricity bills, which are typically higher.

She would also like the government to extend access to pension credit, a means-tested benefit for people who have reached state pension age and are receiving £238 or less per week. Christine currently receives £241 and so just misses out.

She was unconvinced by Andy Burnham's pledge to end the triple lock so that from 2030 the state pension will rise at least by inflation or 2.5%, with the money saved used to create a free-at-the-point of use national care service for England sometime "in the next parliament".
Christine thinks the new service will take time to come in. In the meantime, she fears she will "get less pension and still have to pay out the same for any care I need".
What are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

articles.title: Energy bill help, minimum wage rise and bank taxes - what could be in the Budget?
articles.standfirst: Chancellor John Healey will set out his plans for UK taxes on 28 October.
paragraphs: Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget at around 12:30 on Wednesday.
The speech, which usually lasts about an hour, will be broadcast live on BBC iPlayer and on the BBC News website.
He and Prime Minister Andy Burnham are hoping to give households "breathing space" amid the ongoing high cost of living and they have already announced measures to change gas bills.
But Healey has also refused to rule out some tax increases to potentially pay for support he could distribute elsewhere.
The government has run an unusually tight ship, preventing policies leaking out ahead of time, but here are the key measures expected.
LIVE: Follow all the Budget coverage
Household energy bills are set to see their biggest rise in four years in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276.

Healey has announced that standing charges for household gas bills will be removed for about 23 million homes. These charges are fixed daily fees that are paid by households no matter how much gas they use, and average £108 a year.
The government says energy regulator Ofgem will aim to deliver the removal of these charges in 2027 or "as soon as possible after".

However, this will be offset by higher unit costs for gas. Overall the Treasury estimates that three-fifths of households will see an average saving of £45 a year. Lower gas users will save more but higher users will end up with bigger bills than they have now.

The government also plans to remove tariffs from 100 food items, which it calculates could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June.
The BBC understands the chancellor will keep fuel duty frozen at the Budget and keep in place the 5p fuel duty cut introduced by Rishi Sunak in 2022, as first reported by The Sun.
The Your First Home scheme is aimed at helping people get on the property ladder
The Budget will contain more details on Burnham's planned Your First Home scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property.
The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.
The threshold for eligible buyers will be those with combined incomes of £110,000 outside London, and £140,000 in the capital.
A minimum wage increase will be announced in the Budget, but 18- to 20-year-olds are set to see lower increases than in previous years, the BBC understands.
Pay for younger workers will rise in line with the increase in minimum pay for employees aged 21 years and over.
The increase for younger workers is lower than that seen in the previous two years

However, the increase for younger workers is lower than that seen in the previous two years, when Labour raised the rate to meet a manifesto promise that it would remove "discriminatory age bands" with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage.
Pensioners who only get an income from the state pension are expected to be shielded from paying income tax through a new personal allowance.
But the full state pension is set to rise above the current £12,570 threshold, to £13,036.40 - which would force one million people to pay tax on it.
In his Budget, Healey will explain how these pensioners will be exempted.
An easy target for a Labour chancellor, bank bosses are expecting Healey to raise the amount of tax they pay in order to offer support with energy bills and costs affecting households elsewhere.

Top executives told the BBC they believe the chancellor could reverse a Conservative cut to the surcharge banks pay on their profits, which lowered it from 8% to 3%. Healey could also raise the levy banks pay on the size of their balance sheets.
Online retail giants such as Amazon and eBay are expected to be made responsible for collecting tax owed by traders using their platforms, according to The Times.
The money raised is expected to be used by the government to cut business rates for High Street shops, by raising the threshold at which small companies start paying rates from £12,000 to £18,000.
He is also planning support for small breweries.

Healey has also said the government plans to slash "form-filling and pointless paperwork" to save UK businesses up to £800m. Ministers believe changes in regulations will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy for businesses.

Healey has repeatedly praised the UK's resilience. The UK is the fastest growing G7 country so far this year, and performing better than expected in the face of energy price shocks caused by the US-Israel war with Iran.
But UK growth is expected to slow in the months ahead as those costs continue to weigh on households and businesses.

Prices for goods and services are still rising faster than wanted. Inflation hit 3.1% in the year to August, the highest rate in five months and above the Bank of England's 2% target, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.
Healey's aim in the Budget is to give people "breathing space" to help them cope with the challenges ahead.
When the chancellor sits down, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) will publish economic forecasts for the next five years.
It will set out whether the government is likely to meet the rules it has set for managing the public finances, and how the economy is expected to perform.
Its judgement on the government's plans is keenly watched by financial markets and can have a significant impact on confidence, in turn affecting government borrowing costs.
Leader of the Opposition Kemi Badenoch will respond to the speech in the House of Commons.
MPs then debate the measures for three days before voting on them.
If approved by MPs, tax changes can come into effect immediately.
However, the government must pass a finance bill to make them permanent.

articles.title: Plaid demands more cash, but how could the Budget affect Wales?
articles.standfirst: Welsh Finance Minister Elin Jones has called for a spending plan that "finally treats us fairly".
paragraphs: Plaid Cymru ministers say they want extra cash for railways and public services in Wales ahead of the UK government's Budget on Wednesday.
Welsh Finance Minister Elin Jones called for the Chancellor John Healey to set out a spending plan that "finally treats us fairly".
The Budget announces Westminster's tax and spending plans for the year ahead - and more cash given to English public services could result in extra spending in Wales where they are devolved.
A UK government spokesperson said the chancellor would focus on giving households and businesses "a bit of breathing space where we can".
Meanwhile, shoppers in one of Wales' busiest markets told BBC Wales that once again the cost of living was their biggest concern before the spending announcement.
Any extra spending for things in England that are controlled in Wales by the Welsh government - like healthcare, schools and roads - could trigger additional cash for the country.
Elin Jones had asked the chancellor to bring forward £1bn of the £14bn the UK Labour government had promised for long-term rail funding in Wales.
She also asked for extra money to help the Welsh government set its budget for 2027-28, which currently faces a real-term cut in day-to-day spending.
She previously claimed Wednesday's settlement could be the worst for the Welsh government since the Covid-19 pandemic.
Elin Jones says Wales needs a budget that treats the country "fairly"
Jones said Wales had been short-changed "for years".
"This UK Budget is the moment of truth, and we need the chancellor to act, not just acknowledge the problem," she said.
"Wales pulls its weight in the UK economy. We contribute. Now we need the UK government to match that ambition with action and deliver a budget that finally treats us fairly."
There have also been calls from Labour MP Nia Griffith to give the Welsh government greater flexibility to borrow to fund investment projects.
A senior Welsh Labour source said they had been "pressing really hard for fiscal flexibility", along the lines of Griffith's request.
Ahead of Wednesday's announcement, shoppers and traders at Swansea Market said the cost of living was their biggest concern.
"Will we be able to see through the winter without having to borrow money," said shopper Louise. "It's quite a worry."
Like others at the market, Louise admitted feeling "anxious" about the winter, despite having saved some money with her supplier.
Help with energy costs was the top of many people's lists of things they wanted help with in the Budget.
Prices rose at the beginning of the month and typical bills are forecast to increase by 16% in January because of the conflict in the Middle East.
Louise says she is worried about the winter because "everything is getting more expensive"
Dad-of-two Richard said his wage did not keep up with rising energy bills, leaving his family "penny pinching towards the end of the month".
"Things that we used to have as a bit of luxury are out of the question, days out with family cost a fortune," he said.
Rural homes that use heating oil have also seen a dramatic increase in costs. The chancellor had already announced he will remove import taxes to bring the price down a little.
Healey has talked about giving people "breathing space" from cost-of-living pressures, and revealed a package of small measures he is calling "everyday fixes" ahead of the Budget.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham also wants to cut standing charges from gas bills.
If further support is offered in the Budget, it would be likely limited and targeted to the poorest households.
Richard, from Swansea, says "a lot of things that used to be affordable are now out of reach"
The cost of filling up cars soared this year as the conflict in the Middle East pushed up the price of oil.
Petrol prices hit a four-year high in September, and diesel has also shot up.
The cost of transporting fruit and veg is one issue putting pressure on Gareth Evans, who is the fourth generation of his family to run the Get Fresh stall at Swansea Market.
"It's a struggle at the moment," he said.
"We get costs passed on to us from our suppliers.
"We've also got vans ourselves and we supply caterers and diesel is very expensive."
Emma, who runs a pet store, said her rising costs meant she has had to increase prices for customers, as "it goes down the line".
She believes many working people are "struggling to live now".
The chancellor is expected to freeze the planned increase in fuel duty in January.
The rate was reduced by 5p by the previous Conservative government in 2022 and that measure has already been extended twice.
Gareth took over the running of the family fruit and veg stall from his dad Chris who had worked there for 50 years
One of Elin Jones' requests is for the UK government's help for a flagship scheme to help address child poverty.
The Welsh government is planning a trial scheme paying 15,000 children in families on universal credit £10 a week.
The Cynnal scheme is modelled on the Scottish government's child payment which helped to reduce child poverty in Scotland.
Welsh ministers have asked the UK government to exempt the payments from tax and benefits calculations, so recipients do not see a cut to their income.
BBC Wales has been told discussions about the child payment are still ongoing, which suggests there will be no announcement on Wednesday.
Burnham had previously said he was "open" to considering this, and it has already been granted to facilitate the scheme in Scotland.
The chancellor will also announce how much the state pension will increase by next year.
It looks likely to top £13,000 a year with the full, flat rate expected to increase by £488 a year in April due to the triple lock guarantee.
One thing that has already been announced is that pensioners who rely entirely on the state pension will be shielded from paying income tax, which usually kicks in at £12,570.
The specific details will be announced in the Budget.
On working age welfare, Healey has been rolling the pitch to prepare Labour MPs for potential cuts to the benefits bill, with a carefully scripted speech at this year's party conference.

There are reports that young people not in education, work or training may see big changes to their support, but that could be unveiled after the Budget when former Health Secretary Alan Milburn publishes his recommendations for reform.

Reform UK Senedd member Cai Parry Jones said his party "would stop using Welsh people as cash cows", and would build an M4 relief road, scrap family farm tax, and "reward working people" by raising tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.

Welsh Conservative Senedd leader Darren Millar called for the UK government to make money available for major road projects, including an M4 relief road, and more defence spending in Wales, calling for a "pro-union Budget deal".

David Chadwick, Welsh Liberal Democrat MP, said his party wanted a Budget that gave Welsh families "some much-needed breathing space", calling for a 10p cut in fuel duty, a guarantee to bring down energy bills, and a temporary VAT cut for hospitality.

The Budget comes ahead of the first substantive meeting between the prime minister and the first minister at the National Economic Council later this week, where devolution is expected to be discussed.

A UK government spokesperson said: "The chancellor is focused on giving households and businesses a bit of breathing space where we can. That's why we have removed VAT from electricity bills, extended the 5p fuel duty cut and frozen rail fares."

articles.title: Why bond yields and term premia are likely to remain high
articles.standfirst: Term premia are now back to their mid-2000s levels – high compared to the last 10 years.
paragraphs: To understand the recent surge in government bond yields and whether high yields are here to stay, it’s useful to look at the main yield components over a longer horizon. A 10-year government bond yield can be decomposed into the expected path of safe short-term rates and a broadly defined term premium that compensates investors for risks in holding the bond. Since 2020, more than half of the increase in advanced-economy government bond yields came from the term premium.
Reliable and consistent economic forecasts, analysis, models and scenarios provide the insight necessary to make informed decisions in a fast-changing world.

articles.title: How will central banks react to higher bond yields?
articles.standfirst: We expect major central banks will continue to tighten in coming months.
paragraphs: The recent surge in government bond yields – which is spilling over into higher financing costs for households and businesses – is unlikely to deter central banks from raising policy rates further. We expect major central banks will continue to tighten in coming months.

articles.title: Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase
articles.standfirst: Chancellor John Healey will reveal the new pay rates in the Budget, and has also announced measures to help households with the cost of living.
paragraphs: The rise in the minimum wage is expected to be announced in the Budget, but 18-to-20 year-olds are set to see lower increases than in previous years, the BBC understands.
Pay for younger workers will rise in line with the increase in minimum pay for employees aged 21 years and over.

However, the increase for younger workers is lower than that seen in the previous two years, when Labour raised the rate to meet a manifesto promise that it would remove "discriminatory age bands" with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage.
Chancellor John Healey is also announcing measures to give families what he is calling "breathing space" with the cost of living.
"The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies but we were always clear it could happen over time," Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told the BBC:
"Of course, you want not just good wages but good work, " he added. "It is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account."
The Times reported that the National Minimum Wage for 18-to-20 year-olds is likely to rise by 3.9% from £10.85 an hour to around £11.27.
That is a smaller rise than the 26% increase the Labour government has put in place for younger workers since returning to power in 2024.
Even after the reported rise, the rate remains below the National Living Wage for older workers, which is currently £12.71 an hour. It is set to rise by 3.9% to £13.20, the Times said.
Andrea Egan, general secretary of the union Unison, said it was "deeply unfair" to keep paying different rates for the same job.

"Twenty year-old care workers, teaching assistants and security guards do the same work as their older colleagues," she said. "They don't pay less in the supermarket or at the petrol pump. They must be paid equally."
The government has also announced a number of measures, including removing import taxes on some food and ending the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments.
It says removing tariffs from 100 food items could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June.

"We're not going to say it is everything," Reynolds told the BBC, but taken alongside the changes implemented in the summer on goods such as pasta, fruit juice and tuna, he said it would save around £500m a year.
Other measures the government announced on Tuesday included:
Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that
Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead. However, this will not come in until 2030
Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period
And rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes to make sending parcels easier
Speaking to the BBC's Newscast, Healey said: "None of this is going to change the world. But if it helps around the margins and its action the government can take, then I want try and fix it."

The government will also freeze fuel duty again in the Budget, the BBC understands. The 5p duty discount is also set to continue. That discount was first introduced in 2022, and was due to last 12 months, but has been extended ever since.
The list of products the government is removing tariffs on includes:
Baked beans
Garlic
Gherkins
Chocolate-coated wafers and waffles
Boiled sweets
Toffees, caramels and similar sweets
Citrus jams, marmalades and pastes
Throat pastilles and cough drops
Plant-based drinks including soya, nut, cereal or seed
Kerosene
Fertilisers
The government said removing tariffs on fertiliser aimed to help farmers, while changes to import levies on kerosene is targeted at households that rely on heating oil.
The Treasury said it would publish on Wednesday a full list of the products that will have tariffs removed.
A tariff is an import duty paid by domestic businesses buying products from overseas.

Asked why the government was making it cheaper to buy goods from abroad rather than cutting business costs for UK firms, Reynolds said: "Where you can make a reduction in the cost of importing goods into the UK, when you think you can balance that with your domestic economic interests, that's a decision we will take."

But Balwinder Dhoot, director of sustainability and growth at the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said: "It's more expensive to make food and drink here in the UK than in many of our close neighbours, as businesses face such high energy costs."
The Conservatives said the government's "everyday fixes" had already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises."

articles.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
articles.standfirst: The latest figures mark a major milestone as Beijing grapples with an ageing population.
paragraphs: Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.

Official data released in the last week show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.
The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children.
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.

No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.

The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.

The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.
Birth rates in China have been falling for years now
China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy, which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.

The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.
The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.
But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.
Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.
Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.

Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.

The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.
The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.
Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.
It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

articles.title: Donald Trump's biggest economic problem looks strangely familiar
articles.standfirst: Donald Trump heads into the US midterm elections with an issue similar to his political foe Joe Biden.
paragraphs: US President Donald Trump and his predecessor Joe Biden
The White House is confronting a familiar dilemma. The economic numbers aren't necessarily bad - but the public mood is.
It's a disconnect that haunted Joe Biden in 2024, when solid headline data failed to convince many voters that the economy was working for them.
Now, Donald Trump faces a version of the same challenge.
During the 2024 campaign, Trump promised voters swift relief from rising prices.
"When I win, I will immediately bring prices down," he said.
Delivering on that promise has proved harder than expected.
Economic growth is holding up, unemployment remains low and the stock market is near record highs.
Yet the final inflation report ahead of the midterm elections confirms what voters already know: prices remain high.

The causes are different. Biden was grappling with the aftermath of the Covid pandemic. Trump faces higher energy prices linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran and the fallout from some of his own trade and immigration policies.

The political reality, however, is much the same. Voters are not judging the economy by GDP figures or record highs on the stock market. They are judging it by what they pay at the supermarket, petrol prices and whether they can keep up with the bills.

US economic growth of 2.2% would be respectable by the standards of many wealthy economies. Germany, for example, has struggled to generate comparable momentum. And a stable US unemployment rate of 4.2% hardly suggests an economy in freefall.
Trump argues that he inherited an economic mess from Biden, and points to strong growth, investment and stock market performance as evidence that his policies are working.
Following the most recent inflation report, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said the administration's "aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda" had blunted "Biden's inflation crisis".
Larry Kudlow, a Trump ally and economic commentator, has described the current expansion as "the greatest story never told", arguing that "nobody is getting fired".
But voters appear to be reading a different story - one in which Trump won the presidency promising to tackle the cost of living, only for prices to keep rising.
Part of the problem is that wage increases have not kept pace with prices. Average hourly earnings have risen 3% over the last year, while consumer prices have increased 3.7%.
That helps explain why polls continue to show voters giving Trump poor marks for his handling of the economy.
For Democrats, the dynamic feels familiar.
Celinda Lake, a veteran Democratic pollster, says the problem begins with the way economists and voters use the same language to mean different things.
"When economists say inflation comes down, they mean the rate of increase has come down," she says.
"When voters say inflation has come down, they mean the price has returned to what it was. Well, of course, it never returns to what it was."
Joe Biden campaigned in 2024 on the economy but voters saw things differently
The Biden administration spent much of 2024 highlighting low unemployment, solid growth and falling inflation. However, many voters remained focused on the higher prices they faced every day.
Lake, who advised Biden's 2020 campaign but was not involved in the 2024 race, says voters judge the economy through personal experience, not economic indicators.
"You can't argue with people about their own lived reality," she says.
That may help explain why Trump's challenge looks so similar to Biden's.
Biden's critics blamed him for inflation. But he could point to forces largely outside his control, including the pandemic and its supply chain aftershocks.
Trump has less room to do that.
Some economists argue that today's higher prices are at least partly the result of his own policies, including tariffs, as well as the economic fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran.
"The inflation is clearly traceable to Donald Trump," says Peter Morici, a University of Maryland economist who aligns with Republicans.
"It's his tariffs and the war. People know that. They see it."
Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, announced in April 2025, have added to costs for consumers.
A study by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found the tariffs increased consumer goods prices by about 2.9%.
Donald Trump pledged to lower prices for US households
The impact might have been larger if Trump hadn't later paused some tariffs, struck new trade deals and been blocked by the Supreme Court from using emergency powers to impose many others.
Then came another shock. Conflict with Iran pushed oil prices higher, lifting the cost of petrol and putting fresh pressure on household budgets.

The White House points to tax cuts, job growth and lower prescription drug costs as evidence that the administration is delivering for American families. And it is increasingly embracing policies aimed at easing pressures.
Trump has called for a cap on credit card interest rates and floated the idea of a $5,000 payment to American adults if Republicans retain control of Congress.
The measures reflect a political reality familiar to both parties: when voters are anxious about prices, arguments about solid growth and low unemployment are rarely enough.
Biden never found a way to bridge the gap between economic performance and economic sentiment. The question heading into the midterms is whether Trump can.
If recent political history is any guide, perceptions of the economy may matter more than the economic data itself.

articles.title: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
articles.standfirst: Figures obtained by BBC Newsnight show large spikes in sales of torches, radios and power banks.
paragraphs: This video can not be played
UK prepper stores see massive sales following government campaign
Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.
The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.
The rise in sales came after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event.
Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.
The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month.

"Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin.
"These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."

On 22 October, Streeting said that people should ensure they have three litres of water per person per day; tinned goods in the cupboard; baby food; battery powered torches and mobile phone charging packs.
Many of the items cited by Streeting appeared in the list of goods gathered by Newsnight whose sales have shot up.

In response to the increase in retail sales of certain items, the defence secretary told Newsnight: "It's encouraging that people are taking practical steps to be ready. Having a few everyday essentials at home, from tinned food to torches, helps households prepare for disruption, whether that's flooding, power cuts or burst pipes. We can all play our part in making Britain more resilient."

An Iceland spokesperson told the BBC programme: "It's clear consumers have listened to the government's message as we have seen a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend and strong sales of bottled water too. Our supplies of these products remain healthy."
Sales of torches and radio have risen sharply for some UK retailers
Newsnight also spoke to independent retailers who reported a spike in sales of goods highlighted by the defence secretary.

Josh Pringle, from Sgt Prepper's online store, said his sales had increased tenfold: "We were a small outfit on Wednesday. And then the government launched the Be Ready campaign and we couldn't believe what we were seeing – order after order after order. Most of them were for a wind-up radio."

Lincoln Miles, founder of Preppers Shop UK, told Newsnight of a 650% increase in sales after the government announcement. "Everything about off grid seems to be the key of what people are buying for the minute."

IfG DevoLab #7: How can mayors help to tackle health-related inactivity? Maisie.Jack Tue, 27/10/2026 - 16:05 48 Arundel Gate, Sheffield City Centre, Sheffield S1 2PP Burnham government Hybrid event Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government Monday 23 November 2026, 03:00 Yorkshire and the Humber North West Millennium Gallery
Local government Growth Regional economic growth Health Policy innovations and successes Welfare Metro mayor Institute for Government IfG DevoLab Monday 23 November 2026, 01:30 GMT Devolution Join us in Sheffield to explore how mayors can use devolved powers to tackle health-related inactivity.

The IfG DevoLab is dedicated to exploring the innovations enabled by devolution, learning from the results, and sharing the lessons so that places can take better decisions about how to use devolved powers and budgets.  

Health related inactivity is one of the biggest challenges facing many parts of the country, with approximately 2.8 million working-age people now out of work due to ill health.  

In this DevoLab event, we will hear from three mayoral strategic authorities that have taken different approaches to tackling rising levels of health inactivity. With the Burnham government ambitious to devolve more employment support powers and budgets, we will explore what all levels of government can learn about how to respond to this urgent challenge.

The case studies presented at the IfG DevoLab #7 will be:  

  • ‘Pathways to Work’, by David MacDougall, Director of Work and Skills at South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority
  • ‘Live Well’, by Greater Manchester Combined Authority

The speakers will be joined by Ben Paxton, Senior Researcher at the Institute for Government.  

This event will be chaired by Akash Paun, Programme Director at the Institute for Government.  

Insights from this discussion will inform a published policy briefing containing the three case studies and a synthesis of key lessons.

articles.title: The government should back up its impressive savings and efficiencies figures by showing where they have come from
articles.standfirst:
The government should back up its impressive savings and efficiencies figures by showing where they have come from melissa.ittoo Tue, 27/10/2026 - 15:19 The chancellor should commit to publishing the same level of detail on savings and efficiencies as the last government. 4 Comment Ben Paxton Institute for Government Yes John Healey, chancellor of the Exchequer, outside the Treasury. Public finances Budget Economy Public sector Public spending Labour Chancellor of the exchequer Burnham government HM Treasury
No

Last week, the Treasury published departments’ performance against the 2% efficiencies and saving target for 2025/26 that was set at the autumn 2024 budget. 5 HM Treasury, 2025–26 departmental efficiency and savings performance, 21 October 2026, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6ad8c4e14e6a61c502e89fd0/Departmental_efficiency_performance_2025-26.pdf  This is welcome. More transparency around departments’ efficiency and savings targets, and progress against them, can improve accountability and galvanise efforts in departments.

The headline numbers are also impressive: efficiencies of £9.2bn and savings of £7.2bn, together worth 4.1% of day-to-day spending. 6 Excluding depreciation and overseas development aid, as per HM Treasury’s calculations.  But the credibility of these figures is undermined by a lack of detail on where these are coming from.

Different departments took very different approaches to savings and efficiencies

Measuring public sector savings and efficiencies is tricky. The Treasury defines them as: 7 HM Treasury, 2025–26 departmental efficiency and savings performance, 21 October 2026, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6ad8c4e14e6a61c502e89fd0/Departmental_efficiency_performance_2025-26.pdf   

  • “Efficiency is defined as the ability to spend less to achieve the same or greater outputs, or to achieve greater outputs for the same spend. This definition explicitly excludes decisions to reduce costs where the intended result is a reduction in outputs or service quality.”
  • “Savings are reductions in planned expenditure that do not arise from efficiency improvements as defined above – for example, reductions in demand, policy changes, or decisions not to proceed with planned spending.”

The efficiencies included in this analysis have had to meet the ‘Government Efficiency Framework’ criteria. 8 HM Treasury, ‘The Government Efficiency Framework’, 2025, www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-government-efficiency-framework/the-government-efficiency-framework--2#data-and-reporting  But on savings, it is far less clear what counts as a saving, or the level of ‘planned expenditure’ against which they are measured. Having clear definitions is important, both for scrutiny and for making sure targets are incentivising the right kinds of activities. A lack of detail on where savings and efficiencies have been found further brings undermined their credibility. Going forward, the Treasury should be clearer about what counts as a saving, and where both savings and efficiencies are coming from.

All departments have met the target of 2% savings and efficiencies from the day-to-day budgets, but some have exceeded it by a long way. 63% (£10.3bn) of their overall cash-value comes from DHSC – which reportedly found 3.2% efficiencies and 2.0% savings.

Despite the blanket 2% savings and efficiencies target, the balance of savings versus efficiencies varies. MHCLG, for example, found £588m of savings, but just £7m of efficiencies. DfT found £190m of efficiencies but zero savings. This suggests that different approaches have been taken across government to meeting this target (or at least reporting against it) – rather than, for example, all departments using technology to improve productivity (which makes up just 4% of reported efficiencies).

This range of approaches should have produced lots of lessons about what does and does not work well in finding efficiencies. The Treasury must ensure these lessons are shared in the future, particularly given the lack of published detail on how savings and efficiencies were found.

The Treasury should focus on reforms that improve long-term value for money

Not all efficiencies and savings are equal. Identifying cuts or streamlining processes to free up cash or capacity in the short-term is important, but government should be careful to avoid changes which compromise long-term value for money.

A classic example of this has been successive governments cutting back-office management capacity in order to re-direct funding to ‘frontline’ public services. But this is often a false economy. Many public services are chronically undermanaged, which makes it harder to allocate resources effectively and improve productivity in the long run. 10 Hoddinott S, Performance tracker 2026: Cross-service Analysis, Institute for Government, 2026, www.instituteforgovernment.org.uk/publication/performance-tracker-2026/cross-service-analysis  The government’s current NHS reforms, halving staff numbers across DHSC and NHS England, as well as in all NHS integrated care boards, are repeating this counterproductive pattern.

The Treasury must ensure departments focus on the changes that will deliver better long-run value – and should use greater transparency to do this.

Budget 2026

John Healey's first budget as chancellor will be the biggest indication yet of the priorities of Andy Burnham's government.

Explore our work

Greater transparency would enhance Healey’s credibility

The Treasury has provided very little detail on where these savings and efficiencies have come from, except for a few examples and an aggregate breakdown of efficiencies by broad categories such as ‘Policy and service redesign’ (28.2%) and ‘Workforce and organisation’ (21%). This lack of transparency undermines the credibility of these seemingly impressive figures.

The Starmer government put in place ‘Departmental Efficiency Plans’ as part of the 2025 spending review, which set out in more detail than before how efficiency targets would be delivered. Departments also committed to reporting their efficiency savings in annual reports and accounts from 2026/27, with explanations of how programmes and activities have released efficiencies. 13 HM Treasury, ‘The Government Efficiency Framework’, 2025, www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-government-efficiency-framework/the-government-efficiency-framework--2#data-and-reporting  The Burnham administration, however, has so far only said that “large ministerial departments will disclose efficiency performance against targets”.

John Healey should be ambitious on finding efficiencies and savings. Spending plans are under pressure, and he will want to find cash for higher defence spending and Burnham’s other priorities.

At tomorrow’s budget, he should commit to publishing the same level of detail on savings and efficiencies as the last government, and to updating ‘Departmental Efficiency Plans’ at the next spending review. This would bolster the credibility of both existing savings and efficiency plans, which are already ambitious compared to historical productivity performance, 14 IFS, The Outlook for Public Sector Productivity, 2025, https://ifs.org.uk/sites/default/files/2025-09/IFS_Report_The_Outlook_for_Public_Sector_Productivity_0.pdf  and any further measures he announces tomorrow.

articles.title: What should be in the fiscal devolution roadmap?
articles.standfirst:
What should be in the fiscal devolution roadmap? melissa.ittoo Tue, 27/10/2026 - 09:45 The fiscal devolution roadmap will set out changes to how mayors raise and spend money. 6 Comment Thomas Pope Institute for Government Yes The fiscal devolution roadmap will be a key milestone in Andy Burnham’s agenda. Public finances Devolution Budget Economy Regional economic growth Growth Public spending Tax Local government Labour Chancellor of the exchequer Burnham government HM Treasury
No

Alongside his budget, John Healey will unveil a new fiscal devolution roadmap, setting out how income tax and business rates revenues will be assigned to mayors, replacing grants that have funded them historically. This process was originally initiated by Rachel Reeves at her Mais lecture earlier this year, but it has gained momentum and ambition as a key plank of Andy Burnham’s wider emphasis on speeding up and deepening devolution.

Control over tax revenues for strategic authorities would be a radical development for the UK, although it is commonplace in other countries. While the roadmap is unlikely to set out the full details, it will set the broad parameters of the new system. But the policy changes are not without risks and trade-offs, and an early test of the document is how it deals with these. The roadmap needs to lay out the government’s case for the change, explain how it will deal with national and local shocks, and how the government intends to ensure the wider system, including accountability arrangements, allows mayors to take advantage of the new flexibilities it should offer.

Related content

Budget 2026

Andy Burnham’s devolution announcement is a strong start on his priority agenda

Changes on tax, new powers and institutions show Burnham means business.

Read the comment

The government should be clear about why it is pursuing fiscal devolution

Rachel Reeves’ Mais lecture was clear that she wanted to pursue fiscal devolution as a route to higher growth. There is some support for this in international evidence. But neither Reeves’ lecture nor the international evidence are clear about the mechanism. There are broadly two possible approaches. One approach is based on the idea that allowing local leaders to keep more of their own tax revenue provides an incentive to pursue growth-enhancing policies that might otherwise falter if local people see costs without benefits. The second idea is that a guaranteed share of tax, rather than dependence on grants set in spending reviews, gives subnational government more long-term certainty, allowing them to plan and commit to projects outside short funding windows.

Of course, both approaches, and the incentives behind them, could be important. But the government’s judgment of which is more important matters. A key decision for the roadmap will be how far to allow places to keep their own revenues, and how much equalisation will happen through countervailing grants that take from the highest-income authorities and give to those with less. If growth incentives are the key driver of good outcomes, a strong equalisation system would undermine them, effectively taking away any local benefit. If what matters is long-term certainty, having a credible commitment of tax revenue sharing beyond the next few years will be more important than making sure mayors keep revenue growth.

Others would favour fiscal devolution for non-economic reasons – for example, democratic legitimacy. If this is your priority, it might lead the government to prioritise local autonomy, for example changing rates or allowing total freedom over how the money is spent. The roadmap should clarify the government’s position.

Related content

Andy Burnham’s devolution announcement is a strong start on his priority agenda
How can devolution deliver regional growth in England?

The system needs to be robust if it is to be durable

A move away from grants to income tax and business rates as the main form of mayoral strategic authorities (MSA) funding will be a major shift. Most local funding in England is currently allocated according to formulas based on need, not taking account of local revenue raising power. Shifting away from that will mean difficult political decisions, and if the system is not set up well future politicians may be tempted to reverse course.

One risk is that equalisation mechanisms are too weak, so badly performing places see big reductions in spending power compared to places that grow more quickly over time. Such a system may not be politically viable over the longer term. This suggests equalisation is an important part of the system.

A second risk concerns national economic downturns. MSA spending is currently insulated from such downturns because central government normally maintains spending and accepts higher borrowing in the short term. However, if MSA spending depends on their tax take, by default MSAs would spend less in recessions. Given MSAs spend heavily on long-term economic investments like transport, this is the opposite of sound economic policy. The roadmap will need to address this situation: will central government step in, or will MSAs be able to borrow in bad years and pay it back in good?

The chancellor should ensure the wider system allows benefits to be realised 

The rules around how finances will flow is just one part of how fiscal devolution will change how MSAs operate. A shift from grants to tax revenue should also mean less Whitehall influence over how money is spent, which will in turn allow MSAs to make decisions appropriate for their areas. That means a shift from the current, onerous outcomes frameworks MSAs must abide by, which in practice limit their policy freedom. If funding flows change but wider accountability relationships do not, many of the potential benefits of fiscal devolution will not be realised.

The government needs to design a system that balances providing MSAs freedom with ensuring there is good scrutiny and accountability of their choices. More details on the government’s plans for a stronger local scrutiny and accountability system to replace some of the current accountability to Whitehall is expected in the Rewiring the State white paper later this year, and will be crucial to making fiscal devolution work. 

One aspect the roadmap next week should cover is how MSAs can borrow: either to deal with economic shocks or to allow major investments now that will be paid back from future tax revenue. This will be an early test of the government’s approach to MSA accountability. A system without checks and balances would not be appropriate, but nor is the current system of extensive Whitehall oversight and approval working.

Another is whether the money can be used for tax rebates, as well as spending on core MSA functions. This will make it clearer how far the government’s commitment to local autonomy extends even to mayors and policies they disagree with.

Budget 2026

John Healey's first budget as chancellor will be the biggest indication yet of the priorities of Andy Burnham's government.

Explore our work

The pace of fiscal devolution will reveal this government’s appetite for risk

Some MSAs are more advanced, with greater institutional history and capability, than others. And almost half of England still does not have a mayor at all. Fiscal devolution implies a new level of autonomy and freedom for local decision makers, but with it comes a risk of failure, especially in places with less capacity. The government will, rightly, prioritise capacity building in these institutions, but not all will be ready by the proposed April 2028 fiscal devolution start date.

This poses a key early choice that will tell us much about this government’s approach to devolution, and views on the relative balance of the risks and possible benefits of devolving much more quickly and widely than previous governments. Should fiscal devolution be available everywhere, or at least for all places with a mayor? Or should only those who are ready get full freedom, in which case how does this fit with the government’s commitment to growth in every postcode?

As both a key plank of the devolution agenda, and an early sign of how radical this government will be, the fiscal devolution roadmap will be a key milestone in Andy Burnham’s agenda. It probably won’t be the biggest story, but it may be John Healey’s most consequential announcement on budget day.

Related content

Regional mayors

The second idea is that a guaranteed share of tax, rather than dependence on grants set in spending reviews, gives subnational government more long-term certainty, allowing them to plan and commit to projects outside short funding windows.

Of course, both approaches, and the incentives behind them, could be important. But the government’s judgment of which is more important matters. A key decision for the roadmap will be how far to allow places to keep their own revenues, and how much equalisation will happen through countervailing grants that take from the highest-income authorities and give to those with less. If growth incentives are the key driver of good outcomes, a strong equalisation system would undermine them, effectively taking away any local benefit. If what matters is long-term certainty, having a credible commitment of tax revenue sharing beyond the next few years will be more important than making sure mayors keep revenue growth.

Others would favour fiscal devolution for non-economic reasons – for example, democratic legitimacy. If this is your priority, it might lead the government to prioritise local autonomy, for example changing rates or allowing total freedom over how the money is spent. The roadmap should clarify the government’s position.

A move away from grants to income tax and business rates as the main form of mayoral strategic authorities (MSA) funding will be a major shift. Most local funding in England is currently allocated according to formulas based on need, not taking account of local revenue raising power. Shifting away from that will mean difficult political decisions, and if the system is not set up well future politicians may be tempted to reverse course.

One risk is that equalisation mechanisms are too weak, so badly performing places see big reductions in spending power compared to places that grow more quickly over time. Such a system may not be politically viable over the longer term. This suggests equalisation is an important part of the system.

A second risk concerns national economic downturns. MSA spending is currently insulated from such downturns because central government normally maintains spending and accepts higher borrowing in the short term. However, if MSA spending depends on their tax take, by default MSAs would spend less in recessions. Given MSAs spend heavily on long-term economic investments like transport, this is the opposite of sound economic policy. The roadmap will need to address this situation: will central government step in, or will MSAs be able to borrow in bad years and pay it back in good?

The rules around how finances will flow is just one part of how fiscal devolution will change how MSAs operate. A shift from grants to tax revenue should also mean less Whitehall influence over how money is spent, which will in turn allow MSAs to make decisions appropriate for their areas. That means a shift from the current, onerous outcomes frameworks MSAs must abide by, which in practice limit their policy freedom. If funding flows change but wider accountability relationships do not, many of the potential benefits of fiscal devolution will not be realised.

The government needs to design a system that balances providing MSAs freedom with ensuring there is good scrutiny and accountability of their choices. More details on the government’s plans for a stronger local scrutiny and accountability system to replace some of the current accountability to Whitehall is expected in the Rewiring the State white paper later this year, and will be crucial to making fiscal devolution work.

One aspect the roadmap next week should cover is how MSAs can borrow: either to deal with economic shocks or to allow major investments now that will be paid back from future tax revenue. This will be an early test of the government’s approach to MSA accountability. A system without checks and balances would not be appropriate, but nor is the current system of extensive Whitehall oversight and approval working.

Another is whether the money can be used for tax rebates, as well as spending on core MSA functions. This will make it clearer how far the government’s commitment to local autonomy extends even to mayors and policies they disagree with.
John Healey's first budget as chancellor will be the biggest indication yet of the priorities of Andy Burnham's government.

Some MSAs are more advanced, with greater institutional history and capability, than others. And almost half of England still does not have a mayor at all. Fiscal devolution implies a new level of autonomy and freedom for local decision makers, but with it comes a risk of failure, especially in places with less capacity. The government will, rightly, prioritise capacity building in these institutions, but not all will be ready by the proposed April 2028 fiscal devolution start date.

This poses a key early choice that will tell us much about this government’s approach to devolution, and views on the relative balance of the risks and possible benefits of devolving much more quickly and widely than previous governments. Should fiscal devolution be available everywhere, or at least for all places with a mayor? Or should only those who are ready get full freedom, in which case how does this fit with the government’s commitment to growth in every postcode?

As both a key plank of the devolution agenda, and an early sign of how radical this government will be, the fiscal devolution roadmap will be a key milestone in Andy Burnham’s agenda. It probably won’t be the biggest story, but it may be John Healey’s most consequential announcement on budget day.

articles.title: GCC recovery tracker shows initial rebound has stalled
articles.standfirst: The GCC economy faces challenges with a fragile recovery, varying regional performances, and resilient oil revenues amid ongoing disruptions. Discover more.
paragraphs: The GCC recovery tracker indicates a notable stall in economic rebound, with a forecasted GDP contraction of 5.7% for this year, followed by a gradual recovery to 5.5% growth in 2027. This trend reflects a decline in the diffusion index, which fell by 5.4 points to 51.0 in September, signalling a fragile recovery environment.

Flight disruptions and declining equity prices have contributed to this slowdown, particularly in Saudi Arabia, where ongoing attacks on civilian infrastructure have undermined confidence. Conversely, shipping activities have shown some resilience, with Saudi Arabia restarting exports, although oil production remains at only 77% of pre-conflict levels.

The outlook varies across the region, with Oman performing relatively well due to stable energy production, while Kuwait and Qatar continue to lag behind. Despite a drop in tourist arrivals and uneven fiscal impacts, Saudi Arabia’s oil and gas revenues have exceeded pre-conflict levels, demonstrating some resilience in the face of adversity.
Reliable and consistent economic forecasts, analysis, models and scenarios provide the insight necessary to make informed decisions in a fast-changing world.

articles.title: How Much Does the US Government Lose to Tax Fraud?
articles.standfirst: While the government will never close the tax gap or fully eliminate tax fraud, lawmakers and the IRS can institute several reforms to reduce the gap, including simplifying the tax code, increasing third-party information reporting, and coordinating anti-fraud efforts.
paragraphs: A recent report by the nonpartisan Government Accountability Office (GAO) estimates the federal government loses $116 billion to $304 billion annually to taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. fraud. That amounts to between two and six percent of federal taxes owed. It also exceeds the entire budget of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), a leading anti-poverty program.
The report adds to the case for a simpler tax code and better-coordinated fraud enforcement at the IRS.

Tax fraud is one component of the larger tax gapThe tax gap is the difference between taxes legally owed and taxes collected. The gross tax gap in the U.S. accounts for at least $441 billion in lost revenue each year, according to the latest estimate by the IRS (2011 to 2013), suggesting a voluntary taxpayer compliance rate of 83.6 percent. The net tax gap is calculated by subtracting late tax collections from the gross tax gap: from 2011 to 2—the gap between estimated federal taxes owed and actual federal taxes paid on time each year. The GAO study is novel in its attempt to formally measure tax fraud within the tax gap; the IRS does not offer a separate estimate of tax revenue lost due to fraud.

GAO reports that much of the revenue lost due to tax fraud occurs in the so-called “shadow economy.” The shadow economy, which economic literature reviewed by GAO suggests could equal anywhere from two to nine percent of GDP, includes:

The larger tax gap measures taxpayer noncompliance through intentional fraud and unintentional errors, and was about $696 billion as of tax year 2022. That amounts to 15 percent of taxes owed and indicates fraud is about 17 to 44 percent of the tax gap—a substantial share.
After the IRS collected late payments and money recovered through audits (about $90 billion), the remaining gap was $606 billion.

Most of the tax gap, about 77 percent, is from underreporting, with the remainder due to nonfiling and underpayment of tax. Most of the underreporting, about 71 percent, occurs in the individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source, concentrated in sole proprietorship income, representing $117 billion or 17 percent of the tax gap. The IRS finds that sole proprietorship income and other sources of income with little to no third-party reporting or withholdingWithholding is the income an employer takes out of an employee’s paycheck and remits to the federal, state, and/or local government. It is calculated based on the amount of income earned, the taxpayer’s filing status, the number of allowances claimed, and any additional amount the employee requests. tend to have high rates of noncompliance.

A related issue—and one component of the tax gap—is improper payments associated with refundable tax credits, such as the earned income tax creditA tax credit is a provision that reduces a taxpayer’s final tax bill, dollar-for-dollar. A tax credit differs from deductions and exemptions, which reduce taxable income rather than the taxpayer’s tax bill directly. (EITC) and the child tax credit (CTC). Improper payments are either overpayments or underpayments that the government should not have made or could not verify were made to the correct person in the correct amount. According to the latest estimates by the Treasury Department and the IRS, improper payments in fiscal year 2025 totaled $28.1 billion for four major refundable tax credits.

As with the overall tax gap, not all improper payments of refundable credits are due to intentional fraud. The complex rules and confusing structure of the EITC, CTC, and PTC can lead to unintentional errors—and ultimately overpayments or underpayments—which are all labeled improper payments in government data.
It is not possible to eliminate fraud completely, which GAO recognizes, nor is it possible to eliminate the tax gap. However, improvements could be made to reduce fraud and the tax gap.

And what of the bulk of the tax gap that is not due to fraud? Based on IRS analysis of the tax gap as well as our understanding of the problems associated with tax complexity in the US and other countries, we recommend the following:

Tax complexity is a serious problem. It leads to taxpayer confusion and errors and imposes a significant compliance cost, about $544 billion this year—nearly the size of the tax gap. Much of the tax code’s complexity and compliance cost falls on businesses.

The complexity of the business tax code reflects the challenge of defining business income, including rules that differ by business form (C corporations, S corporations, partnerships, sole proprietorships, etc.), and a multitude of information reporting requirements (such as 1099 forms) that generally serve to bolster compliance across the broader federal tax system. In that sense, it is challenging to streamline the tax code in a way that boosts compliance.

One option is fundamental reform that replaces complicated corporate and other business income taxes with a tax on distributed profits, combined with a simplified individual income tax at the same rate. This approach has been successful in Estonia and other countries, resulting in low compliance costs, a low corporate tax gap, and a competitive tax code with revenues on par with other developed countries. A more piecemeal approach would eliminate unnecessarily complicated deductions, credits, minimum taxes, and other special provisions from the tax code.

Congress can also reduce improper payments of refundable credits by simplifying the tax code and streamlining definitions. For example, the EITC currently differs by filing status and number of children, and parents and guardians must go through a complex set of steps to determine if their child is eligible. The qualifying child rules also differ between the EITC and CTC, adding to taxpayer confusion.

The EITC and CTC could be simplified by consolidating the child benefit in one credit—a reformed child credit—and limiting the EITC to a per-worker incentive regardless of family dimensions. This was proposed by former Sen. Mitt Romney (R-UT), for example.

Another way to reduce improper payments is to expand Treasury’s Do Not Pay system. As noted by Romina Boccia, Treasury has recently bolstered the system and found some success in preventing payments to deceased recipients. However, Treasury lacks statutory authority to expand the system to effectively check improper payments related to employment status, income, and identity.

The federal government loses hundreds of billions of dollars per year to tax fraud, and hundreds of billions more to unintentional noncompliance. While it is impossible for the federal government to eliminate tax fraud or fully close the tax gap, Congress can make improvements to the tax code—and the IRS to tax administration—that reduce the gap and close openings for fraudsters. At the top of the list should be simplifying a Byzantine tax code that contributes to the gap between taxes owed and taxes paid.

Dr. William McBride is the Chief Economist & Stephen J. Entin Fellow in Economics at the Tax Foundation, where he oversees major research projects primarily related to reforming the federal tax code, advancing sound tax policy, and improving the federal government’s fiscal outlook.

Andrew Lautz is Senior Director of Federal Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Before joining Tax Foundation, he was Director of Tax Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center and Director of Federal Policy at the National Taxpayers Union. Andrew’s research and perspectives on federal tax policy have been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and other major publications.
