articles.title: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
articles.standfirst: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
paragraphs: Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.
The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.
Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.
The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.
Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.
Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.
Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.
Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.

As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.
Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".
Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.
Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.

It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.

However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.
"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.
Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.
The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.

Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise.
"Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC.
Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence".
He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development.

articles.title: Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget
articles.standfirst: Changes are needed to prevent the full, flat-rate state pension becoming liable for income tax after it rises in April.
paragraphs: Pensioners on low incomes will be shielded from income tax by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget on Wednesday.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to increase by 3.9% to £13,036.40 a year from April. This would take the payment above the £12,570 personal tax allowance and therefore be liable for income tax if no changes are made.

The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension. Healey will explain this pledge will be met by plans for a new tax allowance for low-income pensioners.
Healey's plans come as the Conservatives and Reform UK unveil their alternative Budget proposals, including deep cuts to the welfare bill.
The chancellor's allies argue his plans for pensioners will mean they do not need to face an administrative burden just to pay a small amount of tax.
More specific details, including how many pensioners this will affect, have yet to be confirmed by the Treasury.
The Budget is due to be printed this evening, with Healey's speech likely to be fine-tuned right up until it is delivered on Wednesday lunchtime.
Treasury sources concede it will not involve the scale of tax and spending announcements seen from Labour and Conservative governments in recent years.
The Tories are calling on the chancellor to cut green taxes, red tape and benefits to bring down energy bills.
Reform is recommending the chancellor adopts 60 policies which they claim will create jobs - including approving the controversial Rosebank oil field - a project Healey is understood to back.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper has called on the government to agree a new growth and defence partnership with the EU, including joining the single market. She argued this would help "ease the huge tax burden weighing people down".
The Green Party has urged Healey to use his first Budget to "make the UK affordable", including by funding energy bill support by ending a tax relief for data centres.
Senior Green politicians, including leader Zack Polanski, MPs and peers, made clear their suggestions in a letter to Healey.

articles.title: The Budget should not price young people out of work
articles.standfirst:
As part of the Budget the Chancellor usually announces any changes to the minimum wage. As AI is eating into entry level jobs, Grace Lordan makes the case for why the Government should refrain from further increasing the youth minimum wage relative to the adult rate. Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a … Continued
The post The Budget should not price young people out of work first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: As part of the Budget the Chancellor usually announces any changes to the minimum wage. As AI is eating into entry level jobs, Grace Lordan makes the case for why the Government should refrain from further increasing the youth minimum wage relative to the adult rate.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

John Healey is about to deliver his first Budget, and the first fiscal event of Andy Burnham’s premiership. The figures from the Office for National Statistics, put vacancies at 691,000, below pre-pandemic levels, with payrolled employment still falling. Youth unemployment is 15.6 per cent, with 54,000 more young people out of work than a year ago. In the three months to July the rate reached 16.4 per cent, the highest since 2014. Around a million young people are not in education, employment or training, and the Learning and Work Institute counts 5.3 people out of work and wanting a job for every vacancy.

The Government is already trying to help, paying firms to take on young people, through a £3,000 Youth Jobs Grant and a Jobs Guarantee that funds six months of part-time wages for the long-term unemployed. Healey has also added £100 million for mayor-run apprenticeship services.

Yet within weeks of the Budget, the Low Pay Commission will recommend the minimum wage rates for April 2027, and its remit still says the Government remains committed to aligning the 18-20 rate with the National Living Wage. That rate rose already by 8.5 per cent in April, to £10.85, against a 4.1 per cent raise for adults. One arm of the Government pays firms to hire young people. Another makes them more expensive. In a time when AI is eating away at entry-level jobs and the country has one million NEETs, the Government should stop raising the youth minimum wage faster than the adult rate.

For most of the minimum wage’s life, the evidence supported raising youth rates. Employers absorbed the cost, trimmed hours or raised prices, and jobs did not vanish. The Low Pay Commission still finds no robust evidence linking the youth rate to youth unemployment, and the Resolution Foundation concludes that minimum wage policy has not been a key driver of the rise in the NEET rate since 2019, and the IFS finds no clear evidence that it has been.
Once a worker and a machine are close substitutes, the price of the worker decides which one gets hired.

That held while the tasks a younger worker did had no substitute. That is no longer the case. Generative AI now drafts, summarises, codes, answers tickets and reconciles data. This is the routine work that was the first rung of a professional career. Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab finds that in the US since generative AI spread, employment of 22 to 25-year-olds in the most exposed occupations has fallen 13 per cent relative to other workers, concentrated where AI automates rather than augments. Britain’s figures point in the same direction. Fifteen months after graduating, 72 per cent of employed graduates were in professional-level jobs, down from 75 per cent a year earlier.

My work with Cecily Josten found that the jobs safest from automation are those needing non-linear abstract thinking, or people skills combined with brains, with codifiable routine jobs going first. Entry-level work is codifiable by design. Once a worker and a machine are close substitutes, the price of the worker decides which one gets hired.

But most minimum wage jobs are not knowledge work; they are in cafés, supermarkets and warehouses. What reaches them is then the second-round effect. When graduates cannot find professional work they move down the ladder. This is not just theory: one in ten employed graduates are in retail, catering, waiting or bar work fifteen months after graduating. Beaudry, Green and Sand found the same cascade in the United States after 2000, as high-skilled workers took less skilled jobs and pushed lower-skilled workers further down the ladder, some out of work altogether.

With David Neumark I studied US data from 1980 to 2015 on jobs that are easy to automate. Raising the minimum wage cut the share of those jobs held by low-skilled workers, who became more likely to end up out of work or in worse jobs. The effects were largest for older workers in manufacturing, and we found some evidence that opportunities improved for the higher-skilled workers who tend the machines.

I then repeated the exercise for Britain in a report commissioned by the Low Pay Commission. Using data from 1994 to 2017, a £1 rise in the minimum wage cut the share of automatable low-skilled employment by 0.24 percentage points, and by 0.58 in manufacturing. The effects were very modest, implying substitution had so far been limited. In the main estimates, workers under 25 were not the group affected. The machines of that era were robotic arms, replacing older men on assembly lines. But the report warned that the set of automatable jobs was evolving, and that the past was no guide to who would be replaced next.
the 18 to 20 minimum wage rate has risen 45 per cent in three years, from £7.49 to £10.85, taking it from 72 to 85 per cent of the adult rate.

If you raise the price of a worker whose tasks a machine can do, some of that work can move to the machine. In 2017 it was older factory workers. In 2026 it is younger professional workers, and also possibly school leavers on tills and counters that self-service machines can replace. In fact, the Bank of England’s agents report warehouse operators looking to automate after recent labour cost inflation, and retail and hospitality have shed 117,000 employees in a year, more than all other industries combined. Out-of-work benefit claims have risen most among 18 to 20-year-olds, from 7.2 to 9.4 per cent between 2022 and 2025. Meanwhile the 18 to 20 minimum wage rate has risen 45 per cent in three years, from £7.49 to £10.85, taking it from 72 to 85 per cent of the adult rate. A price rise of that size, for workers who have just become substitutable, lies outside anything in the Commission’s known evidence base.

Picture a café manager choosing between a graduate who cannot find professional work, a school leaver with few qualifications, and a kiosk. The school leaver costs £10.85 an hour, the graduate £12.71. Convergence would close that gap, removing the one thing the school leaver can compete on, so the job goes to credentials or to the machine. After minimum wage rises in the US, employers became more likely to demand a high school diploma for low-wage jobs, and more-skilled teenagers left school for work, pushing less-skilled teenagers into neither work nor study. The Bank of England’s agents report British firms favouring “experienced, immediately productive hires”.

That is why this is so dangerous. Those pushed out have the fewest alternatives. 84 per cent of NEETs aged 18 to 24 carry at least one disadvantage, and unemployment in youth raises the risk of unemployment well into adulthood, at least for men. The gains, meanwhile, flow up. At a large US retailer, the extra teenagers employed after a minimum wage rise were disproportionately the more affluent. In Britain, full-time students make up more than a quarter of young people in low hourly pay, and university students are disproportionately from better-off homes. A policy meant for the low paid might end up favouring the student with a bedroom at home over the school leaver whose only income is the job.

The Resolution Foundation estimates that holding the youth rate at its 2023 share of the adult rate would have put 15,000 more 16 to 20-year-olds in work in 2025-26, at no cost to the Exchequer. It is not a free lunch. The 230,000 young people already paid the current rates would be worse off. But a pay rise is worth nothing to someone who is not hired, and the Foundation itself now recommends pausing convergence and dropping the commitment to it.

The Government has expressed concern over the future of NEETs, so one thing the Chancellor could do is announce that the 18 to 20 rate will not move further towards the adult rate while youth unemployment is rising, and the Commission’s remit should be amended to match.

The Commission should measuring the substitutability of young workers directly. Its evidence base was built on robotic arms, not language models or self-service kiosks. For each job where the youth rate bites, it should ask how close the machine substitute is and how many over-qualified applicants are queuing for it, and let the answers steer the rate.
The test for 28 October is simple. Taken together with the rates for April 2027, does the Budget make a young person cheaper or dearer relative to the machine that can now do their first job?
Nine years ago my report for the Commission concluded that substitution had so far been limited, and asked policymakers to monitor the trend. The trend has arrived. The “so far” has run out.

articles.title: Could an Employer Compensation Tax Save Social Security?
articles.standfirst: With Social Security insolvency rapidly approaching and policymakers exploring changes to benefits and taxation, Congress could look to base-broadening reforms like the ECT as a guide for how to think about taxing compensation and broadening the tax base.
paragraphs: Most taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. proposals to increase Social Security trust fund revenue have focused on raising the payroll taxA payroll tax is a tax paid on the wages and salaries of employees to finance social insurance programs like Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance. Payroll taxes are social insurance taxes that comprise 24.8 percent of combined federal, state, and local government revenue, the second largest source of that combined tax revenue. rate or lifting the payroll tax cap to increase the amount of wages subject to the payroll tax. Less attention has been given to other kinds of base broadeners, such as adding fringe employer benefits to the payroll tax base, which have the potential to raise substantial revenue.

Under current law, one of the largest tax exclusions is for employer-sponsored health insurance (ESI), which is excluded from both income and payroll taxes. Other types of fringes, such as commuter benefits, education assistance, employer contributions to employee retirement plans, and stock options, are also excluded from both.

One novel idea to tax fringes has been proposed by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB): the employer compensation tax (ECT). The ECT would replace the current employer-side payroll taxes, 6.2 percent for Social Security and 1.45 percent for Medicare, with a 7.65 percent payroll tax on all compensation, including compensation above the taxable maximum ($192,300 in 2027). Self-employed workers would pay half their payroll tax under the current Self-Employed Contributions Act (SECA) tax rules and the other half under the ECT.

Tax Foundation modeled the ECT as part of our Options for Reforming America’s Tax Code 3.0: A Policymaker’s Guide to Tax Reform Trade-Offs (Option 41). We find that the ECT could raise $2.5 trillion from 2027 through 2036. The top quintile of taxpayers would experience the largest decrease in after-tax incomeAfter-tax income is the net amount of income available to invest, save, or consume after federal, state, and withholding taxes have been applied—your disposable income. Companies and, to a lesser extent, individuals, make economic decisions in light of how they can best maximize their earnings., 1.5 percent in 2036, largely due to applying the employer-side payroll tax to income above the taxable maximum. This makes the ECT a progressive reform overall.

The ECT would also come at a significant cost to the US economy. We estimate that the ECT would reduce long-run GDP by 1.1 percent. After accounting for this reduction in economic growth, revenue over the next decade would fall to $1.4 trillion on a dynamic basis. Incorporating changes in interest costs, the publicly held debt-to-GDP ratio would decrease in 2056, from its baseline value of 176 percent to 168 percent.

Applying the ECT to compensation above the taxable maximum would also somewhat decouple the relationship between taxes paid while working and benefits earned in retirement. Currently, Social Security replaces income in retirement up to the taxable maximum: workers do not pay payroll taxes on income above $184,500, but they also do not receive benefits based on income earned above that threshold.

One way to partially restore that link would be to only apply the ECT to compensation below the taxable maximum. This would not fully preserve the tax-benefit link, as fringes would still not be counted as part of the benefit calculation, but would be more consistent with current policy. Alternatively, policymakers could count fringes as part of the benefit calculation, but this would blunt the revenue-raising impact of the proposal.

The ECT would make the tax code more neutral in some ways and less neutral in others. By removing the payroll tax exclusion for all fringes, the tax code would not favor certain types of employee compensation over others (although the distortions from the income tax exclusion would remain). It would also reduce the asymmetrical tax treatment between employer and employee contributions to retirement accounts. For example, employee contributions to both traditional 401(k) plans and Roth 401(k) plans face payroll taxes, while employer matching and nonelective contributions are excluded.

The ECT could also create new arbitrage opportunities for self-employed workers. Although most fringes for self-employed workers are already non-deductible, removing the payroll tax cap on half of the payroll tax base might encourage some businesses to reclassify their wage income as business income. Applying SECA to cover the active component of partnership and S corporationAn S corporation is a business entity which elects to pass business income and losses through to its shareholders. The shareholders are then responsible for paying individual income taxes on this income. Unlike subchapter C corporations, an S corporation (S corp) is not subject to the corporate income tax (CIT). income could help address this.

With Social Security insolvency rapidly approaching and policymakers exploring changes to benefits and taxation, Congress could look to base-broadening reforms like the ECT as a guide for how to think about taxing compensation and broadening the tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates..

Alex Durante is a Senior Economist at the Tax Foundation, working on federal tax policy and model development. Alex worked as a research assistant at the Federal Reserve Board and served as a staff economist on the Council of Economic Advisers.

articles.title: Cigarette Taxes and Cigarette Smuggling by State, 2024
articles.standfirst: Cigarette smuggling is costly for states. We estimate that the forgone revenue from smuggled cigarettes totaled more than $4.6 billion in 2024. California lost nearly $1.4 billion in cigarette excise tax collections, and New York missed out on more than $1.2 billion.
paragraphs: Higher taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. rates incentivize tax avoidance. As tax rates increase, consumers and suppliers search for ways around these costs. In cigarette markets, consumers tend to shop across borders where the tax rates are lower, and dealers develop black and gray markets to sell illegally to consumers, paying little or no tax at all. Growing cigarette tax levels and differentials have made cigarette smuggling both a national problem and a lucrative criminal enterprise.

Each year, in partnership with scholars at the Mackinac Center for Public Policy, we estimate cigarette smuggling rates for each continental US state. The most recent report uses data from 2024. As in previous years, the data show a strong positive relationship between cigarette smuggling and tax rates across the country.

New York retook its usual status as the nationwide leader in cigarette smuggling after being surpassed briefly by California last year. A significant majority of cigarettes consumed in New York, an estimated 61.1 percent, weren’t purchased legally in the state. California followed New York, with an estimated smuggling rate of 54.4 percent.

On the other end of the spectrum, net outbound smuggling rates—where cigarettes are purchased in the state and consumed elsewhere—were highest in Wyoming (58.6 percent) and Virginia (54.4 percent). Wyoming and Virginia are well-positioned to accept cross-border shoppers looking to avoid higher taxes in neighboring states and areas like Colorado and Washington, DC.

Cigarette smuggling is costly for states. We estimate that the forgone revenue from smuggled cigarettes totaled more than $4.6 billion in 2024. California lost nearly $1.4 billion in cigarette excise taxAn excise tax is a tax imposed on a specific good or activity. Excise taxes are commonly levied on cigarettes, alcoholic beverages, soda, gasoline, insurance premiums, amusement activities, and betting, and typically make up a relatively small and volatile portion of state and local and, to a lesser extent, federal tax collections. collections, and New York missed out on more than $1.2 billion.

Virginia was the largest beneficiary of smuggling-related cigarette tax revenue, which nets the state more than $61 million. Indiana was the second largest, with net smuggling generating the Hoosier State nearly $57 million.

There is a strong positive relationship between cigarette smuggling and cigarette tax rates across the country. The data also show that when states increase their cigarette taxes, their smuggling rates also increase—just like New York this year—both in the form of increased purchases in neighboring states and through illicit international channels.

Cigarette smuggling clearly correlates with high cigarette taxes, but it also correlates with excessive regulations. Namely, states with menthol bans like California and Massachusetts also tend to have particularly high rates of smuggling as consumers shop across borders to avoid the ban.

Our previous analysis detailed the impact Massachusetts’s flavor ban had on the state’s tobacco revenue and smuggling. California’s flavor ban continues to cost the state hundreds of millions of dollars annually as previously predicted, while smoking behavior in the state has remained largely unchanged. The void in legal sales continues to be filled by illicit products.

Evidence from flavor bans in states like Massachusetts and California indicates that, just as with alcohol prohibition in the 1920s, consumers can and will acquire prohibited products. While overall consumption remains steady, consumers are pushed to illicit markets that often have more dangerous products and prop up sophisticated organized criminal enterprises supplying their demand. Flavor bans, nicotine bans, or effective bans from FDA inaction all burden consumers, domestic legal businesses, and states that lose tax revenue and face higher enforcement costs.

While some states may benefit from cross-border trade, no state benefits from the illicit market of smuggled and counterfeit cigarettes. Many of these illicit cigarettes are smuggled from China, where an estimated 400 billion counterfeit cigarettes are produced annually. Counterfeit cigarettes are often more dangerous, containing toxic heavy metals and other contaminants. Some of the billions of dollars moved through cigarette smuggling internationally have been linked to terrorism.

State enforcement agencies bear additional burdens trying, and almost entirely failing, to combat these large-scale smuggling operations. Anti-smuggling task forces in various states seize hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of contraband cigarettes. However, these seizures are often a minuscule amount of the overall market. A recent arrest and major seizure of approximately 43,700 packs of cigarettes by a multi-agency investigation in New York, for instance, represented 0.019 percent of estimated annual smuggling activity in the state.

Illicit markets for tax avoidance and smuggling are also becoming an increasingly prominent issue in the vaping market as well. Lawmakers could learn the lessons of cigarette taxation and prohibition and apply them to vaping regulation, but states are often falling into the same pitfalls that hurt revenues, legal businesses, and consumers.

Legal markets suffer when untaxed and unregulated products receive significant competitive advantages from high taxes and prohibitions. Illicit markets create additional dangers for consumers, and subsequently additional burdens on public health, and undermine both legitimate domestic businesses and state revenue generation.
Policymakers should consider the unintended, but foreseeable, consequences as they determine tax rates and regulatory regimes for tobacco and nicotine products.

Adam Hoffer is the Director of Excise Tax Policy at the Tax Foundation. Dr. Hoffer earned his PhD in Economics from West Virginia University and his undergraduate degree from Washington & Jefferson College.

Jacob Macumber-Rosin is an Excise Tax Policy Analyst with the Tax Foundation. Jacob holds a BS in economics (politics and the economy) as well as a BS in civic and economic thought and leadership from Arizona State University.

articles.title: Spain’s Tax Competitiveness Has Declined Since 2018
articles.standfirst: Under Spain’s current Social Democratic government, the country has fallen from 27th to 35th (out of 38 OECD countries) in the International Tax Competitiveness Index.
paragraphs: Spain’s central government could learn some valuable lessons about sound taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. policy from its regional governments and other European countries. According to the 2026 International Tax Competitiveness Index (ITCI), Spain has dropped from 27th to 35th (out of 38 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development [OECD] countries), reflecting multiple tax increases, new taxes, and weaker performance across all major tax categories under Pedro Sánchez’s government. While the central government is the main driver behind this drop, regional policies also affect Spain’s overall competitiveness.

Spain’s tax system reflects competing regional and central policies. While some regions have offset distortive central taxes, particularly on wealth, inheritance, and personal income, overall tax competitiveness has declined markedly over the past eight years. Strengthening competitiveness at both levels of government should therefore be a policy priority.

To capture these differences, the Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index (RTCI) compares the country’s 19 regions across more than 60 variables covering individual income taxes, wealth taxes, inheritance taxes, transfer taxes and stamp duties, and other regional taxes. The contrast between central and regional approaches offers important lessons for future reform.
By repealing the taxes and tax increases introduced during Pedro Sánchez’s administration, Spain could improve its position in the ITCI, moving from 35th to 22nd place.

Spain ranks 33rd on corporate tax competitiveness. Several policy choices explain this poor result. First, Spain has both a patent boxA patent box—also referred to as intellectual property (IP) regime—taxes business income earned from IP at a rate below the statutory corporate income tax rate, aiming to encourage local research and development. Many patent boxes around the world have undergone substantial reforms due to profit shifting concerns. regime and a research and development (R&D) tax creditA tax credit is a provision that reduces a taxpayer’s final tax bill, dollar-for-dollar. A tax credit differs from deductions and exemptions, which reduce taxable income rather than the taxpayer’s tax bill directly.. While intended to encourage innovation, these incentives favor specific activities rather than treating investment neutrally, increasing complexity and distorting business decisions. Second, Spain’s corporate tax system has become increasingly complex following the introduction of the national minimum tax in 2021, which limits the practical value of deductions, credits, and investment incentives available to large businesses. Third, Spain is one of the10 OECD countries that levy a digital service tax (DST). Since DSTs tax gross revenues rather than net income, they can disproportionately burden low-margin firms. Finally, Spain’s 25 percent corporate income tax (28 percent in Navarra) remains slightly above the OECD average of 24.2 percent.

Spain’s individual tax component also declined from 15th in 2017 to 20th, largely due to repeated increases in taxes on capital income. Since 2019, the top tax rate on capital gains and dividends has increased by seven percentage points. Spain also has one of Europe’s highest top income tax rates. When the central government increased the national top marginal income tax rate from 45 percent to 49 percent, several regions moved in the opposite direction. Madrid reduced its overall (central and regional) top rate to 45 percent, while Andalusia, Castilla-La Mancha, Galicia, and Murcia lowered theirs to 47 percent, and Castile and León cut it to 46 percent.

However, tax rates are only part of the picture. An equally important issue is bracket creepBracket creep occurs when inflation, or real income growth, pushes taxpayers into higher income tax brackets. Bracket creep results in an increase in income taxes without an increase in real income. Many tax provisions—both at the federal and state levels—are adjusted for inflation. Over time, bracket creep can increase how much income tax people owe as their income grows, either due to inflat, which occurs when inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin pushes taxpayers into higher tax bracketsA tax bracket is the range of incomes taxed at given rates, which typically differ depending on filing status. In a progressive individual or corporate income tax system, rates rise as income increases. There are seven federal individual income tax brackets; the federal corporate income tax system is flat. even if their real income has not increased. While most European countries index their income tax to inflation, Spain’s central government refused to do so. Regional governments have been more proactive. In 2026, the Canary Islands and the Basque provinces indexed tax brackets to inflation. The Valencian Community and Extremadura reduced their personal income tax rates, while La Rioja became the first Spanish region to adopt automatic inflation adjustment for tax brackets and personal deductions.

Spain ranks 18th on consumption taxes. However, only 45 percent of consumption is covered by the value-added tax (VAT) due to exemptions that complicate the overall system and distort consumer choices. Consumption taxes that exempt certain goods and services from VAT, or tax them at a reduced rate, require higher standard rates to raise sufficient revenue. A broader VAT base could create fiscal space for lowering the overall VAT rate from 21 percent down to 12 percent.

Spain performs worst in the property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. category, ranking 35th internationally. The country levies a variety of taxes on assets and transactions, including taxes on real property, property transfers, capital duties, financial transactions, net wealth, inheritances, and gifts. Together, these taxes contribute significantly to Spain’s weak competitiveness.

Spain remains one of the few OECD countries that still impose a net wealth taxA wealth tax is imposed on an individual’s net wealth, or the market value of their total owned assets minus liabilities. A wealth tax can be narrowly or widely defined, and depending on the definition of wealth, the base for a wealth tax can vary.. While the country abolished the tax in 2008 and later reinstated it, some regions adopted substantial relief measures. Madrid maintained a 100 percent exemption, later followed by Andalusia and Extremadura. Galicia introduced a 50 percent reduction.

The central government moved in the opposite direction in 2022 by creating a temporary solidarity tax on high-net-worth individuals, which complements the regional wealth tax and acts as a top-up in regions that provide substantial rebates. Initially introduced for 2022 and 2023, the measure was later made permanent.

Several regions responded by creating offsetting mechanisms. Andalusia, Cantabria, La Rioja, Madrid, and Murcia designed regional rebates that effectively redirected revenue from the central government to regional budgets without materially changing taxpayers’ liabilities.

Unlike other regions, Extremadura kept the 100 percent relief and did not introduce an offsetting mechanism, enabling the central government to collect solidarity tax from residents with net wealth exceeding €3 million.
Other regions reduced wealth tax burdens through different reforms. The Balearic Islands increased the exemption threshold to €3 million, while the Valencia Community increased it to €2 million.

Inheritance and gift taxation is also administered by regional governments. Following RTCI recommendations, many regions have introduced 99 percent relief for close heirs, bringing the total number offering significant relief to 11. Several regions have also expanded relief to more distant relatives.

Even so, Spain still imposes some of the highest inheritance taxAn inheritance tax is levied upon the value of inherited assets received by a beneficiary after a decedent’s death. Not to be confused with estate taxes, which are paid by the decedent’s estate based on the size of the total estate before assets are distributed, inheritance taxes are paid by the recipient or heir based on the value of the bequest received. rates in Europe. For distant or unrelated heirs, top rates can reach 87.6 percent in Asturias and Murcia.

Although inheritance and gift taxes raise little revenue, they can reduce wealth inequality because inheritances are relatively larger for lower-wealth households. This effect is particularly relevant in Spain, where inherited wealth accounts for 95.6 percent of net wealth.

While inheritance and gift taxes collect little revenue, a recent study reveals that inheritances can reduce wealth inequality as inheritances are proportionately larger for lower-wealth households. This effect is particularly relevant in Spain, where inherited wealth accounts for 95.6 percent of net wealth. Therefore, given their limited capacity to collect revenue and negative impact on entrepreneurial activity, saving, and work, policymakers should consider repealing inheritance and gift taxes.

Spain should implement principled tax reforms that support economic growth by making the tax code more neutral and competitive. Instead, over the past decade, Pedro Sánchez’s government has adopted a number of tax policies that have increased complexity and weakened the country’s tax competitiveness.

One recent example is the extension of the bank windfall tax, originally introduced as a temporary measure for 2023 and 2024, through 2026. Although the tax is set to expire in 2026 and is unlikely to be renewed, it arguably should never have been introduced. It does not target profitability (windfall or not) as it is based on banks’ net interest income and net fees. The new tax is progressive, ranging from 1 to 6 percent, and is partly deductible from the corporate income tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates..

The European Central Bank has warned that such taxes could reduce credit availability, weaken banks during economic downturns, raise interest rates, distort competition, and increase litigation. Because the tax applies only to a specific sector, it also departs from the principle of tax neutrality.

Spain has likewise continued raising capital income taxes, increasing the rate on capital gains above €300,000 by 2 percentage points to 30 percent. Although expected to generate little revenue, the increase continues a trend begun in 2019, marking a seven-percentage-point increase since then. Higher taxes on capital income are unlikely to generate substantial additional revenue but can discourage investment and weaken Spain’s attractiveness relative to competing jurisdictions.

Policymakers should also reconsider its domestic minimum tax regime, introduced in 2021, as it limits the practical value of deductions, tax credits, and investment incentives for large businesses, especially those already covered by Pillar Two’s qualified domestic minimum top-up tax (QDMTT).

Policymakers should refrain from raising taxes and consider repealing the taxes introduced during Pedro Sánchez’s administration, including the windfall profits, digital services, financial transactions, national minimum, solidarity, and wealth taxes. Together with a reduction in the top tax rate on capital gains and dividends from 30 percent to 23 percent, these reforms would move Spain from 35th to 22nd place in the ITCI. Spain could also follow Portugal’s lead and use the additional revenue raised during past years to cut taxes. Finally, Spain should adopt nationwide inflation indexingInflation indexing refers to automatic cost-of-living adjustments built into tax provisions to keep pace with inflation. Absent these adjustments, income taxes are subject to “bracket creep” and stealth increases on taxpayers, while excise taxes are vulnerable to erosion as taxes expressed in nominal dollars, rather than rates, slowly lose value. similar to the model pioneered by La Rioja, preventing bracket creep. To increase its internal and international tax competitiveness, perhaps Spain’s central government should look to its successful regional governments and overseas competitors for ideas.

Cristina Enache writes on the economics of tax policy and is the author of the Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index. She was formerly the Director of Research at Civismo, an economic research organization based in Spain. She also served as head of research at Institución Futuro, a regional think tank based in Navarra in northern Spain. She is also currently Secretary-General at the World Taxpayers Associations and General Manager of the Spanish Taxpayers Union, which she joined in 2016.

articles.title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI
articles.standfirst: Indian workers are being paid to film themselves at work and the footage is used to train AI.
paragraphs: Mohammed Ashim is paid to film his hands at work
Mohammed Ashim has been cutting hair and trimming beards for four years in Bengaluru.
But recently the 22-year old has been strapping a camera to his head to record his work.
The camera only records his hands and fingers - his client's faces are blurred out.

"The routine is simple, but you have to be disciplined about how you move. The operations team taught me that my hands always have to stay cleanly inside the frame, the lighting has to be sharp, and I can't tilt my head too abruptly while working."
He wears the camera for five or six hours a day.
"It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited. I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim.
He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities.
Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work.

That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world.
Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data.

"Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making. We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig.
His company pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work.
"For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says.
Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says.

"We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out. No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off."
But his customers are getting more demanding.
"Now clients are asking for four to six cameras rigged around a person's head to cover the entire scene, not just the hands.

"Getting someone to agree to one small camera is one conversation. Getting them to agree to wearing what's effectively a five-camera headset is a completely different, and harder, one. We pay more for that tier of data collection because of what we're asking of people."
And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year.
Shahil Baig expects dozens more firms to start collecting video of workers
Why is such data so important?

If you want robots to navigate the real world, they can't just be trained inside computer simulations, argues Manish Agarwal, the founder of Humyn Labs, which collects and processes human-generated data.
Most of that data comes from video, but sometimes collectors wear hardware on their hands and fingers to capture physical contact.

"Physical tasks require high-quality signals involving limb movements, fingers, wrists, elbows, shoulders and dynamic force application. For example: applying the correct grip force so a plastic bottle doesn't crumble versus a steel glass," he says.
And until recently, that data was not available.

"There is no existing internet archive of embodied human activity - no dataset of a kitchen being cleaned, or a car being assembled by hands that know exactly how much force to apply. That data has to be captured from scratch, in the real world, across diverse environments," says Agarwal, whose company has bases in Bangalore and San Francisco.
At the moment his firm has 96,000 data collectors across countries in Latin America and Southeast Asia.

Humyn Labs filters the thousands of hours of video supplied by those collectors, selecting the most useful content. It's then labelled so the AI knows what it is looking at and packaged in a format that can be used by clients.

"You need to source across a variety of factories, a variety of tasks, in different geographies because if you want to build deployment for US factories or US houses, you'd want environments that are a proxy for that. Residential houses in India may not be the right context for building a robotics use case for the US."
This video can not be played
The factory workers teaching robots how to work like humans
But are workers collecting data for machines that will one day do their jobs?
At the moment it's too early to tell says Bino Paul, senior professor at the School of Management and Labour Studies at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) in Mumbai.
For some workers AI might be a useful tool, but robots could automate other jobs, he says.
The problem is that, if machines do start to take over, there will be little workers can do about.
"By the time workers realise what they have participated in, things may have gone too far," he says.
Like many others, he wants governments to regulate AI.

"AI cannot be viewed merely as a technical system. We need to develop a socio-technical system in which ethics is upheld through human agency, ensuring that AI delivers beneficence rather than maleficence."
Despite concerns over where AI is heading, money is still being poured into its development.
Some of that trickles down to workers in India, where there is no shortage of workers prepared to wear a camera for a few dollars a day.
Mohammed Arman has been working in the textiles industry in Bangalore for 10 years.

"Garments stitching and cutting. I know this work so well I could probably do it with my eyes closed. Cloth, thread, needle, machine after 10 years, your hands just know what to do before your mind even tells them," he says.
He has recently started wearing a head-mounted camera that records his work.

"For me, it's simple. This is survival. I have a family back home in Bihar, and every rupee I send back matters. If someone offers me extra money to wear a camera while I do the exact same work I've been doing for 10 years, I'm not going to say no.
"It doesn't cost me anything. I'm already doing the stitching, already doing the cutting. Now I just get paid a little more for it," he says.
Mohammed Arman has been filming his tailoring work
While there is demand for such footage it will be collected somewhere.

"India's current role in this industry is largely as a supplier of raw material - people strap on cameras, record themselves doing ordinary tasks, and that footage gets shipped off to labs abroad," Agarwal says.
But he argues the value of that kind of work will quickly become eroded, as more companies compete for collection contracts.

"India can't afford to stay a footage supplier. It needs to move up the value chain: from recording raw video to owning the pipeline that turns that video into something usable - cleaning it, structuring it, validating it, and ultimately setting the standards for what counts as high-quality training data," he says.
Jolly Arifur has been filming domestic work for a few hours a day
For some people collecting data is attractive part time work.
Science teacher Jolly Arifur was looking for work she could do from home that would fit around her young son.
"For the past seven months, I strapped a rig-mounted camera on my head while doing my routine domestic work scrubbing, cooking, sweeping tile floors, and folding laundry."
Arifur, who lives in Guntakal, Anantapur, fits the recording work around her teaching.

"I get paid two to three dollars per hour. If I record three to five hours a day, that's a good amount in hand it's become an extra source of income for me, on top of teaching. I'm managing both honestly, fantastically."

articles.title: The Minimal Credibility Test For The Autumn 2026 Budget
articles.standfirst: The ground has been prepared for a quiet Budget, albeit one in which the Chancellor’s buffer against the fiscal rules comes in perhaps £10 billion lower than the £23 billion...
paragraphs: The ground has been prepared for a quiet Budget, albeit one in which the Chancellor’s buffer against the fiscal rules comes in perhaps £10 billion lower than the £23 billion the OBR found in March. This so-called “headroom” is nothing more than the margin by which the OBR expects the current budget to be in surplus three years out, the point at which the fiscal rules are now tested. Running it down means a higher expected level of borrowing three years from now than previously planned (and nothing about the years in between).

In this week’s blog, Ben Caswell and I consider whether that is the right call from a macroeconomic standpoint. Our answer is no, for three reasons. First, the economy does not need a fiscal stimulus. Second, the rise in borrowing costs this year looks mostly persistent, so the argument for borrowing through a temporary shock does not apply. Third, markets are jittery and looking for the next shoe to drop. This is the environment to strengthen our fiscal position, not weaken it, and the case is stronger still if one believes the risk outlook has deteriorated.

Assuming we do end up with extra borrowing at the Budget, the minimal test of credibility is whether the higher borrowing through year three of the forecast is accompanied with correspondingly lower borrowing in the years after it: whether, in the language of control theory, the framework delivers “integral control”, so that overshoots in the stock of debt are made up later rather than forgiven. It is the minimal test because the government’s planned consolidation path is already time-inconsistent: back-loaded towards the last possible date for the next general election, when governments are not traditionally incentivised to deliver fiscal restraint. Our recent survey with Ipsos suggests that the public are ahead of the politicians in understanding the scale of fiscal retrenchment needed to bring the public finances into good shape.

Growth has proved far more resilient than almost anyone expected in March. GDP has grown by 1.8 per cent so far this year, with four months still to go. That is remarkable, and it exceeds anyone’s estimate of trend; our own is 1.3 per cent. The labour market tells the same story. Unemployment has fallen since the start of the year and is now half a percentage point below the OBR’s March forecast.

Inflation, meanwhile, is above target and rising. CPI inflation was 3.5 per cent in September, up for three months running, and with energy prices higher again since the summer most of the shock has still to reach consumer prices. We expect inflation above 4 per cent in the first quarter of next year. Some of the direct effect of the energy shock of course. But pay growth is running close to 4 per cent, against the 3 per cent or so the Bank of England regards as consistent with the target, and the main round of pay settlements falls early in the new year, when inflation will be above 4 per cent. The risk of second-round persistence has grown.

If we take the OIS curve literally, markets already price 100 basis points or more of increases in Bank Rate over the next twelve months. A Budget that adds to demand would push that path higher still; the looser the fiscal stance, the more of the work falls to the Bank of England. The policy mix the economy needs is tighter fiscal policy and, in time, easier monetary policy, not the reverse.

The case for dipping into the buffer rests on a respectable piece of economics: borrowing should be used to absorb temporary shocks, while taxes and spending should adjust to permanent ones (Barro, 1979). Borrowing through a permanent shock, however, postpones the adjustment and makes it bigger. So the judgement call for the Chancellor is whether the shock he would be borrowing through will pass.

Our assessment is that part of shock to global yields will dissipate if there is a resolution to the conflict in the middle east. The ten-year gilt yield has risen by around 110 basis points since the conflict began in February, to about 5.4 per cent, its highest since 2007, and the rise has been global. Roughly a third of the UK move reflects higher inflation compensation and the policy rates expected to deal with it.

The rest is likely to prove persistent. The real rate the market prices for 2031 to 2036 has risen by 75 basis points in the UK and by almost 100 in the US. That is harder to square with a temporary energy shock story. It is easier to rationalise as a global shift in the real interest rate, driven by the AI investment boom and the scale of government borrowing everywhere, with a term premium on gilts that has been rising since July on top. Around two-thirds of the rise in borrowing costs, on this reckoning, is here to stay.

The interest rate on new government borrowing is now above the growth rate of the economy, which turns the debt arithmetic from a tailwind into a headwind: the primary surplus needed simply to hold the debt ratio steady has risen, and every pound borrowed at today’s rates adds to that bill. With interest rates at 5 per cent, say, and a primary deficit of -1.5 per cent of GDP, the economy would need to grow in cash terms by 6.5 per cent annually to keep debt stable.

None of this is certain of course. But standard frameworks for decision-making under uncertainty point to fiscal conservatism. A Bayesian would treat most of the move as persistent, because changes in real rates historically are. A robust control approach asks which mistake is worse: tightening now and finding that rates fall back is a reversible error. Borrowing more and finding that they stay high may be harder to reverse.

The environment in which the Budget will be delivered next week is not a forgiving one. Global bond markets are looking for the next weak link. Attention is on France today, but the UK has been there twice in four years, in autumn 2022 and January 2025, and its 10-year yield is already the highest in the G7. It is not hard to imagine how the UK could come under the bond market’s spotlights in the months ahead. The risk outlook has, in our judgement, deteriorated: adverse shocks are more likely than they were a year ago. These are circumstances in which to build fiscal buffers, not run them down.

The public share the concern. In our survey with Ipsos, 52 per cent think a severe loss of market confidence in the UK’s ability to repay its debt is likely within five years, and 16 per cent of which think it very likely. Those are sobering numbers.

There is also an opportunity here, and an asymmetry. A Budget that markets judged credible could take 10 to 20 basis points off gilt yields through a lower term premium, worth £1 to 2 billion a year by the end of the Parliament. A Budget that they did not could cost several times that: on the OBR’s own reckoner, a 50-basis point repricing adds around £6 billion a year to debt interest by the end of the decade. The downside is larger than the upside, and the buffer is the one thing in this the Chancellor controls.

Suppose the Chancellor does borrow more. The minimal test of credibility is whether higher borrowing through the third year of the forecast is matched by correspondingly lower borrowing in the years after it, so that the stock of debt (relative to GDP) returns to the path planned in March rather than settling on a higher one. Engineers call this approach “integral control”—monetary economists will recognise it as the difference between a price-level target, which claws back an overshoot, and an inflation target, under which bygones are bygones.

The figure below illustrates this strategic choice facing the Chancellor. Both borrowing paths meet the fiscal rules (which do not require integral control), but only one delivers the same debt reduction path planned in March.1

It is a minimal test because the plan it would be applied to is already back-loaded and already hard to believe. The March forecast requires the primary balance to improve by around £100 billion a year by the end of the decade, a swing from the current primary deficit of 1.5 per cent of GDP to a primary surplus of the same magnitude. Almost all of it comes after 2027, with the largest single step in 2029-30, the year of the latest possible general election. If borrowing costs remain elevated, the debt interest bill could be £11-17 billion higher by 2030-31, raising the surpluses required further still. And at today’s borrowing costs, this would do no more than hold the debt ratio at 95 per cent.

The record on delivering surpluses of that kind is shown below. With the exception of the forecasts made at the height of the pandemic, every OBR forecast since 2010 has shown a primary surplus within its horizon. None of them has arrived; the UJ has not run one since 2001.

There is a further risk to the plan. The March forecast and the Spending Review settlements were set before the conflict pushed up inflation. On unchanged plans, the same cash buys 2.1 per cent less by 2030 than departments were promised. The flip side is that higher inflation flatters the near-term public finances precisely because cash spending plans stand still while cash receipts rise, and the OBR’s Budget forecast is likely to show that gain. It is only real if the squeeze is delivered. The record suggests it will not be, and the pressure points are already visible: pay review bodies reporting against inflation above 4 per cent, and the calls to raise real spending on the NHS and defence.

Pulling this together, the case for higher borrowing at this Budget is thin. It rests on a gamble that that the Bank of England won’t respond to the fiscal stimulus by raising Bank Rate; that market yields will fall back to pre-conflict levels; that there are no further adverse shocks; and that the government will deliver a 2 per cent annual real spending squeeze on departmental budgets relative to what it promised a year ago.

It also seems blind to the scale of debt reduction the country needs to deliver over the medium term. On this, the public appear to have a better appreciation of the problem than is evident in political discourse. In our survey with Ipsos, 58 per cent expect further significant steps to reduce debt within five years, beyond what is already planned, and four in ten of those expect them only after the next election. Two-thirds expect higher taxes at this Budget. When half the sample was shown the facts on debt and debt interest, neither expectation moved, because people already knew. Voters are divided on how the adjustment should fall, between taxes and spending and between high earners, business and waste, which is why the conversation to have now is about its size and timing rather than how. The public, it seems, are ready for that conversation.

1 The current fiscal rules are analogous to inflation targets. The stability rule tests whether the current budget is in balance in the third year of the forecast; the investment rule tests whether the debt ratio is falling in that same year. Both are tests of a single year, and neither asks where the debt ratio is relative to where it was meant to be.

articles.title: My final newsletter – fewer meetings, less management, slower pay growth?
articles.standfirst:
Morning all, As I step back from my role as Deputy Chief Executive at RF (I’ll be sticking around as a Research Associate, so you may still spot my by-line here and there), I’ll also be hanging up my Top of the Charts pen. Thank you for occasionally welcoming me into your inboxes over the … Continued
The post My final newsletter – fewer meetings, less management, slower pay growth? appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: As I step back from my role as Deputy Chief Executive at RF (I’ll be sticking around as a Research Associate, so you may still spot my by-line here and there), I’ll also be hanging up my Top of the Charts pen. Thank you for occasionally welcoming me into your inboxes over the past few years.

But the world very much keeps spinning, as the deluge of data we experienced this week demonstrates – from the labour market, to inflation, to rental prices, to pay, there was plenty to dig into (and scroll down to Chart of the Week to find out what the latest pay data tells us about pay inequality).

Next week brings Halloween Chancellor Healey’s first Budget. The team at RF is gearing up for their traditional all-nighter – I recommend signing up for the morning-after-event to get the lowdown on our overnight analysis before the last in-person tickets are gone.

This could have been an email. How many hours this week did you spend in meetings? And how many of them were useful? (RF colleagues: this is a rhetorical Q). This write-up of research into the prevalence of meetings notes the widespread disdain for their abundance. The analysis finds the average (Norwegian) worker in their survey spends 4.7 hours per week in meetings (one hour a day doesn’t sound so bad??), but that increases substantially for managers. There’s a perk, though: spending more time in meetings is correlated with faster wage growth. Plus, firms with higher salaries tend to meet more. That’s notable because the more you pay your workers, the more expensive it is to convene them away from their spreadsheets (that is all people do at work, right?), so there must be something in it. If only I had read this before I cut my working hours and excused myself from management duties…

Not doing so well. Life in the UK is not getting any better, according to Carnegie UK’s latest Life in the UK index. Drawing on a survey of around 6,700 people, it puts the UK’s collective wellbeing at 61 out of 100 this year, the first fall since the index began in 2023. Unsurprisingly, cost of living pressures knocked economic wellbeing down two points to 70 out of 100. Our focus is on living standards, but research like this provides an alternative insight into issues like intergenerational differences (people aged 55+ have a wellbeing score six points higher than people aged 16 to 34 or 35 to 54), social inequalities (people who are not heterosexual report lower wellbeing than the heterosexual majority), and deep-rooted structural inequalities (social renters score a whopping 25 points below homeowners on economic wellbeing, at 50 versus 75). Here’s hoping Andy Burnham can put us back on an upward track.

Working out welfare. There is much focus now on how to reform welfare, but alarm bells should have been ringing a lot earlier, given the rapid rise in out-of-work benefit recipients since 2016 (up by about 1.5 to 2 million, with the uncertainty caused by the move to Universal Credit over the period) despite a stronger labour market. So argues Paul Gregg, former RF Research Associate and current labour market policy royalty, in an essay on how the welfare system has “malfunctioned”. In the 2000s and early 2010s, Paul argues, job-search conditionality, strong part-time work incentives, caseworker support and scaled-up job placements worked well together to get benefit recipients into work. Since then, employment support has reverted to a cheaper sanction-based regime; in-work benefits have been cut back; and “the binary nature of our welfare system pushes our ageing and increasingly impaired population to claim incapacity benefits over limited working with in-work financial top-ups.” Paul argues that the current Government does not seem to have a coherent strategy for how to reform welfare to get people into work – although the imminent Milburn review may change some of that – and that its focus so far has been more on cost-cutting. Do the other political parties have the answer? You’ll have to come back later for part 2.

Tot(ting) up. More policy design issues this week, as a new report suggests how to reform England’s three (!) childcare subsidy schemes, each run by different parts of government and with their own eligibility rules, rates and payment methods. This is not only inefficient for government but (unsurprisingly) confusing for parents: only two-fifths of families on Universal Credit who pay for childcare claim the childcare element, and take up of Tax-Free Childcare is under half. Low take-up, the report says, is due to stigma, low awareness, administrative burdens and the reliability of payments. A simpler system would help; the report suggests the Government should consider a single system for supporting parents with childcare costs which varies the subsidy rates smoothly by income to prevent cliff-edges, something we’ve previously called for too.

Total recall. We have all randomly decided to clean the house, cook or stare out the window to shield ourselves from a mountain of work. However, a new paper – which feels directly targeted at people who have to write a weekly newsletter – argues that selective memory (or wishful thinking), not just weak willpower, can be a culprit behind procrastination. Over four weeks, around 500 German students had to finish a tedious transcription task of unknown length and were sent hints about their workload size. Among those who received bad news, those who weren’t reminded later on quietly ‘forgot’, and put the chance of a light workload 10 percentage points higher than those who had been reminded. Each 10 percentage point rise in hoped-for ease meant 7 per cent less work done early, leaving more to pile up. So, just keep telling yourself how much work you have to do, and it should get done.

It wouldn’t be a Mike TOTC without some mention of inequality, and yesterday’s ONS Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings data dump gave us the definitive take on earnings inequality, with data now up to 2026. The headline was that the share of workers in low pay failed to fall for the first time in 15 years, but Chart of the Week takes a closer look at overall pay inequality, measured by the 90:10 ratio (where higher numbers mean more unequal pay) for hourly pay and weekly earnings. Women’s weekly earnings have long been less equal than men’s – due to their higher share of part-time workers – but the genders have been slowly converging since this series began in 2002. More recently, overall earnings inequality has ticked up across the board, after a decade of decline. This is partly because the National Living Wage, which used to outpace median pay, is now only keeping pace with it, but is also because high earners are pulling away: weekly pay for the 90th percentile grew by 7.3 per cent in nominal terms this year (to reach £1,433 a week), against just 1.1 per cent at the 10th percentile. Among men, earnings inequality is now at its joint highest on record (alongside 2014), thanks to increasing numbers with a low weekly paycheck (the 10th percentile fell in cash terms from £309 in 2025 to £301 in 2026).

articles.title: Burnham and Badenoch need to reckon with Britain’s exposure to the rest of the world
articles.standfirst:
Burnham and Badenoch set out their visions for the country last month at their Party conferences. Next week’s Budget is the first test of whether Burnham can set it in action. But as Roli Asthana argues, neither politician has acknowledged the degree to which the fate of the economy and the country depend on the … Continued
The post Burnham and Badenoch need to reckon with Britain’s exposure to the rest of the world first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: Burnham and Badenoch set out their visions for the country last month at their Party conferences. Next week’s Budget is the first test of whether Burnham can set it in action. But as Roli Asthana argues, neither politician has acknowledged the degree to which the fate of the economy and the country depend on the state of the wider world.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

In July, as Andy Burnham prepared to enter Downing Street, I argued that his politics of place could ground a new internationalism, one in which Britain’s foreign relationships are judged by whether they deliver for its towns: stable jobs, secure energy, resilient supply chains and access to global markets. Next Wednesday’s Budget is the first serious test of that idea, and of the opposition’s alternative to it.

Conference season was about abstract principles and Party identities. Badenoch promised “a battle for the soul of this nation”. Burnham offered “a new economy and a new politics”, with water, energy and housing brought under stronger public control. On 28 October, John Healey’s first Budget, published alongside the OBR forecast, will have to turn vision into hard numbers.

A battle for the soul of the nation has to be paid for, and the spreadsheets will show who pays. But much of the bill is set abroad: in energy, food, fertiliser and capital markets, in allied defence industries, in the global growth on which Britain’s own prospects now depend. On Wednesday, neither the Chancellor nor the opposition will say much about the state of the wider world. The numbers will say it for them.

Both parties are chasing the same voter groups in a bid to attract them back from further left and further right parties to the centre ground. Households struggling with bills, regions struggling with deindustrialisation and sluggish growth, and young persons entering the labour market, and their families. These groups are concentrated largely in economically lagging regions.
On Wednesday, neither the Chancellor nor the opposition will say much about the state of the wider world. The numbers will say it for them.

The two leaders present different paths based on different visions of the economy and the state. For instance, in The Times on Monday, Burnham called the plight of a million young people outside work and education a moral failure, and attacked a welfare system that offers “an assessment, a payment and, after that, a goodbye”. Badenoch’s answer is to halve employer National Insurance for 21- to 24-year-olds. The same applies to approaches to energy security, job-creation and tax and spend. Both measure success by the cost of living, growth and jobs.

This is the electorate of Will Jennings and Gerry Stoker’s “two Englands”: towns on a different trajectory from the growing cities, and sceptical of mainstream politics. Daron Acemoglu’s new book, What Happened to Liberal Democracy?, explains why this still holds. He argues that deindustrialisation did more than hurt particular workers: by leaving a working class stranded, it shrank the coalition on which democracy itself depends. The next technological shift could repeat the pattern. An AI economy left to the market will reward the cities and graduates already ahead. Without a deliberate industrial strategy that brings new work to towns, it will widen the very gap that is eroding faith in liberal democracy. The Budget is a key event in this test of confidence.

The IMF has already set the backdrop. Its October World Economic Outlook raised UK growth this year to 1.3 per cent but cut 2027 to 1.2 per cent, just as it expects the world economy to accelerate. Britain’s prospects are being revised by events abroad, and 2027, the year of its G20 presidency and the run-up to several consequential European elections, now looks economically more fraught.

Energy costs make the point most sharply. Healey may extend the electricity VAT cut, but the household bill is set in a global gas market that no Budget controls. After war broke out between Iran, the US and Israel in March, fuel prices climbed and ministers faced calls for rationing. A tax cut softens such a shock, but it cannot prevent the next one. Badenoch’s alternative, to maximise North Sea extraction, hits the same wall: North Sea gas sells at world prices, which is why the government says new licences would not take a penny off bills.
No Party yet owns the link between domestic and international in their policy visions.

Defence is no different. Healey arrives at the Treasury having resigned from Defence on budget issues. But, this is not a domestic industrial strategy issue. Post-war security has been managed through a shared approach, and every defence pound goes through supply chains that run through allies. Similarly, Badenoch’s £10bn “Britannia Shield” would be built from American, European and Israeli industry, using minerals processed largely in China.

Foreign policy rarely decides British elections directly; but competence does. As Jane Green and Will Jennings show in The Politics of Competence, voters reward the party they trust to handle the problems they care about. But international conditions are the implicit (and increasingly explicitly) drivers of many of those problems, especially in an open economy like ours.

No Party yet owns the link between domestic and international in their policy visions. Burnham came closest by tying weaker control of immigration to the loss of cooperation with Europe. Badenoch has said little on migration and treats Europe as a closed question. Neither directly connects energy, defence or jobs to the international bargains beneath them.
One Budget cannot close Britain’s exposure to the world, but it can begin to turn that exposure into a political offer. Three steps would help.

First, a Foreign Office that treats resilience as its core domestic task, judged by whether shocks to energy, food, supply chains and critical minerals reach households more slowly and less severely, and answerable to Parliament for it.

Second, a place-by-place map of Britain’s critical dependencies: which towns rely on one foreign-owned employer, which industries on one supplier country, which areas would feel an energy shock first. A Budget that promises power to every postcode should give mayors and councils the means to own that map.

Third, a 2027 G20 presidency built around the cost of living and jobs for young people. Burnham wants AI at its centre. It belongs there as the test Acemoglu sets: whether young people outside the big cities can gain the work it creates or lose the work it replaces.
Parties may disagree about the soul of the nation. But the promises they make at home will be paid for, or broken, abroad and the Budget must target resilience and growth taking that into account.
