articles.title: What Is Taxable Income? How It’s Calculated for Tax Filing
articles.standfirst: Want to know how much you'll owe during tax filing season? Then you need to know your taxable income.
paragraphs: *This amount is your adjusted gross income, or “AGI.” Your federal AGI is also what most states start with to determine your state income tax.
* Once these steps are complete, you have your taxable income.
Want to know how much you’ll owe during tax filing season? Then you need to know your taxable income.
Your taxable income is the amount of your income that’s subject to tax.
There’s a maze of variables to navigate to get to that number, but here’s how it is determined:
To calculate your taxable income, we start with your gross income.
Salary, bonuses, tips, unemployment—include every dollar you brought in for the year. There are a few types of income that aren’t taxed, so you can exclude those.

The next step is your filing status. Whichever status you choose has its own deductions and exemptions, which cover things like child care or student loan payments. These deductions and exemptions reduce the amount of taxes you owe by lowering the amount of income you’re taxed on.
What’s left is your adjusted gross income, or “AGI.” Your federal AGI is also what most states start with to determine your state income tax.
Then, you can take either the standard deduction, which reduces your taxable income even further by a set amount determined by the government each year, or you can itemize your deductions.

Now apply the marginal tax rates to that, and you get your tax liability. There’s just one last step. It’s time to apply any available credits to your tax liability. Credits directly reduce how much you owe.
Congrats! You’re done. Now you know what you owe or if the government owes you a refund.

articles.title: Jackdaw is a distraction from Aberdeen’s much bigger problem
articles.standfirst:
This article was originally published on our Substack. After years of back and forth and months of mounting speculation, this week the Government gave the green light to the Jackdaw gas field. But one small hydrocarbon project dominating headlines risks missing the much bigger – and more important – question over where tomorrow’s good jobs … Continued
The post Jackdaw is a distraction from Aberdeen’s much bigger problem appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: After years of back and forth and months of mounting speculation, this week the Government gave the green light to the Jackdaw gas field. But one small hydrocarbon project dominating headlines risks missing the much bigger – and more important – question over where tomorrow’s good jobs in Aberdeen will come from.

When we visited Aberdeen earlier this year, we saw what the city has to offer and the incredible depth of expertise and infrastructure it has built over decades, but to put this to best use, we need to start focusing more on the city’s future and less on its past.

Aberdeen remains at the centre of the UK’s oil and gas industry, and when the industry has boomed so has the city. In the early 2010s, total disposable incomes in Aberdeen exceeded the UK average by a fifth, and the earnings of people working in the city by almost half (47 per cent).

The flip side to this is that when the industry has suffered so too has the city. When oil prices halved between 2014 and 2016, the city sank into decline, and Aberdeen’s earnings premium over the rest of the UK has since fallen by three-quarters, while payrolled employment is down 8 per cent since 2015.

Now, Aberdeen faces a new problem: after extracting close to 48 billion barrels of oil equivalent, reserves are running dry. UK oil and gas production is down 76 per cent on its 1999 peak and is set to fall by another 40 per cent by 2030 (and by over 90 per cent by 2050). While Jackdaw will increase output, its contribution will only be marginal: the new field will generate fewer than 30 permanent roles.
For Aberdeen and its specialised workforce there is now no other option than to look elsewhere for jobs that can fill the gap the oil and gas industry is already leaving behind.
Green jobs can help but aren’t arriving fast enough or are arriving in the wrong order

Aberdeen is a natural fit for offshore wind thanks to its subsea engineering capability, offshore logistics, deep harbour, and long experience with operating in harsh North Sea conditions. But despite Scotland’s largest offshore wind farm, Seagreen, sitting nearby, the city hasn’t seen the green jobs boom it was hoping for.

Much of this is down to timing, as wind capacity has arrived before the grid upgrades that would enable the electricity generated to be used by households across Britain. As a result, much of Scottish wind capacity is being wasted (‘curtailed’). In 2024, energy from Seagreen was curtailed in 71 per cent of the hours it was available at a cost of £65 million.

To prevent future bottle necks, ministers will need to ensure that infrastructure is built in a sensible order by aligning Scottish capacity targets with the grid timetable. As it stands, the grid reinforcements that are needed to carry Scottish wind south will not be complete until the 2030s – several years after a wind farm consented today would start generating.

With oil already declining and more green jobs years away, there’s a risk that Aberdeen loses the highly skilled engineering base that took half a century to build. In the year to mid-2023 alone, 4,400 Aberdonians voted with their feet and left for overseas destinations.

In the short-term, decommissioning work (making safe old rigs, wells and pipes) can help bridge the gap and draw on the skills that the city already has. The part of the North Sea currently serviced out of Aberdeen is expected to account for 60 per cent of national decommissioning spending over the next 10 years, with demand for workers increasing to a peak in 2029.

To get the most out of this inherently temporary work, the Government should attach domestic content conditions to the tax relief that funds much of decommissioning and treat dismantling capacity at ports as national infrastructure to ensure as much of the work as possible is based in Scotland, rather than hubs on the other side of the North Sea.

Decommissioning activity, grid investment and wind infrastructure all need to be timed against one another so that workers and the firms employing them can clearly see where the next five years of work comes from.

This kind of coordination would be a major departure from the reliance on market timing that has characterised the North Sea hydrocarbon industry, and that underpins the UK Government’s competition-led, ‘place-blind’ approach to renewable energy subsidies. But to future-proof Aberdeen’s workforce the UK and Scottish Governments will have to be more hands-on: no single operator, regulator or local authority holds all the levers.
Read ‘Second wind’ to find out more about how green industries can contribute to local economic growth in places like Aberdeen.

articles.title: Jackdaw was well handled – but government needs a coherent net zero strategy
articles.standfirst:
Jackdaw was well handled – but government needs a coherent net zero strategy melissa.ittoo Thu, 22/10/2026 - 16:18 Miatta Fahnbulleh made a good case for the government decision on the Jackdaw gas field. 4 Comment Jill Rutter Rosa Hodgkin Institute for Government Yes Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey during a visit to Shell UK's St Fergus Gas Terminal in Peterhead, Aberdeenshire. Policy making Net zero Energy Climate change Environment Labour Burnham government Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
No

The secretary of state for energy security and net zero finally retook the decision on the exploitation of the Jackdaw gas field. It was a decision long in the making after the Scottish courts found that the initial decision by the then Conservative government had failed to take proper account of the impact of licencing the field on the UK’s ability to deliver net zero.

The government aced its Jackdaw communications

The announcement itself was testament to the political skill of the Burnham operation. It made clear that the decision was – as it had to be – for the secretary of state. Miatta Fahnbulleh was clear about the implications – this was about energy security, tax revenue and jobs, not reducing gas prices set by the international market. She, the chancellor and the secretary of state for Scotland shared the press release, and the publicity, with the prime minister, emphasising the positives for the Scottish economy.

Meanwhile, hypothecating future revenues to an “Energy Wealth Fund”, which will sit within the National Wealth Fund and invest in green energy infrastructure, made it clear that exploiting UK supplies for residual gas could (in theory at least) help speed the reduction in fossil fuel dependence. Jackdaw’s shelf life means that the UK will stop using gas quite some time after the field has to be decommissioned.

The government lined its ducks up – and they quacked appreciatively. And this is useful in the run-up to the budget to show what “Burnham pragmatism” means in practice and that government is prepared to listen to business concerns.

Critics of the plan missed the target 

Authorisation has inevitably triggered criticism from green campaigners and Green politicians. Some has been about the UK losing ground on climate leadership. This is a genuine concern, but the UK was already on shaky ground after cuts to the aid budget and a raid on international climate finance paid for the bus fare cap two days into Burnham’s premiership.

But the second criticism was that there were alternatives – more investment in electrification, decarbonising power, upgrading homes, all of which could create wider benefits, more jobs and speed the green transition.

That posed a false dichotomy: Jackdaw or the green transition. But in truth they were not competing: all net zero scenarios still have the UK using gas into the 2040s. The choice on Jackdaw was UK or imported gas. That was the supply side question the secretary of state had to answer. The government now has – at the margin – a little bit more resource to put into the transition that matters which, looking ahead, is primarily on the demand side.

Related content

Jackdaw and Rosebank

Jackdaw and Rosebank

What are Jackdaw and Rosebank, and what position has the government taken on North Sea licences?

Read our explainer

Rosebank is a very different decision

There have been two readings of the implications of the Jackdaw decision for the bigger one on the new oil field at Rosebank. One is that the secretary of state will be able to use similar rationales, and it would not be worth establishing the Energy Wealth Fund for Jackdaw alone. The other is that Miatta Fahnbulleh has been emphasising the differences – not least the lesser domestic security angle when it comes to oil versus gas, and she is rolling the pitch for a no. The key thing is that this is a separate, and quite different, decision which she needs to show she has taken on the merits.

The bigger issue is a credible net zero strategy

Jackdaw should not be a distraction from the much bigger issue of whether the government has a coherent strategy to get the UK off fossil fuels in the longer term. Jackdaw alone does not blow a hole in that strategy, but the strategy had numerous holes already and will look even more patchy if the government rolls back on some of its key levers to drive electrification. There are stories that the Boiler Upgrade scheme may be cut to pay for the uplift in defence spending and that the EV mandate may be watered down (and if getting inside Made in Europe means applying EU style tariffs to Chinese EVs that change may slow anyway).

The government has made a good case for why approving Jackdaw makes sense in the short term, but a plan for getting off fossil fuels that actually adds up when combined with concerns on energy security and affordability – and fits with a strategy to adapt to the climate change that is already baked in – is the real issue. That needs to be the secretary of state’s next priority.

The government has set out its case for approving Jackdaw clearly, but it needs a more credible roadmap for getting the UK off fossil fuels, write Jill Rutter and Rosa Hodgkin Off Net zero

paragraphs: This holiday season will remain deeply bifurcated. High-income consumers will keep a floor under spending, helped by the surge in equities this year.

We forecast holiday retail sales to rise 4.2% in dollar terms and 2.2% in volume after adjusting for inflation. That would beat last year’s volume, when tariffs hurt sales and shifted purchases forward into October, but it trails a typical holiday season, reflecting the hit to spending power from higher energy prices.

High inflation is holding down real disposable income growth, high diesel prices are raising shipping costs, and Federal Reserve rate hikes are raising borrowing costs for those planning to spend by credit card.

articles.title: In Wyoming, Are Two Homestead Exemptions Enough?
articles.standfirst: No one enjoys paying taxes, but the property tax serves an important purpose, and Wyoming has already implemented significant property tax relief. Proposition 1 would undercut local finances to a degree that would likely force reliance on worse taxes (local or state) and prompt spending cuts that reduce homeowners’ property values.
paragraphs: If having one property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. exemption is good, then having two is preferable, and three is better still. Or at least, that seems to be the logic of many states, where lawmakers and voters keep piling on new property tax relief measures that rarely cohere and sometimes work at cross purposes. But in Wyoming—Big Wyoming, as they say—it’s “go big or go home,” with voters deciding this November whether to create a choose-your-own-adventure system with three different homestead exemptions.

Taxes should be simple, neutral, transparent, and stable. Wyoming, however, is merely the latest state to offer an alternative: what if we made the taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. system more complex, arbitrary, opaque, and volatile?

In 2024, lawmakers adopted a long-term homeowner exemption, which now stands at 50 percent of the first $3 million in market value on primary residences of owners or spouses 65 or older, who have paid Wyoming residential property taxes for at least 25 years, with the condition that they must live in the home at least eight months per year.

In 2025, lawmakers adopted a 25 percent exemption on the first $1 million in market value, both land and structures, for owner-occupants of single-family residential housing who reside in a home at least eight months per year. Those claiming the 50 percent long-term homeowner exemption may not simultaneously claim the 25 percent exemption.

Lower-income households, moreover, can receive property tax refunds. Those with household incomes at or below 125 percent of their county or the statewide median household income, with assets (beyond their home, one vehicle, and retirement accounts) less than about $160,000, receive a refund of the lesser of 75 percent of the previous year’s property taxes or 50 percent of the median residential property tax liability in their county. Those with incomes between 125 and 145 percent of the median household income, and still under the asset limit, receive 65 percent of those amounts. These refunds are subject to appropriations.

This year, voters will decide whether to adopt a third exemption with Proposition 1, worth 50 percent of the assessed value of the home itself (excluding the value of land), with no cap, for those who have been Wyoming residents for at least one year and who lived in the home for at least six months of the preceding tax year. Under anticipatory legislation enacted this year, the new exemption could not stack with the long-term homeowner exemption, but nothing prevents it from being claimed in tandem with the 25 percent exemption, which would allow eligible homeowners to claim an exemption for 25 percent of all value (land and structures), plus another 50 percent of the home’s value.

Owner-occupants of duplexes and other multi-family buildings would be eligible for the new 50 percent exemption but are not eligible for the existing 25 percent exemption. Those who have lived in Wyoming for less than a year are eligible for the 25 percent exemption but wouldn’t be eligible for the new initiative-created exemption. Those who live in a home for at least six months but less than eight months per year could qualify under the new exemption but not the existing ones. And whereas both the 25 percent exemption and the long-term exemption are capped, the new exemption is not. The exemptions also have different application dates, further complicating matters. The existing exemption applications are due March 1, the Proposition 1 application would be due the fourth Monday in May, and refund applications are due the first Monday in June.

This is the wrong way to do tax policy. In tandem, these three exemptions wipe out a significant share of Wyoming’s residential real property tax, forcing Wyoming governments to rely even more heavily on taxes on the oil, gas, and mining industries—a concerning lack of diversification, particularly for industries with high volatility and potential long-term decline.

Consider a $400,000 property, consisting of $325,000 in home value and $75,000 in land value, taxed at the statewide average levy (about 68.5 mills on 9.5 percent of market value). Without any homestead exemptions, annual property taxes would run $2,603. If the homeowners qualify for the existing 25 percent exemption, that trims the property tax bill to $1,952. If Proposition 1 passes, their tax bill gets slashed to $895, with homestead exemptions eliminating almost two-thirds of the household’s property tax liability. If their income is less than 125 percent of the county’s median, they’ll get a refund of up to $671 of that, leaving a net annual tax bill of $224 on a $400,000 property.

That may sound like an incredible deal for homeowners, but it severely undercuts the property tax, and it may seem like a worse deal as local governments scramble to find revenue to fund basic services.

Property taxes, as Gov. Mark Gordon explains in outlining his opposition to Proposition 1, pay for local services that directly benefit homeowners, and they offer a level of local control that other taxes do not. Properties in a community are more valuable because of the services—roads, schools, courts, parks, police, and emergency services—that local governments provide, and if a locality gets the balance wrong, voters can force a correction. If the state eventually has to come in and backfill an eroded property tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates., that local control—and the ability of localities and their voters to make decisions that benefit the community and local property values—will be lost.

No one enjoys paying taxes, but the property tax serves an important purpose, and Wyoming has already implemented significant property tax relief. Proposition 1 would undercut local finances to a degree that would likely force reliance on worse taxes (local or state) and prompt spending cuts that reduce homeowners’ property values.

Jared Walczak is a Senior Fellow at the Tax Foundation, where he spent five years as Vice President of State Projects, and president of Walczak Policy Consulting.

articles.title: Options to Reform the Tax Treatment of Exempt Hospitals
articles.standfirst: Nearly half of all hospitals are exempt from paying US corporate income taxes. As healthcare spending rises, lawmakers have questioned whether hospitals are providing as much in community benefits as they derive from tax exemptions.
paragraphs: TaxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities.-exempt hospitals provide a substantial share of medical care in the United States. Of the 6,100 hospitals operating in the country in 2026, nearly half are nongovernment, tax-exempt community hospitals. As hospitals consolidate into larger systems and their revenues rise, the value of their tax exemptionA tax exemption excludes certain income, revenue, or even taxpayers from tax altogether. For example, nonprofits that fulfill certain requirements are granted tax-exempt status by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), preventing them from having to pay income tax. and the cost of forgone revenue grow.

Not-for-profit hospitals are tax-exempt. They do not usually pay federal income taxes, state income taxes, or local property taxes. They may also use tax-exempt bond financing and benefit from tax-deductible charitable donations.

A variety of studies have attempted to measure the value of these tax exemptions. Recent estimates covering 2018 through 2022 put the value of the federal corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. exemption for hospitals at $8.3 billion to $11.5 billion per year. Several studies have also compared the value of hospitals’ tax exemptions with the benefits they provide for their communities.

Lawmakers in both parties have scrutinized the hospital tax exemption in recent years, questioning whether the community benefits provided by tax-exempt hospitals justify the value of their tax exemptions. Some have debated requiring hospitals to report more information on the community benefits they provide or even limiting tax exemptions for the largest hospital systems.
Below, Tax Foundation models and analyzes several options to reform the tax treatment of exempt hospitals.

We estimate that applying the 21 percent corporate income tax to large hospital systems would raise $147.6 billion in federal revenue over ten years. More targeted reforms, like applying taxes on investment income or recapturing tax benefits in excess of community benefits, would raise less revenue. If policymakers choose to reform the tax treatment of tax-exempt hospitals, they face complex choices along the way, such as how many hospitals would be covered, how community benefits would be defined, and which tax benefit to prioritize within a reform effort.

A tax-exempt organization is one that is generally exempt from federal income tax on income related to its exempt purpose. The first corporate income tax exemption came in 1894, with the imposition of a temporary corporate income tax that was subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court the next year. Congress again exempted charitable organizations from an excise tax on corporations in 1909, and that exemption carried through to the modern income tax first levied in 1913.

Hospitals were not included in the 1909 or 1913 laws by name, but in practice received tax exemptions as nonprofits “affiliated with either religious groups or philanthropic foundations.” A 1956 revenue ruling from the Internal Revenue Service established the “charity care” standard by which hospitals could earn and retain their federal tax exemption. The IRS replaced the 1956 ruling with a broader “community benefit” standard in 1969, which is still in place today.
Hospital systems today are much larger and more sophisticated than they were a century ago. In 2024, 2,271 hospital filers collectively reported:
These figures heavily reflect the influence of the top 100 tax-exempt health filers ranked by tax year 2024 revenue, as demonstrated in the chart below:

In all, hospital filers reported a combined $87.9 billion in net income in 2024. If the hospital tax exemption did not exist, much of that net income would be subject to the 21 percent US corporate income tax rate. Hospitals would also be subject to state corporate income taxes, local property taxes, and federal unemployment taxes.

Table 1 below summarizes several studies that measured the value of hospital tax exemptions between 2011 and 2022. The estimates are not directly comparable with Tax Foundation estimates as they use different years, methods, and definitions of tax benefits.

We estimate the conventional revenue effects of five different ways to reform the tax treatment of large hospital systems, along with several variants. Each reform option is imposed on hospital systems with $1 billion in average total revenue over the three preceding years (indexed for inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin for future years). The $1 billion threshold would cover 287 systems in 2027, making up about 85 to 89 percent of the sector revenue, income, assets, bonds, and gifts.
The options above are illustrative, and policymakers reforming the tax treatment of exempt hospitals might choose different parameters.

Congress could levy a 21 percent income tax on large systems based on book (financial statement) income rather than taxable income. A 21 percent book income tax on large hospital systems would increase revenue by $224.7 billion on a conventional basis, compared to $147.6 billion if levied on taxable income. About half of the difference in these two measures is 100 percent bonus depreciationBonus depreciation allows firms to deduct a larger portion of certain “short-lived” investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings in the first year. Allowing businesses to write off more investments partially alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. for machinery and equipment, with the other half being regular MACRS depreciation deductions faster than deductions allowed under financial rules.

Lawmakers could also levy the 21 percent income tax on individual hospitals surpassing the $1 billion threshold rather than on consolidated hospital systems. A tax on individual hospitals would raise less revenue, as fewer entities would meet the threshold.

The 4 and 8 percent excise tax rates mirror the top two rates of the existing university endowment tax as it was restructured in 2025, while the 21 percent rate would match the corporate income tax. Policymakers could also decide whether to apply a graduated rate structure, although higher marginal rates could increase incentives for tax avoidance.
The charitable deduction could be restricted incrementally, rather than a full denial of charitable deductions for covered systems.

Policymakers could apply limits on hospital tax-exempt bond financing for existing bonds or only for bonds issued moving forward. Our option only applies prospectively, so existing bond and bond refundings are not included in the tax base. The revenue effect therefore starts small and grows slowly over time as the share of bonds issued since the options took effect rises.

Congress could measure tax benefits or community benefits in different ways. A narrower definition of community benefits, such as charity care alone, would produce more revenue than a broader definition.

Policymakers, academics, and hospital representatives have fiercely debated how to measure community benefits. The hospital sector takes a broad view, including charity care as well as research, education, Medicaid shortfalls, Medicare shortfalls, and bad debt. The IRS takes a narrower view in its Schedule H reporting requirements for hospitals. The IRS includes free care, unreimbursed Medicaid, community health programs, and community building activities but excludes items like bad debt and Medicare shortfalls.

The nonpartisan health think tank Lown Institute produces a widely cited annual report, the Lown Hospitals Index, with a narrower measure still of “meaningful” community investment: financial assistance, subsidized health services, community health improvement services, cash and in-kind contributions, and community-building activities. The Lown Index notably excludes Medicaid shortfalls, as well as education and research funding.

For the recapture option, we model two definitions of community benefits: charity care alone and the broader community-investment measure developed by the Lown Institute. The broader the measure of community benefits, the fewer hospital systems who have tax benefits greater than community benefits, resulting in less revenue from recapture.

Our estimates do not include certain behavioral effects for hospitals. For example, hospital systems would reasonably change their behavior in response to any of these options, especially for systems near the $1 billion threshold we chose for the tax.

Some systems may sell or spin off affiliated hospitals to avoid the tax. We used a threshold based on gross revenue, but thresholds using a net income measure could encourage profitable hospitals to acquire revenue-losing hospitals so that their consolidated entity falls under the threshold. Other hospitals may even shift to for-profit status or seek acquisition by a for-profit entity. We exclude such behavioral responses from our revenue estimates.

Other options incorporate limited behavioral effects; for example, when restricting the charitable deduction for donations to large hospital systems, we assume that overall giving will decline in response to the higher, after-tax cost of charitable giving but we do not assume any shift in the composition of giving (i.e., from donors shifting their giving from covered systems to other charities).

While each option would raise federal revenue and increase horizontal equity between hospitals and similar private sector health care providers, they would involve tradeoffs. Each option would need to be designed to minimize possible impacts on capital investment. Preserving full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. within the corporate income tax base would be an important feature of an income tax design, for example.

From a principles perspective, each of these options would move the tax code toward greater neutrality between similarly situated taxpayers in the health sector. Applying tax rules already in place for most other taxpayers earning similar forms of income is the most defensible approach, especially if it was done in concert with other changes in the tax code.

For example, more broadly limiting tax-exempt bond issuance, imposing stricter rules on nonprofit tax-exempt earnings, and limiting the scope of all charitable deductions would move in the same direction as these sector-specific options. If policymakers wish to keep some tax benefit for hospital operations, tailoring them to the specific societal benefit (such as charity care or other operations) would be an improvement over the status quo.

Our estimates suggest that incremental options focused on the top of the sector would raise revenue and only focus on the largest hospital systems. Reforming the treatment of tax-exempt hospitals is also an opportunity to improve the horizontal treatment of health providers in the tax code. Policymakers have a range of reform options to consider, but the design details matter to ensure we benefit from the neutrality improvements while minimizing unintended consequences on the sector and patients.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

To construct our estimates, we used IRS Statistics of Income (SOI) Exempt Organization study files from tax years 2019 to 2022 and IRS Form 990 e-file returns from tax years 2022 to 2024 to construct a model of hospital filers. We omitted the pandemic years 2020 and 2021 to avoid pandemic-era noise in the data.

We used Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services ownership data to group filers into systems under common control from control trees on Schedule R, resulting in 2,452 total hospital filers in 1,771 total systems from tax year 2019 to tax year 2024 (2,271 filers and 1,045 systems in tax year 2024). Systems exclude gifts between members and exclude university hospitals, which tend to file returns with their affiliated universities. As a check, we cross referenced our estimates of the 25 largest systems with their audited consolidated revenue, and the median value came within 4 percent of the audited figures.

SOI and CMS cost report data provide information on financials, Schedule K bonds, Schedule H community benefits, and itemized sources of revenue. Our growth paths for each modeled item follow CMS projections of national hospital spending through 2034, and from there Congressional Budget Office’s February 2026 baseline for nominal GDP, the 10-year Treasury rate, and CPI-U where applicable.

A system is covered under each option if its total average revenue over the three preceding years exceeded $1 billion as of 2027, indexed to CPI-U after that and rounded down to $10 million, reaching a threshold of $1.2 billion in 2036. In 2027, 287 systems would be covered, holding between 85 percent and 89 percent of sector revenue, income, assets, bonds, and gifts.

We use the Tax Foundation General Equilibrium Model to capture interactions with individual and payroll taxA payroll tax is a tax paid on the wages and salaries of employees to finance social insurance programs like Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance. Payroll taxes are social insurance taxes that comprise 24.8 percent of combined federal, state, and local government revenue, the second largest source of that combined tax revenue. revenue, charitable deductions, and depreciation allowances.

The 21 percent corporate tax swaps book depreciation for tax depreciation for investment prospectively using BEA hospital asset mix data. Bonus depreciation for eligible investment is assumed to be taken up 80 percent of the time when profitable and 45 percent in loss years.

The 4 percent investment excise tax includes net investment income as under IRC Section 4940: interest, dividends, royalties, and investment income booked as “other revenue.” Realized securities gains are also included.

The option ending tax-exempt bond financing uses Schedule K data to derive new money bonds net of refundings (refundings of pre-2027 bonds are exempt). Coupons are estimated at the CBO 10-year Treasury rate plus 1.9 points (the average gap between A-rated corporate bond yields and 10-year Treasury yields from 2010 to 2025). Holders of the taxable bonds follow Federal Reserve figures for ownership of corporate bonds.

We use data on gifts to covered systems split by donor type using Giving USA shares for individual, corporation, and foundation and/or donor advised fund giving, with individual gifts run through the Tax Foundation General Equilibrium Model to capture existing charitable giving. Corporate gifts are counted above the existing 1 percent floor at 21 percent. We assume foundation and donor advised fund giving is included in the denial of deduction base, though this is a policy design choice and an avoidance mechanism that could lower the estimate under certain designs.

Federal benefit recapture uses the method established by the Lown Institute, defining community benefit as charity care, community health, cash and in kind-contributions, subsidized services, and community building. Federal benefits are defined as taxable income under a corporate tax base at 21 percent plus bond financing savings. The proposal recaptures 100 percent of benefits above the community benefit per system, tested each year for each system with no carryforward. We exclude state and local tax benefits in our estimates.

Garrett Watson is Vice President of Federal Tax Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. His work has been featured in The Washington Post, The Atlantic, Politico, the Associated Press and other major outlets.

Andrew Lautz is Senior Director of Federal Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Before joining Tax Foundation, he was Director of Tax Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center and Director of Federal Policy at the National Taxpayers Union. Andrew’s research and perspectives on federal tax policy have been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and other major publications.

articles.title: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroad
articles.standfirst: With graduate jobs hard to come by, more young adults are reported to be considering emigrating.
paragraphs: Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseas
Last year Rachel James quit her corporate job in London, packed a suitcase and booked a one-way ticket to Sydney, without a job lined up or a plan in place.
"I went for a fresh start," says the 26-year-old from Surrey. "To take a risk and try something completely different. With the worst case being there will always be a flight home if all fails."

More than one in 10 UK university students are now planning to move abroad for better opportunities after they have graduated, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to a survey of 15,000 final year university students.
Meanwhile, a study by the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) says that competition for graduate jobs in the UK was at a three-decade high.
UK employers now receive 140 applications per graduate vacancy on average, an increase of 14% from 2025, and up from just 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago, according to the ISE's report.
For young British adults going abroad, where are they heading?
While there is no age-specific data for which countries people go to, Australia remains by far the most popular nation for British adults overall who move abroad, official figures show.

In addition to Australia's weather and use of the English language, another reason is its visa-friendly policy. Under its Working Holiday Maker programme, British passport holders between the ages of 18 and 35 can live in Australia for up to three years.
Rachel James says that Sydney is a nicer place to live and work than London

Rachel, who graduated from Loughborough University in 2022 with a degree in English, had been working for accountancy giant PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK. She now has a job in marketing in Sydney for gym chain Fitness First.

She says her annual salary has gone down from £42,000 to £37,000, while she now pays $AUS 2,000 (£1,000) a month to rent a two-bedroom apartment with a friend, similar to what she was paying in London.
Despite having less disposable income, she has no regrets. "The weather's beautiful, even in the winter, and the walks on my doorstep are unmatched.

"People want to leave work at 5pm so they can go and do their hobbies - whether it's surfing, running, enjoying the sunset, a picnic or sunset yoga. I didn't come with career progression as a focus - it's more about the different way of life."
Around two-thirds of British nationals who emigrate are aged between 16 and 34, according to the most recent figures from the UK's Office for National Statistics.
It said that 75,000 more people in that age bracket left the UK in 2025 than arrived.
After Australia the next most popular destination for British adults is the US.
Charlie West says that working in the US has given him better pay and more opportunities
Charlie West, 25, from Cheshire, moved to the States in 2024 for better pay and opportunities in academia after he completed a masters in medieval studies at Oxford University.
West is now two years in to a six-year funded PhD course at Yale's Department of Italian Studies, which includes him teaching.

"I really wanted to do a PhD but it's difficult to get funding in the UK, particularly in the humanities, and funded stipends are about £21,000. I'd have had to work [outside academia] at the same time to afford to live.
"In the US I'm paid $51,000 a year (£37,770), about to rise to $52,000, and it comes with a lot more opportunities to teach and travel to conferences."
The European Union also remains popular with young Britons looking to move abroad, although the visa requirements since Brexit have made it more difficult.
One way to get into the European jobs market is to have studied in the EU. International graduates can apply for a permanent residence permit after their degree ends.
Owein Iveson has no plans to return to the UK from Finland
This is what Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is doing as he is about to graduate from Finland's Aalto University with a masters in design.
Owein says he "fell in love with the country" after visiting for the first time in 2020.
"Finland's a beautiful country," he says. "The streets are very clean. It's a very quiet lifestyle. The nature is fantastic and the public transport works really efficiently."
Owein lives in Espoo, a city about 15 minutes on the metro from Helsinki, and doesn't expect to return to the UK anytime soon.
"To be honest the jobs market is not great in Finland, but there is high demand for IT workers, and if you can work across the EU there are many more opportunities."
Immigration lawyer John Kiely, a London-based partner at international law firm Howard Kennedy, says it is easy to see why more UK graduates are looking overseas.
"When you combine student debt, high housing costs, relatively weak wage growth and uncertainty about future employment, the willingness to roll the dice somewhere else becomes quite rational."
Back in Sydney, Rachel says the city simply offers a better quality of life than London.
"I don't see life in Sydney as any more expensive than if I was in London, but personally I have found the perks in Sydney better."

articles.title: Inflation Could Climb Above 5% in Early 2027
articles.standfirst: Annual CPI inflation increased to 3.5 per cent in September from 3.1 per cent the previous month.  Monthly price growth between August and September in 2026 was high at 0.4...
paragraphs: Annual CPI inflation increased to 3.5 per cent in September from 3.1 per cent the previous month. Monthly price growth between August and September in 2026 was high at 0.4 per cent compared to 0 per cent in 2025, leading to the increase of 0.4 percentage points in annual inflation.

The monthly inflation of 0.4 per cent corresponds to an annualised rate of 4.9 per cent and flows on from the high monthly inflation of 0.5 per cent in August. This suggests that the continuing energy supply issues caused by the American war on Iran are feeding into general price inflation. These effects are likely to escalate until a resolution to the conflict is found. Under our preferred forecast scenarios, inflation looks set to reach
The Bank of England will face pressure to tighten policy as inflation continues to increase.
If we look at the broad categories of inflation over the last 12 months, we see:

Services inflation this month is pretty much in line with wage data reflecting a cooling labour market: the latest ONS figures on wage increases excluding bonuses, covering June to August 2026, came in at 3.7 per cent.
The biggest contributors to the change in headline inflation between August and September were:

However, these overall contributions combine the “base effects” of inflation dropping out from the previous year with the new inflation “dropping in”. We need to unwrap these to get the true picture. Figure 1 (below) shows the sectoral contributions to overall inflation, with the previous year’s monthly inflation dropping out (blue) and the current month’s new inflation dropping in (brown). The overall impact is the sum of the two, shown by the burgundy line.

Focusing on the new monthly inflation (brown), eight sectors registered an increase in prices this month, with two registering falls (interestingly these two were Transport and Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverages). The blue dropouts from the previous year are negative or close to zero in eight sectors, and positive in two (also Transport and Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverages). Overall, the burgundy line, showing the total effect for each sector, is significantly negative in one sector, and significantly positive in three sectors, as listed above.

We can look ahead over the next 12 months to see how inflation might evolve as the recent inflation “drops out” as we move forward month by month. Each month, the new inflation enters the annual figure and the old inflation from the same month in the previous year “drops out”. We depict the following scenarios for future inflation dropping in:

The Iran war makes the future path of inflation highly uncertain. In my initial blog, The Possible Effects on UK Inflation in 2026 of the US-Iran Conflict, published on 23 March, I contrasted the possible effects of two scenarios, a “good scenario” with a short conflict that left most of the energy infrastructure in the Gulf intact and an “ugly” scenario with a prolonged conflict in which most of the infrastructure is destroyed. With the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and now the additional closure of the Bab-el-Mandeb, we seem to be heading into the “ugly” scenario, with a major inflationary spike. In addition, the direct conflict between Saudi Arabia and Ansar Allah (the Houthis) has led to the destruction of significant pipelines and refineries in Saudi Arabia. Unless the conflicts are resolved soon, there is likely to be more inflation coming our way and also negative impacts on output and employment across much of the world as we move into 2027.

I have therefore revived our old friend from 2022, the “sanctions” scenario, now renamed the “Hormuz” scenario. This and the very high scenario seem to be most relevant at present, and we also depict the high and medium scenarios for reference. The low scenario seems unlikely to be relevant so we have not depicted it.

If we look at the very high and Hormuz scenarios, inflation might be at 4.2-4.7 per cent in December 2026. Even the medium and high scenarios suggest that inflation will be at 3.4-3.7 per cent by December. So, under all scenarios, inflation looks set to rise in the final quarter of 2026.
For further analysis of inflation in the United Kingdom, see:
Seasonal Adjustment of CPI and CPIH, Huw Dixon and Monica George Michail. NIESR Policy Paper 45, May 2025

articles.title: Japan’s low-leverage economy should withstand rate hikes
articles.standfirst: The rate hikes we expect over the next few months are unlikely to derail Japan’s economy from its modest but steady growth path. Most firms and households will be able to withstand a rise in interest rate costs thanks to their healthy balance sheets.
paragraphs: The rate hikes we expect over the next few months are unlikely to derail Japan’s economy from its modest but steady growth path. Most firms and households will be able to withstand a rise in interest rate costs thanks to their healthy balance sheets.

Most companies will likely maintain a reasonable spread between return on assets and interest rate costs thanks to their low leverage and rising profitability. However, an analysis of small firms shows that a 1ppt rise in effective interest rates could increase the share of loss-making small firms from 27% to 31%.

On aggregate, the Japanese are net savers and rate hikes will have a net positive impact by raising deposit rates. However, people in their 30s and 40s tend to be net debtors due to large, overwhelmingly floating-rate mortgages, making them vulnerable. Although higher rates will weaken already stagnant residential investment, their impact on overall economic growth should be limited.

The economy’s overall resilience to higher interest rates may allow the Bank of Japan to hike its policy rate beyond 1.75% to prevent further weakening of the yen and/or the de-anchoring of inflation expectations driven by prolonged cost-push inflation. However, the potential damage to vulnerable small firms and stretched household finances could make the government more cautious, exerting pressure on the bank.

articles.title: Expensing Concentrates the Corporate Tax Burden on Economic Profits
articles.standfirst: As scrutiny over data center investment and AI rises, some commentators are concerned about how expensing interacts with these ongoing investments. Most of these concerns misunderstand what expensing does.
paragraphs: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) improved the corporate taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. system with permanent bonus depreciationBonus depreciation allows firms to deduct a larger portion of certain “short-lived” investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings in the first year. Allowing businesses to write off more investments partially alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. for machinery and equipment investment and immediate expensing for research and development (R&D) costs. But now, as scrutiny over data center investment and AI rises, some commentators are concerned about how expensing interacts with these ongoing investments. Most of these concerns misunderstand what expensing does. Expensing stops the tax code from discouraging marginal investment, but it doesn’t subsidize investment that isn’t worthwhile on its own merits, nor does it eliminate taxes on profitable projects.

Full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. allows firms to immediately deduct what they expend on capital investment in the same year the capital investment starts being used. Aligning the timing of the deduction to the timing of the expense preserves its full value; firms fully recover investment costs, as opposed to taking deductions over time and experiencing the erosion brought on by inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin and opportunity cost. This treatment eliminates the burden of the tax system on the normal return to investment, the amount needed to break even. It does not eliminate tax on the supernormal return, which arises when firms earn economic profits.
Imagine two firms that each undertake a $100 investment in a world of 2 percent inflation and a 3 percent real discount rate (which we approximate with a 5 percent rate for simplicity).

Firm A’s investment will just break even, returning $105 in year 2, equal in present value terms to the $100 upfront cost. It’s a marginal investment, and the firm wouldn’t undertake it if the tax system imposed a burden on marginal investment. Firm B’s investment will earn economic profits, returning $110 in year 2. It is not a marginal investment, but is something so profitable the firm would undertake it even under a biased tax system.

Now we’ll add taxes, using the 21 percent corporate tax rate and an illustrative depreciationDepreciation is a measurement of the “useful life” of a business asset, such as machinery or a factory, to determine the multiyear period over which the cost of that asset can be deducted from taxable income. Instead of allowing businesses to deduct the cost of investments immediately (i.e., full expensing), depreciation requires deductions to be taken over time, reducing their value and disco system that requires the firms to use straight-line depreciation over the two-year period, deducting $50 in year 1 and the remaining $50 in year 2. Firm A’s investment broke even before taxes, but the requirement to delay depreciation deductions imposes a tax burden on the normal return to investment, making the project no longer pencil out. Firm B still clears a profit, even in the presence of depreciation.

Waiting to take the depreciation deduction in year 2 reduces its real value: the $10.50 of tax savings in year 2 ($50 depreciation deduction x 21 percent corporate rate) is only worth $10.00 today. This erosion in the real value of the deductions flips Firm A’s after-tax net present value negative, while it costs Firm B $0.50 of its after-tax net present value.

But if the tax system instead permitted the firms to deduct the investment cost upfront, the tax burden on the break-even investment would be eliminated. Firm A would break even, while Firm B still earns a profit of $3.76 in present value, down $1.00 from the no-tax scenario and up $0.50 from the depreciation scenario. Expensing concentrates the tax burden on the supernormal returnSupernormal returns are payoffs to investment greater than the typical market rate of return. They are often approximated as company profits that exceed 10 percent. This additional return on capital or labor is above breaking even on an investment relative to the amount of risk and time that investment required. (21 percent of $4.76) and leaves the normal return untaxed.

Expensing would not make an unprofitable investment worthwhile. For example, consider Firm C, with the same $100 upfront investment cost but a return of $104 in year 2. In present value, the project loses $0.95 before taxes. Under full expensing, it would still lose $0.75, so Firm C still would not invest. Expensing makes the tax code neutral toward investment; it does not turn a pre-tax loss into an after-tax gain (see the discussion on potential interactions with interest deductions below).

Table 4 separates each firm’s tax into the normal and supernormal return components. Depreciation taxes both, while expensing removes the burden on the normal return and places it entirely on the supernormal return. Expensing thus removes most of the corporate tax’s adverse impact on economic efficiency and growth, while still generating revenues from projects with positive economic profits.

Some argue that in the presence of deductions for business interest paid, full expensing more than eliminates the burden on the normal return and leads to negative effective tax rates. Under the current tax code, business interest deductions are limited to 30 percent of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA). Further, the concern over negative effective tax rates typically excludes consideration of the tax that applies to the interest income received by lenders, as Stephen J. Entin explains for Tax Foundation:

Some students of taxation claim that the two deductions result in a negative tax rate on some businesses, because between the two write-offs the business would appear to be writing off more than the cost of the asset. But that argument looks only at one side of the financial transaction (the borrower’s side) and misses a key point. The interest payment deducted from the borrower’s income is added to the lender’s income. Looking at lender and borrower together shows there is no excess deduction. Some of the earnings of the asset are passed on to be taxed on the lender’s tax form instead of on the business’s tax form. The earnings are still taxed. There is no negative tax on the investment and its returns. (Note: some limited lending comes from tax exempt groups, but their endowments are relatively inflexible and are not generally funding new investment, at the margin, which determines the amount of capital formation. The issue with the non-taxable entities is whether they deserve that status; it is not a reason to avoid expensing.)

As Entin explains elsewhere, simply disallowing interest deductions while still taxing lenders on the interest they receive would lead to double taxationDouble taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income.. Consistent reform of interest deductions would move toward cash flow taxation: either disallowing deductions for borrowers and excluding interest income for lenders, or the reverse, permitting deductions and ensuring full taxability. But reforming the treatment of interest is not a prerequisite for a tax system built on expensing.

Expensing is the right policy because it eliminates the tax burden on the normal return to investment—the margin that matters most for growing the capital stock—and it concentrates the burden of the corporate tax on economic profits. Profitable data center investment may be like the economic profits case, and expensing still taxes its economic profits in full. Expensing does not make a higher corporate tax rate fully harmless, as the statutory rate and the burden on supernormal returns affect incentives for profit shiftingProfit shifting is when multinational companies reduce their tax burden by moving the location of their profits from high-tax countries to low-tax jurisdictions and tax havens. and innovation, but it right-sizes the corporate tax system.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Erica York is Senior Economist with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Her analysis has been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The Washington Post, Politico, and other national and international media outlets.

articles.title: 2026 Economics Nobel Laureate Robert Hall Helped Lay Foundation for Pro-Growth Tax Reform
articles.standfirst: Hall’s research helped economists understand how taxes distort investment decisions, while his work with Rabushka shows how to minimize those distortions. Although the US remains far from a pure consumption tax, Hall’s work informs efforts to reduce the tax burden on investment, improve neutrality, and promote long-run economic growth.
paragraphs: Last week, economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.” The award recognizes their foundational contributions to New Keynesian macroeconomics, including how individual decisions by households and businesses shape broader economic outcomes.

Robert Hall is also well known in the taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. policy world. In a landmark 1967 paper written with Dale Jorgenson, Hall helped establish how tax policy affects business investment decisions. Businesses invest when the expected return exceeds the cost of depreciationDepreciation is a measurement of the “useful life” of a business asset, such as machinery or a factory, to determine the multiyear period over which the cost of that asset can be deducted from taxable income. Instead of allowing businesses to deduct the cost of investments immediately (i.e., full expensing), depreciation requires deductions to be taken over time, reducing their value and disco, financing, and taxes. This combined hurdle is known as the user cost of capital.

The Hall-Jorgenson framework shows quantitatively how tax policy can impact both the level and timing of business investment, providing the foundation for why delaying depreciation deductions raises the cost of investment by raising the cost of capital. Immediate expensing, on the other hand, removes the tax penalty on marginal investment imposed by inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin and the time value of money.

Additionally, Hall is known for being the co-author of the Hall-Rabushka flat tax. While some focus on the tax proposal’s flat rate design—the original proposal used a 19 percent flat taxAn income tax is referred to as a “flat tax” when all taxable income is subject to the same tax rate, regardless of income level or assets. rate—it is also, at its core, a tax aimed at consumption.

Policymakers can target a consumption taxA consumption tax is typically levied on the purchase of goods or services and is paid directly or indirectly by the consumer in the form of retail sales taxes, excise taxes, tariffs, value-added taxes (VAT), or income taxes where all savings are tax-deductible. base in many different ways; a value-added tax (VAT) targets value added at each stage of production, while the Hall-Rabushka flat tax splits the base out to tax businesses on their cash flow and individuals on their wages.

Businesses deduct the cost of investment and households pay tax on wages above an exemption, without being taxed twice on investment returns such as interest, dividends, and capital gains. The proposal therefore eliminates the income tax’s bias against saving and investment by providing expensing and avoiding additional taxes on investment returns.

Hall and Rabushka’s work inspired subsequent proposals to tax consumption progressively, including the X-tax proposed by economist David Bradford. The X-tax keeps a cash flow tax for businesses and applies a graduated tax rate for household wages with a top household rate matching the business tax rate. This design helped inform the design of destination-based cash flow taxes (DBCFTs) as a policy option to reform the business tax code.

While the US remains a hybrid tax system between income and consumption tax bases, Hall’s tax policy legacy contributed to the policy motivation behind the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which moved the US tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. toward consumption by reviving 100 percent bonus depreciationBonus depreciation allows firms to deduct a larger portion of certain “short-lived” investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings in the first year. Allowing businesses to write off more investments partially alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs.. The 2025 reconciliation law made 100 percent bonus depreciation permanent and restored domestic R&D expensing, keeping that progress in the tax code.

Hall’s research helped economists understand how taxes distort investment decisions, while his work with Rabushka shows how to minimize those distortions. Although the US remains far from a pure consumption tax, Hall’s work informs efforts to reduce the tax burden on investment, improve neutrality, and promote long-run economic growth.

Garrett Watson is Vice President of Federal Tax Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. His work has been featured in The Washington Post, The Atlantic, Politico, the Associated Press and other major outlets.

articles.title: The Return of the Energy Shock
articles.standfirst: In this blog we present updated forecasts from our Multi-Recurrent Neural Network (MRN) model, extending the outlook from September 2026 to August 2027.1 This is our fourth MRN update of...
paragraphs: In this blog we present updated forecasts from our Multi-Recurrent Neural Network (MRN) model, extending the outlook from September 2026 to August 2027.1 This is our fourth MRN update of the year, following the February, May and July 2026 blogs. Three things have changed since July:

The July blog made a testable claim: our recommended Intermediate Energy MRN projected 3.0 per cent for June 2026, easing to 2.7 per cent by August, before rising to a 4.5 per cent peak in February 2027. The outturns were 2.6 per cent in June and 3.1 per cent in August. The model was 0.4 percentage points too high in June and 0.4 points too low in August, and the sign of the error flipped exactly as the geopolitics did. In June the peace announcement was pulling energy prices down faster than the model’s training data allowed for; by August the collapse of that deal was pushing them up faster. We flagged the first possibility explicitly in July (“a June print materially below this range would suggest the peace-deal energy price fall is passing through faster than the model anticipates”). We did not anticipate the second, and nor, on the evidence of its July Report, did the Bank of England, whose central projection assumed oil prices would drift from $76 to $71, and inflation would peak at 3.2 per cent in the fourth quarter of 2026. Two lessons follow. The first is that the MRN carries no oil price assumption at all; it extrapolates from the energy history it has seen. So its twelve-month path is best read as an unconditional projection of where the data were pointing at end-August. The Bank’s and NIESR’s forecasts are conditional on an assumed path for oil prices. Part of the gap between us is therefore a difference in what is being forecast, not only in how; the fair test is whether the unconditional path keeps moving the right way when the world moves, as it did between June and August. The second is that readers of our May blog will recall that the then-current MRN had inflation “well beyond 5 per cent in early 2027”; the July update, trained during the brief peace, pulled that back to 4.5 per cent. The present round returns to the May reading.

Figure 1 shows the current forecast of two classes of MRN model: the Simple Energy + MPC MRN, which uses CPI level and month-on-month change, ONS UK energy CPI, the monthly Brent average and, new in this round, Bank Rate; and the Intermediate Energy MRN, which adds real GDP, PPI, the 10-year gilt yield and the sterling effective exchange rate to that set. The Intermediate Energy MRN projects annual CPI inflation of 3.7 per cent in September 2026, 4.1 per cent in November, 4.4 per cent in December, and then a step up to 5.4 per cent in January 2027, holding at 5.4 per cent in February and March before easing to 4.3–4.4 per cent in April–May and drifting back up to 4.9 per cent by July and August 2027. The Simple Energy + MPC MRN follows a similar path but peaks later and higher, at 5.7 per cent in June 2027. The Average MRN peaks at 5.3 per cent in February and does not fall below 4.5 per cent at any point in the forecast window. The quarterly averages are 3.9, 5.2 and 4.8 per cent for the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first two quarters of 2027, respectively.

We must state two things about this path clearly. The first is that the peak has moved up by almost a full percentage point since July, from 4.5 per cent to 5.4 per cent, while its timing has stayed put in the first quarter of 2027. That revision is almost entirely the energy channel doing what it is designed to do: the price of Brent crude oil is 50 per cent higher than when the July models were trained, UK wholesale gas prices have risen 78 per cent since the Bank’s July Report, and the Ofgem energy price cap has gone from £1,477 in Q2 to £1,663 in Q3 and £1,723 for October–December, with Cornwall Insight now forecasting £1,999, a 16 per cent rise, for January 2027. The second is that part of the January step is arithmetic rather than economics. The CPI fell by 0.5 per cent month-on-month in January 2026; so, roughly half a point of the first quarter peak is that base effect. It is real, in the sense that the headline rate will print it, but it does not imply a fresh burst of price pressure in that month.

This is the first round in which we forecast the policy rate, and the two classes disagree in a way we think is informative rather than embarrassing. The Simple Energy + MPC MRN, which sees inflation, energy and the rate itself, but nothing of the real economy, has Bank Rate rising from 3.75 per cent to 4.0 per cent by February 2027 and 4.5 per cent by June. The Intermediate Energy MRN, which also sees GDP, producer prices, gilt yields and sterling, has it falling to 3.5 per cent by November, 3.25 per cent by January and 3.0 per cent by March, before settling at 3.25 per cent. The average of the two dips to 3.5 per cent through the winter, touches 3.25 per cent in March, and is back at 3.75 per cent by June 2027.

Read the two classes as the two sides of the Monetary Policy Committee’s own argument. At its 17 September meeting the Committee held at 3.75 per cent by six votes to three, with Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill voting for an immediate quarter-point increase on the grounds that slack “may have already peaked” and that raising rates is “a better risk-management strategy when faced with uncertainty about inflation dynamics and second-round effects”. The six who held pointed to “very limited evidence of emerging second-round effects” and to slack “still evident in a range of indicators”, with Alan Taylor arguing that policy “should respond to evidence of propagation rather than mechanically to volatile ticks in headline energy prices”. The Simple class, which has no measure of slack and reacts to headline energy, is the hawkish minority’s direction of travel. The Intermediate class, which can see weak activity and the restrictiveness of financial conditions, is the majority’s. We do not claim the network understands this debate; we claim that the two feature sets encode the two positions, and that is exactly why we report both rather than only the average.

The September 2026 inflation number from the ONS is due on 21 October and is the first direct test of these forecasts. The Intermediate Energy MRN projects 3.7 per cent, the Simple Energy + MPC MRN 3.9 per cent and the Average 3.8 per cent, all well above August’s 3.1 per cent, reflecting the motor-fuel surge the Bank has already documented. A September number in the 3.6–3.9 per cent range would validate the near-term path; something nearer 3.3 per cent would suggest the VAT cut and the G7 reserve release are biting faster than the model allows. The second test is the 6 November MPC decision: the Simple MRN class implies the hawks gain ground, the Intermediate MRN class implies the first cut arrives by November, and the two cannot both be right. The third is the Ofgem announcement for January 2027, due in late November, which will fix the single biggest input into our peak in the first quarter of 2027. The IMF’s October World Economic Outlook and the NIESR Autumn Economic Outlook both appear before our next update, and we will report how the MRN stands against their revised paths.

1 The modelling approach is described in Binner, J. M., Kelly, L. J. and Tepper, J. A. (2025) ‘Professional Forecasters vs. Shallow Neural Network Ensembles: Assessing Inflation Prediction Accuracy’, Journal of Risk and Financial Management, 18(4), 173 (MRN methodology). https://doi.org/10.3390/jrfm18040173.
