articles.title: Is the minimum wage to blame for falling youth employment?
articles.standfirst:
This blog was originaly published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack.  Once a year the Low Pay Commission (LPC) assemble in their Canary Wharf office to decide the following year’s minimum wage rates. I went along to share my thoughts on falling youth employment. I said that we can’t confidently blame the minimum wage. But the … Continued
The post Is the minimum wage to blame for falling youth employment? appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: This blog was originaly published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack.

Once a year the Low Pay Commission (LPC) assemble in their Canary Wharf office to decide the following year’s minimum wage rates. I went along to share my thoughts on falling youth employment. I said that we can’t confidently blame the minimum wage. But the LPC should still tread carefully and refrain from shrinking the gap between the youth rate and the adult rate next year.
Youth employment rates are ringing alarm bells, having fallen further than for older workers in recent years, as shown below.1

Employment rates among 18-24 and 25-64-year-olds fully recovered after Covid, but the trend for young people then diverged. The youth employment rate fell from 2022 onwards, now standing almost 6 per cent below 2019 levels. By contrast, the rate among 25-64-year-olds held up, reached a new high in 2023, and only then drifted down to 1 per cent below 2019 levels.
Before we get to the minimum wage, it’s worth heading off some challenges to this negative picture.

Firstly – it’s not about studying. Student numbers are flat. This means that the share of young people not in employment or education (the NEET rate) has almost certainly been rising – which is also what the LFS tells us.

What about population growth? If the employment rate is jobs divided by people, then maybe it’s more people, not fewer jobs? If we focus on the numerator for a moment – the number of jobs – it looks like there might be some truth to that. The number of 18-24-year-olds in PAYE employment recovered post Covid and then stayed pretty flat.

Flat jobs and a rising population might be less worrying if we thought the population increase was coming from groups we’d expect to work at lower rates. We know there’s been high migration recently – so maybe it’s just that lots of people arrived with low employment rates?

But that’s not what’s been happening. Firstly, the number of jobs held by young UK nationals has been falling since 2022 – it’s not that population growth from overseas is making a flat picture on jobs look bad.2

Second, the number of UK nationals has probably been growing since 2022, due to a mini baby boom twenty years ago.3 This means jobs among UK nationals would have had to have been growing since 2022 for the employment picture to be stable among that group.

So, the picture is pretty much the same as where we started. There has been a serious fall in youth employment since 2022, which isn’t accounted for by rising education participation, or by population or migration changes.
Honestly, we don’t have great answers. Lots of the obvious candidates don’t line up neatly with a deterioration that began in 2022.

Earlier in the year we dug into rising NEET rates and found that half of the post-2019 increase can be put down to a general labour market slowdown. The rest seems to be to worsening health, but that’s a slower moving trend, not something that accelerated in 2022 specifically. It’s tempting to reach for AI as an explanation, but Claude and ChatGPT weren’t very widely used until fairly recently, so they don’t really help with the 2022 question.

What about the minimum wage? There have certainly been big increases. Between April 2022 and April 2026, average weekly earnings rose 24 per cent, the adult minimum wage rose 34 per cent, and the older youth rate rose 59 per cent.

Lots of people have put two and two together: the minimum wage went up, youth employment went down, what more do you need to see? Well plenty else changed over that period, and it’s hard to strip that out. The IFS did some great analysis on the recent youth rate changes and couldn’t rule out a zero effect. And you find zero effects in some other studies.

What if this is all structural change, not policy? Perhaps the shape of the economy shifted against the young. Retail and wholesale jobs never recovered post-Covid and have been falling since 2022, while hospitality jobs have fallen since 2023. Together those sectors account for 2-in-5 youth jobs, and they stopped adding jobs just as more young people needed work. You can tell a story of big forces here: online shopping; automated warehouses; and a preference for screens to seeing our mates.

But maybe the minimum wage is why they shrank – it makes what they sell more expensive and causes firms to save on low-wage (disproportionately young) labour. That said, it’s not true that recent job shedding is all happening in low-paid sectors. This implies that either recent sectoral changes aren’t being driven by policies affecting low-paid labour costs (like the minimum wage, and employer NICs), or that those policies are having an effect, but there just happen to be other drivers affecting higher-paying sectors at the same time.
So, what to do if you are the Low Pay Commission? They have to make an actual pounds and pence decision for next year’s minimum wage rates – they can’t get away with the hand waving I’ve done here.

I think in the face of big uncertainty about policy effects, and when the labour market is weak, the right choice is caution. We can’t say that the minimum wage is causing the youth employment downturn. But absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. And with the UK’s high minimum wage rates, low hourly pay isn’t the problem it once was. So, I think the LPC should avoid another convergence hike to the youth rates this year.

One LPC Commissioner looked me in the eye and said give me a number. I’d eaten several of their biscuits so I could hardly say no. So my specific recommendation for 2027 was to uprate the whole framework – the adult rate and the youth rates – in line with average wages.

1 Data aside #1: I say ‘employment rate’ because we are using proxies based on tax and population data, because the ONS’s LFS still isn’t very useful for monitoring trends. The 18-24 rate is simply PAYE jobs among this age group divided by the population. This means it doesn’t include any self-employed people in that age group, but there aren’t many so that’s ok. The 25-64 rate nets 18-24-year-olds off the fully-fledged estimates we produce for 16-64-year-old employment rates which do include self-employment.

2 Data aside #2: These charts are counting PAYE jobs not people – because that’s what HMRC published – and there’s a probable discontinuity in 2021 from IR35 changes boosting the number of PAYE jobs per person in the PAYE system. But it’s safe to look at trends before and after this point.

3 Data aside #3: Unfortunately, as far as I’m aware the ONS doesn’t publish population by age by nationality explicitly. But we can make a reasonable guess by ageing forward younger cohorts (specifically – we add up the population aged 16 from previous years). This will differ from the true change in 18-24 UK nationals to the extent that the non-UK share of 16-year-olds and net migration patterns among young UK nationals have changed in this period.

articles.title: Does falling migration spell trouble for the Budget?
articles.standfirst:
Migration rates to the UK are falling. That might sound politically advantageous for a government that is trying to show it has immigration under control, but some argue that it could in fact spell economic trouble for the upcoming Budget. Alan Manning looks at how much reduced migration has cost compared to how much it … Continued
The post Does falling migration spell trouble for the Budget? first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: Migration rates to the UK are falling. That might sound politically advantageous for a government that is trying to show it has immigration under control, but some argue that it could in fact spell economic trouble for the upcoming Budget. Alan Manning looks at how much reduced migration has cost compared to how much it has saved the state.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

As the new Budget looms, and the Government seems to have little room for fiscal manoeuvre, there have been a flurry of articles about whether the reductions in net migration have worsened the situation. On 28 September the Times published an article headlined “Falling migration gives John Healey a headroom headache” suggesting that lower migration could cost the government as much as £7bn. The next day the Guardian published an article with the headline “Cutting immigration to the UK means billions less for the Treasury. Can the country really afford that?”.

The £7bn is probably based on estimates derived from the OBR’s Economic and Fiscal Outlook for March 2024. Like all such numbers it is based on assumptions which, in turn, may not be based on very strong evidence. Migrants will typically pay taxes but also consume public services and may receive welfare benefits (though many new migrants are ineligible for these). There are a number of reasons to think the £7bn is too high.

First, the OBR itself came to recognise that migration required more public expenditure that its March 2024 estimates implied if it was not to have some implicit austerity. In their September 2024 Fiscal risks and sustainability report, the OBR argued that extra public investment of £20k per person would be needed to maintain the public sector capital stock (the hospitals, schools roads etc) in per capita terms (though they also gave some reasons why this might be too high). But if migration is 100k lower for 5 years, then the saving from lower required public sector investment would be £10bn(100k migrants requires investment of £2bn, multiplied by 5 years) – i.e. this could conceivably wipe out the £7bn cost in the March 2024 estimates. At the very least it substantially reduces it.

The March 2024 OBR estimates also do not take into account who the migrants are, how much they work and how much they earn. They assume migrants are the same as the average Brit of the same age and sex (broadly consistent with the data we have). But migrants vary a lot in their employment and earnings, so it’s important to think about the types of migrants that make up the reduction in net migration. The big reductions in migration have come from falls in care workers and their dependents, the dependents of Masters’ students, some family, nurses, and some other work migrants (mostly the lower-paid). Since the 2024 OBR report we know the first three groups have low levels of earnings, in some cases not much above minimum wage and that lower-paid migrants are more likely to stay. Taking account of this would again reduce the cost of the reduction in migration, though how much is uncertain, given the data. What’s more, nurses’ salaries are paid by the Government, so there is an extra expenditure associated with them.

The OBR estimates may also be optimistic in their baseline assumption that investment responds positively to higher migration, leaving the long-run capital-labour ratio unaffected. If this was right, we should be in the middle of an investment boom right now – net migration was about 2.5 per cent of population in 2021/23 – if the capital-output ratio is about 4 this requires extra investment of 10 per cent of GDP to maintain the capital labour ratio. But we do not seem to be experiencing an investment boom. The latest flash productivity estimates show productivity per worker falling in the period of very high net migration and now growing again with lower migration. Some commentators are arguing that higher productivity growth is because of the type of reductions in migration– I don’t think we have enough evidence to be so confident but it is an argument that needs to be taken seriously and, if true, also implies that the fiscal cost of reductions in net migration is much lower than thought, perhaps not negative at all.

Our data and knowledge is simply not good enough to be very confident about the fiscal consequences of the recent reductions in net migration. The £7bn cost is almost certainly a large over-estimate and it is conceivable there is actually a benefit. Even if the reductions in net migration have a small fiscal cost over the forecast horizon they are of migrants who, on average, are likely to be fiscally negative over their lifetime. Immigration of this type is akin to borrowing – it gives you more resources today at the expense of less in the future. Where fiscal rules constrain literal borrowing this migration as disguised borrowing has been an attractive policy for successive governments. But this would not be the first government if it succumbed to the temptations of short-termism.
Enjoyed this post? Sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.
All articles posted on this blog give the views of the author(s), and not the position of LSE British Politics and Policy, nor of the London School of Economics and Political Science.

Alan Manning is Professor of Economics in the Department of Economics at LSE, and co-director of the community wellbeing programme at LSE Centre for Economic Performance. His research generally covers labour markets, with a focus on imperfect competition (monopsony), minimum wages, job polarisation, immigration, and gender.

articles.title: The Model Assistant in action: What would an escalating Iran war mean for bond yields?
articles.standfirst: We ask our Model Agent what would happen if the war escalates again. Here are the results.
paragraphs: In Part 1 of this series, we introduced the AskOEAI Model Assistant, the world’s first AI assistant for scenario modelling, and explained why we built it. In this post, we put it to work on a question many of our clients are asking right now: what would a renewed escalation of the war in Iran mean for the global economy, and for government bond yields in particular?

The war in Iran has already pushed up energy prices and unsettled financial markets. Renewed attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure in the Gulf have lifted oil prices, and global bond markets have sold off sharply. The US 10-year Treasury yield has climbed above 5% for the first time since 2007, and the Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September for the first time since 2023, as we discuss in our latest analysis of the bond sell-off.

Our baseline forecast already reflects the conflict and the market moves seen so far. What many clients want to know is what happens if the war escalates again: how far could energy prices rise, how would inflation and central banks respond, and how much higher could bond yields go? So we asked the Model Assistant, walking through four simple steps:
We started with a single prompt: “Model a scenario of new and sustained escalations in the war in Iran”

We didn’t specify any indicators, shock sizes or timings. In its first response, the assistant pulled in the most relevant Oxford Economics research and set out a complete first draft of the scenario.

The assistant based its calibration on the downside case from our research on a prolonged Iran war, which points to sustained energy disruption, higher inflation risk premia and increased long-term borrowing costs. It translated these channels into four shocks, starting in Q4 2026 (Table 1).
Each input comes with a short rationale and a preview chart showing how the scenario path compares with our baseline.

Once we’re happy with the inputs, a single click on Solve runs the scenario through the GEM. The shocks feed through trade, prices, financial markets and policy responses across economies, and the results are automatically benchmarked against our latest baseline.

Once the scenario had solved, we asked for the impact on US yields, and the assistant returned a chart and a short summary. In our scenario, US 10-year government bond yields are 0.78 percentage points above baseline at their widest gap, in 2028Q2. Higher energy prices and supply-chain stress create inflation pressure and prompt a tighter monetary policy stance, keeping risk premia elevated, lifting yields and tightening financial conditions.
The assistant’s analysis pointed to a tighter monetary policy stance as a key factor behind the initial rise in yields.
To understand this better, we asked the Model Agent: “How does the Fed react?”

Based on our initial assumptions, the assistant gave a concise description of the Fed’s “stagflationary trade-off”, along with further research to review. Higher inflation creates pressure to raise rates, while weaker growth and a softer labour market subsequently lead to rate cuts. This Taylor-rule mechanism drives policy-rate dynamics in the GEM, but users can take their own view and add a new assumption.

A scenario is rarely complete in one go. Having reviewed the results, we assumed a more hawkish Fed reaction: “Assume the Fed is more hawkish, raising rates by 50bps above the baseline until the energy shock subsides.”
The assistant added a fifth shock, raising the US policy rate by 0.5 percentage points above baseline from 2026Q4 to 2027Q4, until the energy shocks fade.
Adding the assumption means solving the scenario again, which takes a single click, and each version is traceable in the chat.

With a more hawkish Fed, US bond yields rise more quickly and stay higher for longer than in our first run. Comparing the two gives a range of ‘what-if’ outcomes under different assumptions, all built through conversation with the Model Assistant.

In four steps, we went from a topical question to a fully modelled scenario grounded in our research, complete with charts and an explanation of the results. We didn’t need to know which variables to shock, by how much, or how to set up the model inputs. Every assumption was transparent and open to change, so we could question the results, adjust the shocks and re-solve within the same conversation.

The Model Assistant is designed to make scenario analysis quicker and open to more people, with economic judgement staying firmly with the user. To find out more about the problem it solves and what sets it apart from general-purpose AI tools, read part 1 of the series.
The Model Assistant is available as an add-on to the Global Economic Model. To see it in action, click here to request a demo.

articles.title: Introducing the Model Assistant: from ‘what if’ to modelled insight
articles.standfirst: Our Model Assistant brings our economic research and modelling expertise into a conversational workflow, helping clients move more quickly from “what if” to a rigorous, quantified assessment of the impact.
paragraphs: When markets shift, policies change or geopolitical risks emerge, the first question is usually “what if?” What if oil prices spike again? What if a trade war escalates? What if bond yields keep rising? Answering those questions rigorously means building a macroeconomic scenario, a job that has traditionally required specialist modelling skills most teams don’t have on hand. Our new AskOEAI Model Assistant changes that.

Scenario analysis sits at the heart of good planning and risk management. Risk managers use it to stress-test portfolios, strategy teams to prepare for contingencies, and investment analysts to judge how exposed their views are to a change in the outlook. But turning a “what if” into a credible, quantified scenario has historically been challenging and time consuming.

First, you need to know which levers to pull. Our Global Economic Model (GEM) contains thousands of variables, but a subset of these are the key ones to generate complete economic scenarios with full transmissions. Second, you need to know how big the shock should be and how long it should last, which depends on research and judgement about how similar events have played out. Third, you need to know how to set up the inputs, solve the model and interpret the results.

For many of the people who rely on scenarios, that has made timely analysis hard to come by. Even experienced modellers can spend much of their time identifying the right indicators and building inputs before any analysis begins, which limits how many scenarios they can explore.

“Organisations need to explore how different economic shocks could affect their decisions, particularly when uncertainty is high. The challenge is turning those questions into scenarios that can be modelled and benchmarked quickly and easily. The Model Assistant brings our economic research and modelling expertise into a conversational workflow, helping clients move more quickly from “what if” to a rigorous, quantified assessment of the impact.” — Neil Walker, Head of Macro Modelling, Oxford Economics

The Model Assistant is the world’s first AI assistant for scenario modelling. It lets you build and run macroeconomic scenarios in the GEM through conversation, with no specialist modelling knowledge required. The workflow has four steps:

General-purpose AI tools can talk fluently about economics. Ask one what an escalation in the Middle East might mean for bond yields and you will get a plausible-sounding answer. But the numbers are not produced by a validated economic model and the assumptions are hard to trace. Our economists and AI experts built the Model Assistant to close that gap, with the work focusing in four key areas：

The Model Assistant is designed for anyone who needs scenario analysis but do not have technical model expertise: risk managers, investment analysts, portfolio teams, strategy and planning teams, and consultants. They know the question they want to answer, and the assistant bridges the gap between that idea and model-ready inputs.

The second is existing GEM users, from economists to model specialists, who want to speed up routine scenario setup. For them, the assistant produces a first-draft scenario in minutes, making it easy to test multiple shocks and freeing up time for interpretation and discussion with stakeholders.

The assistant is built for high-level narrative scenarios and for testing many “what ifs” quickly. Complex bespoke exercises, such as regulatory stress tests or detailed geopolitical scenarios that need client-specific calibration, still benefit from tailored work, and our economists and consultants are always available to help.

In part 2 of this series, we put the Model Assistant to work on a question many of our clients are asking right now: what would a renewed escalation of the war in Iran mean for the global economy and for government bond yields? We walk through each step, from a single prompt to a solved scenario, and show how we refined it through conversation. To read on, find it here.
The Model Assistant is available as an add-on to the Global Economic Model. To see it in action, click here to request a demo.

articles.title: Amendment 3: A Restructuring of Florida’s Local Tax Base
articles.standfirst: Florida has long maintained one of the nation’s most competitive state tax codes, but a fundamental change proposed by Amendment 3 could undermine that competitiveness.
paragraphs: Florida currently maintains one of the nation’s most competitive tax systems. It imposes no individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source and relies relatively less on property taxes than many competing states. Under its current tax structure, Florida has been able to maintain a competitive tax code that attracts individuals and businesses to the state while also investing in the public infrastructure, services, and amenities that help make the state a desirable place to live in, visit, and start and grow a business.

Florida voters are being asked to consider Amendment 3, a constitutional amendment that would substantially increase the state’s current homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes. Amendment 3 would also require the legislature to enact a law prescribing a procedure by which counties and municipalities could increase the amount of assessed value exemption from taxation, up to all remaining assessed value. While the amendment would provide meaningful property tax relief for many homeowners, its fiscal and economic consequences would impact all Floridians.

Amendment 3 would eliminate a significant portion of the local property tax base but not the underlying cost of local public services. As a result, Amendment 3 would create pressures for local governments to shift tax burdens, increase reliance on alternative revenue sources, reduce services, or pursue some combination of all three. This fundamental restructuring of Florida’s local tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. would come with significant fiscal and economic trade-offs that voters should consider.

Florida’s tax code has consistently ranked among the nation’s most competitive, placing it in the top five in nearly every edition of the Tax Foundation’s State Tax Competitiveness Index and its predecessor, the State Business Tax Climate Index, dating back to its inception in 2003.[1]

Research on state tax structures has found that income taxes are among the most economically harmful forms of taxation, as they can reduce incentives to work, invest, and start and grow businesses.[2] Florida imposes no state individual income tax and maintains a relatively competitive 5.5 percent corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. rate. Furthermore, Florida’s combined state and local sales taxA sales tax is levied on retail sales of goods and services and, ideally, should apply to all final consumption with few exemptions. Many governments exempt goods like groceries; base broadening, such as including groceries, could keep rates lower. A sales tax should exempt business-to-business transactions which, when taxed, cause tax pyramiding. rate of 6.98 percent is lower than those levied in many other southern states, including its neighbors Alabama and Georgia, whose average combined rates are 9.46 percent and 7.56 percent, respectively.[3]

Florida’s competitiveness is rooted not only in its relatively low tax burdens, but also in a revenue structure that has provided sufficient funding for local infrastructure, public safety, and other public services that contribute to strong communities and a favorable business climate.

Without question, Florida is a popular destination for tourists, workers, retirees, second homeowners, and entrepreneurs. The strong in-migration of residents, the relocation of businesses from other states, and in-state business expansion have contributed to the state’s economic success. A consequence of that success has been a competitive housing market and the resulting rapid growth in property values. As property values have risen, so has the property tax burden for many homeowners, despite existing constitutional protections. This is especially true for new and first-time homeowners. Florida’s existing assessment limit, Save Our Homes (SOH), has exacerbated the problem. Nearly identical properties on the same street can have significantly different tax burdens based solely on when the property was purchased or how long the occupants have been Florida homeowners.

Against this backdrop, voters will consider Amendment 3 on November 3, 2026.[4] If approved by at least 60 percent of voters, the measure would mark one of the most consequential fiscal policy changes in modern Florida history. The proposal seeks to reduce property tax burdens faced by owners of primary residences who have experienced substantial increases in property values and other broader cost-of-living pressures.

Under current law, Florida homeowners who qualify for a homestead exemption receive an exemption from all property taxes levied on the first $25,000 of assessed value.[5] A second inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin-adjusted exemption of $25,000 (equal to $26,411 in 2026) applies to assessed value beginning at $50,000 but does not apply to school district property taxes.[6] As a result, a homestead property with an assessed value of at least $76,411 receives a total exemption of $51,411 in 2026 for non-school district property taxes.

Amendment 3 would maintain the existing $25,000 homestead exemption for school district property taxes. For all other property taxes, the amendment would increase the homestead exemption to $150,000 beginning in 2027, and to $250,000 beginning in 2028. Starting in 2029, the $250,000 exemption would be adjusted annually for inflation. To qualify for the increased exemption, a property owner must have established a permanent Florida residency as of December 31, 2026.

Property owners who establish a homestead on or after January 1, 2027, would be eligible for the $25,000 homestead exemption for school district taxes. For all other levies, however, they would be limited to a $50,000 homestead exemption for the first five years of ownership. After the five-year period, new owners would become eligible for the larger exemption available to existing homestead owners.

Amendment 3 would also direct the legislature to establish a uniform procedure for counties and municipalities to increase the exemption, if they choose, to any higher level, up to the exclusion of all homestead property value.

Florida’s homestead exemption serves as a gateway to an additional property tax relief benefit: the SOH assessment limitation.[7] Under SOH, the assessed value of a homestead property may increase by no more than 3 percent per year, or the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index (CPI), whichever is lower. Over time, market value may increase faster than assessed value. Many long-term owners have assessed values that are substantially below the market value of their homes.

The difference between the property’s assessed value and market value is referred to as the SOH benefit. As the benefit accumulates over time, a homeowner pays taxes on an increasingly smaller share of the property’s market value. Therefore, a homestead exemption measured against the assessed value can provide a larger tax benefit than its dollar amount may initially suggest. A $250,000 exemption would represent a much larger share of taxable value for a long-term homeowner whose assessed value has been constrained by SOH than for a recently purchased home with an assessed value much closer to market value.

A portability provision in the SOH assessment limit allows most Florida homestead owners to transfer up to $500,000 of accumulated SOH benefit to a new homestead property.[8] If the market value of the new homestead is equal to or greater than that of the previous homestead, the owner may transfer the full accumulated benefit up to the $500,000 cap. If the market value of the new homestead is lower, the transferred benefit is reduced proportionally. Amendment 3 would preserve both the SOH assessment limit and the portability provision. Because long-term homeowners accumulate larger SOH benefits, portability reduces the property tax increase that would otherwise occur when they relocate within Florida.

For property that does not qualify for a homestead exemption, current law limits annual increases in assessed value to 10 percent.[9] Amendment 3 would reduce this assessment limitation to 5 percent beginning in 2027. As under current law, a property’s assessed value would continue to reset to just value, or market value, when ownership changes.

Collectively, these provisions would substantially reduce taxable value for many residential properties while slowing taxable value growth for non-homestead property. The result would be a significantly smaller property tax base available to finance local government services. Understanding the implications of reducing the property tax base requires an examination of the fiscal stability of the property tax and the role it plays in financing local governments.

The property tax aligns closely with the benefit principle of taxation, under which taxpayers help finance the public services from which they benefit. Local government services such as public safety, infrastructure, schools, and other amenities make neighborhoods desirable and enhance property values. Through the property tax, homeowners help finance local services, and in turn, receive corresponding benefits through enhanced property values and quality of life.

For example, homeowners value safety and security, so homes located in communities known for providing quality fire and police protection tend to be more desirable. The market values also reflect the services provided to those homes. More desirable properties lend themselves to higher property values. Because the property tax finances services that are delivered locally and reflected in local property values, it creates a direct relationship between taxpayers, the benefits they receive, and the officials responsible for providing those services. This connection reinforces local accountability in a way that many alternative revenue sources cannot.

Economic literature consistently identifies the property tax as one of the most stable sources of local government revenue. Several characteristics contribute to this stability, including the immobility of the tax base, the resiliency of property values, the diversification of property types, and the tax’s limited effect on economic decision-making.

A key advantage of the property tax is that real property is immobile. Land cannot be relocated, and most structures are not easily moved. This immobility makes tax avoidance difficult and the tax base more reliable. In contrast, increases in state and local sales tax rates could encourage consumers to shift purchasing to lower-tax jurisdictions, leading to more revenue volatility.

In their 2021 report evaluating revenue options for local governments, tax policy experts Adam Langley and Joan Youngman note that the property tax is not only the primary source of local government revenue, but it is also the best tax option available to them.[10] They note that a stable revenue source lessens the need to cut essential public services during economic downturns, often when the need for public services is increased.

Property values are less volatile compared to wages, business profits, and retail activity. During economic downturns, wages, employment, corporate earnings, and consumer spending can decline rapidly, resulting in corresponding reductions in income and sales tax revenues. The existing stock of homes, commercial buildings, and industrial facilities cannot be laid off or temporarily stop existing. Moreover, property values tend to reflect market changes with a delay, and as a result, they adjust more slowly. Because of this lag, the property tax base is less cyclical and less volatile, making the property tax a more predictable revenue stream, which helps to lessen fiscal disruptions during economic downturns.

Homeowners, in turn, benefit from the stability of the property tax and its more predictable revenue streams because it allows local governments to maintain public safety, infrastructure, emergency response, and other essential services without service disruptions.

The composition of the property tax base further enhances its stability. Local property tax rolls are constituted by a mix of properties across a variety of classifications, including residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, and utility properties. A decrease in the aggregate assessed value of one class of property may not equally coincide with changes in valuations of the other property types. A decline in one segment of the tax base could be offset by increases or relative resiliency in others, thereby reducing the likelihood of large fluctuations in overall taxable value. This diversification makes the property tax base less volatile.

The stability of the property tax is important because many local governments rely on various forms of state aid. State revenues are more sensitive to economic conditions because of states’ reliance on income and sales taxes. In Florida, the state’s sales tax accounts for approximately 64 percent of its own-source state tax collections.[11] During an economic downturn, decreased consumer spending could lead to lower sales tax collections, placing pressure on the state budget. The result could be reductions in state aid to Florida’s local governments.

Beyond local accountability and revenue stability, the property tax is one of the more economically efficient forms of taxation. Taxes imposed on income, business activity, or consumption may alter behavior by discouraging work, investment, entrepreneurship, or spending. Property taxes generally have a smaller effect on these economic decisions.

Property taxes generally have a smaller effect on decisions involving labor force participation, savings, business formation, and capital investment than income taxes. Income taxes disincentivize work and investment because additional earnings are subject to taxation. In contrast, property taxes are imposed primarily on land and structures, assets that already exist, rather than income production.

Similar considerations apply when comparing property taxes with sales taxes. Property taxes have less influence on decisions regarding where to purchase everyday consumer goods. Jurisdictions with high sales tax rates could experience less retail activity as consumers are more likely to engage in cross-jurisdiction shopping.

The economic efficiency of the property tax contributes to a more competitive state and local tax structure. Because the property tax imposes fewer distortions on economic decision-making than taxes on income, business activity, or consumption, it allows local governments to raise revenue without disincentivizing work and investment. With the property tax as the major source of local government funding, there is a reduced need for higher taxes on labor, entrepreneurship, capital formation, and consumer spending, all of which are more sensitive to tax rates and can influence economic behavior. As a result, the property tax can help support a more competitive economic environment while still providing a stable source of revenue for Florida’s local governments.

Property taxes are the cornerstone of local government revenues across the country. In Florida, they are the largest source of revenue for local governments, accounting for 41.5 percent of own-source local revenues (taxes, fees, and charges) and 75.8 percent of local tax collections in fiscal year (FY) 2024.[12]

Florida’s non-school district property tax collections grew 68.6 percent from 2019 to 2025, outpacing population growth (9.2 percent) and cumulative inflation (25.9 percent).[13] During this same period, the value of homes in Florida increased by 68.8 percent.[14] While this growth increased local government revenues, it does not necessarily indicate that local governments could easily accommodate the fiscal effects of Amendment 3.

Homestead property is a significant component of Florida’s property tax base. Over 5.2 million parcels in Florida are homestead parcels, accounting for 46.7 percent of all parcels in the state.[15] Homestead property accounts for 46.4 percent of the just value (market value) and 36.1 percent of the taxable value of all real property in Florida.[16] If Amendment 3 is approved by voters, it is estimated that the $150,000 exemption would cost local governments $4.9 billion in the first year, and the $250,000 exemption would cost $8.7 billion in the second year, with annual impacts of $11.8 billion as of tax year 2031. However, the full fiscal impact remains uncertain and could easily exceed current estimates. The Revenue Estimating Conference noted that the effect of provisions authorizing future legislative action to increase exemptions and fully exempt all homesteads is unknown.[17]

Recent revenue growth should not be viewed as evidence that the amendment could be absorbed without fiscal consequences. Rather, Amendment 3 would substantially narrow the property tax base available to support local government services. Although recent revenue growth has been driven in large part by rising property values, those same valuation increases are what make exempting homestead property increasingly costly. Over time, the amendment would remove a substantial and growing share of that value from the property tax base and significantly reduce the future revenue-generating capacity that local governments need to fund the services they provide.

Florida’s SOH assessment limitation, effective as of January 1, 1995, allows substantial differences to emerge between a property’s market value and taxable value. For long-term homestead properties, taxable value may be only a fraction of just value, and in some cases, a proposed $250,000 exemption could eliminate most or all non-school property tax liability.

Because eliminating a substantial portion of the property tax base does not eliminate the cost of local government services, Amendment 3 would instead change who pays. A greater share of the burden of funding local government services would instead be borne by the owners of non-homestead properties. This means that businesses, landlords, second homeowners, and recent buyers would likely see higher effective tax rates, as would renters, in the form of higher rent.

For businesses, this shift could be extremely impactful. In addition to real property, Florida taxes business tangible personal property (TPP) using the same local millage rates that apply to real property. In 2025, business TPP accounted for 5.5 percent of statewide total taxable value.[18] Florida’s business TPP tax is costly to comply with and may distort investment decisions. Although Florida provides a $25,000 exemption, this may represent only a small fraction of assets, especially for capital-intensive industries and industries where short-lived assets like technology can become rapidly obsolete. Higher tax burdens could discourage investment and increase operating costs and consumer prices.

Approximately one-third of Floridians are renters, and the massive tax shift created by Amendment 3 could have tremendous implications for them. In 2024, renter occupancy rates ranged from 14.3 percent in Gilchrist County to 47.8 percent in Miami-Dade County.[19] Because renters do not directly receive homestead tax relief, counties with larger rental populations could experience greater downstream effects if increased property tax burdens are passed through by landlords.

Evidence suggests that property tax increases are frequently borne by tenants. A 2025 study examined California’s Proposition 13 assessment limit and the impact of higher property tax liability when an apartment community changed ownership.[20] It found that landlords passed approximately 50 to 89 percent of increased tax liabilities through to new tenant rents.

A recent analysis specific to Amendment 3 concluded that if local governments raised millage rates to compensate for homestead revenue losses, annual property taxes could increase by roughly 15 percent for both apartment and single-family rental properties by 2031.[21] These increases would likely place upward pressure on rents statewide.

The analysis also noted that Amendment 3 could impact housing affordability, particularly in the case of income-restricted units. Higher tax burdens could reduce funds available for maintenance and capital improvements. Additionally, the construction of new income-restricted units could decline as the capacity to raise rent is restricted, thereby reducing any return on investment.

Increased rents would not only impact renters of residences. A 2018 study examined both urban and suburban commercial rental markets in the Greater Boston Area as well as 93 municipalities in eastern Massachusetts.[22] It found that commercial property tax increases were passed on to tenants much more fully in urban areas than in suburban areas. For every $1.00 increase in property taxes per square foot, rents rose by about $1.06 to $1.39 in urban areas, compared with $0.52 to $0.67 in suburban areas.

Florida is a popular destination for second homeowners. While owners of second homes are often only part-time residents, their footprint is impactful. Under Amendment 3, they too would bear the burden of higher property taxes. Higher property tax burdens on second homes could reduce Florida’s attractiveness relative to competing destination states and influence future location decisions among some prospective buyers.

Second homeowners tend to be high-net-worth individuals who meaningfully contribute to local economies through high-end retail, entertainment, and service purchases. Should would-be homeowners opt to purchase second homes in other nearby states, Florida and its communities could see reduced demand for these amenities accompanied by reduced associated revenues. Second homes are typically a good deal for local governments, because they receive all of the property tax revenue while having to provide fewer services. In particular, second homes are unlikely to increase school enrollment.

Finally, new homeowners, whether Floridian first-time homebuyers or new Florida residents, would, for a period of time, see vastly different tax bills compared with existing homeowners under Amendment 3. While new residents who qualify for a homestead exemption would immediately receive existing constitutional protections, they would not qualify for the proposed enhanced exemption until after the first five years of their residency. As a result, two very similarly situated homeowners could face dramatically different tax bills solely because of when they purchased their homes—tax bills that could discourage new homeownership and make Florida far less attractive to prospective residents.

Additionally, while intended to benefit non-homestead properties, and in particular, small businesses, Amendment 3’s proposed 5 percent assessment limitation has the same distortionary “lock-in effect” associated with most assessment limits, though in practice, a 5 percent cap on commercial property appreciation has nowhere near the effect of the current residential cap at the lesser of 3 percent or inflation. Still, businesses seeking to expand or relocate would experience assessment resets to just value following ownership changes, creating incentives to remain in existing facilities rather than pursue growth opportunities.

These effects extend beyond property owners themselves. If housing costs rise for renters and recent homebuyers while business tax burdens increase, employers could face greater challenges attracting and retaining workers. Over time, the cumulative effect could weaken Florida’s competitive position for workforce recruitment, investment, and economic growth.

Florida law incorporates a rollback requirement under which the millage rate is adjusted to a level that would generate the same revenue from existing property as was collected in the prior year, excluding revenue attributable to new construction.[23] The intent of the rollback rate is to prevent local governments from receiving a windfall due to rising property values without taking formal action to increase taxes. Local governments may exceed the rollback rate, but doing so generally requires a supermajority vote of the governing body, with higher thresholds for larger revenue increases.[24]

If Amendment 3 passes, however, local governments would collect less revenue from existing property owners because a larger share of residential value would be exempt from taxation. As a result, the rollback mechanism itself would not prevent local governments from increasing millage rates to offset some or all of the revenue loss associated with the expanded homestead exemption. Over time, as the amendment is fully phased in and its effects are incorporated into annual tax rolls, a new revenue baseline would be established for future rollback calculations.

Because the property tax is the most stable and significant source of local government revenue, local governing boards would likely evaluate the feasibility of potential millage rate increases before pursuing service reductions or relying on more volatile sources of revenue.

The ability to offset lost property tax revenue through higher millage rates depends largely on a jurisdiction’s existing millage rate and the amount of remaining tax authority available. The Florida Constitution limits county and municipal millage rates to 10 mills each for general operating expenses, meaning $10 for every $1,000 of taxable value.[25] A higher rate is temporarily allowed if approved by a majority of voters. Counties and municipalities already levying rates at or near their authorized limits have little to no ability to replace lost property tax revenue through rate increases without having to seek voter approval. In contrast, jurisdictions with rates moderately to substantially below their authorized limit have a greater ability to increase rates, thereby shifting a portion of the tax burden onto the remaining taxable value.

Tables 1 through 4 identify the Florida counties and municipalities with the highest and lowest general operating millage rates, while Tables 5 and 6 illustrate the statewide distribution of millage rates.[26] The data reveals substantial variation across jurisdictions, though most jurisdictions have enough fiscal capacity under the 10 mill cap to adopt revenue-neutral rate increases if they choose to do so.

Florida’s highest county operating millage rates are concentrated in rural areas in northern Florida, the Big Bend area, and the Panhandle. In contrast, the lowest-rate counties tend to be coastal jurisdictions with tax bases driven by tourism and high-value real estate. At the municipal level, the highest millage rates are split between small rural communities and urban South Florida cities, while the lowest municipal rates are concentrated among affluent coastal municipalities and a handful of very small towns.

More than half of Florida counties levy at rates below 7 mills. These counties generally have greater rate flexibility compared with higher taxing jurisdictions. The distribution is different for municipalities. Municipal rates are generally lower, with nearly one-half of Florida municipalities levying rates below 5 mills.

These patterns suggest that local governments would enter Amendment 3 from markedly different fiscal positions. Some jurisdictions already rely heavily on property taxation and have little remaining rate-raising capacity, while others maintain comparatively low millage rates and retain greater flexibility to raise rates. The extent to which local governments could offset revenue losses through future millage rate increases would vary significantly across jurisdictions, but overall, higher property tax burdens could potentially result across much of the state.
Exempting a large portion of the property tax base does not exempt local governing boards from their responsibility to provide essential public services; it reallocates how they would pay for them.

Property taxes are the principal source of own-source revenue for Florida’s local governments. As previously noted, they currently account for 41.5 percent of own-source local revenues and 75.8 percent of local tax collections.

While the amendment directs local governments to use property tax revenues for defined core services, no minimum funding levels are mandated. Depending on their existing millage rates and available taxing capacity, certain jurisdictions could potentially offset a substantial portion, or even all, of their revenue losses through millage rate adjustments.

In addition to utilizing unused millage capacity, they could turn to alternative revenue streams for funding. Like property taxes, local taxes and fees in Florida are authorized by the state. While local governments would face statutory constraints related to voter requirements, eligibility requirements, tax rates, and permitted uses of the funds, some local governments would likely turn to other existing local taxes and fees to offset some of the lost property tax revenue.

Florida’s local option sales tax, known as the Discretionary Sales SurtaxA surtax is an additional tax levied on top of an already existing business or individual tax and can have a flat or progressive rate structure. Surtaxes are typically enacted to fund a specific program or initiative, whereas revenue from broader-based taxes, like the individual income tax, typically cover a multitude of programs and services. (DSS), is imposed at the county level and applies to transactions subject to the state sales and use tax. For sales of tangible property, it generally applies to the first $5,000 of the sales price of each taxable item, although there is no cap for some service transactions.[27]

In 2024, the DSS accounted for 5.1 percent of total local own-source general revenues and 9.4 percent of total local tax revenues.[28] Aside from property taxes, Florida’s discretionary sales surtax is the state’s largest locally imposed tax revenue source.[29]

Although the DSS could be an alternative revenue option for Florida’s local governments, it faces notable limitations as a substitute for lost property tax revenue. Revenues from the DSS are generally restricted to specific purposes, such as infrastructure, transportation, health care, and schools. While counties may impose more than one surtax, they must observe applicable combined rate limits. Individual rates are typically capped between 0.5 percent and 1 percent, with combined rates currently ranging from 0.5 percent to 2.0 percent.[30]

Eligibility to impose a particular DSS varies based on criteria such as charter or consolidated-government status, population size, and other statutory criteria. While many require voter approval and are frequently adopted with sunset provisions, specific requirements vary.[31] The most widely used ones include the Local Government Infrastructure Surtax, and among eligible jurisdictions, the Small County Surtax.[32]

Florida local governments also have access to several business-related taxes and fees. One example is the Local Business Tax, which counties and municipalities may levy for the privilege of operating a business within their jurisdictions.[33] Because counties and municipalities may independently impose the tax, a business located within a municipality may be subject to it at both the county and municipal levels. Rates vary according to business classification and other characteristics, while state law establishes requirements governing rate structures and subsequent rate increases. Numerous statutory exemptions narrow the tax base.

Local government revenues also include taxes and fees specific to various services. Municipalities may impose the Municipal Public Service Tax (MPST) on specified utility services, including electricity, natural gas, and water.[34] Counties and municipalities may impose a Communications Services Tax (CST) which applies broadly to a variety of modern communications technologies. Currently, state law prohibits increases in local CST rates that were in effect on January 1, 2023, until January 1, 2031.[35] Fees may also be imposed to support services such as wastewater management, solid waste collection, and parking.

Many local governments impose a variety of local option tourist taxes, and while tourism is important to Florida, the revenues from these taxes are heavily restricted and limited to only certain parts of the state.

Impact fees are another source of local revenue, but their use is typically limited more specifically to finance facilities and infrastructure necessitated by new development.[36] Due to this limitation, they generally cannot substitute for revenues used to fund ongoing local government general operations. An increase in impact fees could, however, increase the cost of new development and contribute to higher prices for newly constructed housing and commercial development.

Local governments may also utilize special assessments to finance certain improvements or services that provide a distinct benefit to assessed properties.[37] Special assessments are commonly used for things like sidewalk improvements, lighting of pedestrian areas, stormwater systems, sewer improvements, fire protection, and parking facilities. While special assessments are permitted, a property must receive a specific benefit from the improvement or service, and the amount charged cannot exceed its proportional share of the benefit received.

Local governments must follow specific procedures when looking to impose a special assessment, particularly providing public notice and holding a public hearing for property owners to attend. While some improvements do require voter approval, many only require approval by local governing boards. If millage increases and existing revenue sources prove insufficient to offset revenue losses, local governments could increasingly rely on special assessments to finance specific services and infrastructure improvements.

While this is not a complete list of all local taxes and fees imposed by Florida’s local governments, it illustrates both some of the alternatives available to them along with their limitations. Like millage rates, the extent to which these alternatives could replace lost property tax revenue would vary significantly across jurisdictions. While Florida has substantial non-property-tax local revenue options, many are not general-purpose replacements for the property tax.

The fiscal impacts imposed by Amendment 3 would force local officials to evaluate whether existing taxes and fees could be increased within current constraints and whether they should seek additional authority from the legislature to create new, or expand existing, revenue options.

Some local governments may decide that increasing millage rates or turning to other fees and taxes should not be the sole options for offsetting lost property tax revenue. They may instead defer capital investments, reduce services, or both. Over time, such reductions could affect public safety, infrastructure, and other attributes that contribute to Florida’s desirable quality of life.

Ultimately, the fiscal effects of reduced property tax revenues would extend to all Floridians. Homeowners, renters, consumers, and businesses could all bear some portion of the adjustment through higher taxes, fees, and assessments; reduced services; or a combination thereof. Amendment 3 does not reduce the cost of providing local government services; it merely changes how those costs are distributed and who ultimately bears the burden.

Should major tax policy be embedded in Florida’s constitution? Major tax policy is generally much easier to enact, amend, or repeal through legislation than through constitutional amendment. Laws can be enacted, amended, or repealed during a legislative session and generally take effect shortly thereafter. By design, legislation is more easily adaptable.

In contrast, amending the Florida Constitution is a lengthier and more difficult process. Whether legislatively proposed or citizen-led, constitutional amendments must satisfy extensive procedural requirements before they reach voters. Depending on when a proposal is initiated and when the next general election occurs, the process can take months or even years to complete. By design, constitutions are meant to be more enduring and are therefore much less adaptable.

Florida has embedded several major property tax policies in its constitution, including the homestead exemption, the SOH assessment limitation, and local government millage limitations. These provisions were adopted with the goal of protecting taxpayers from excessive taxation and substantial increases in taxable value. A consequence, however, is that policymakers have less flexibility when responding to changing economic conditions, housing market trends, fiscal emergencies, or shifts in public service needs.

If Amendment 3 is added to Florida’s constitution, any change to the policy would be a major undertaking, requiring another statewide campaign and voter approval. Amendment 3 would fundamentally change Florida’s local tax base. For this reason, it is important to get the policy right the first time.

A recent ballot measure in Missouri illustrates how voters often approach proposed policy changes with skepticism, particularly when there is too much uncertainty about how governments would replace lost revenue from major tax changes. In August, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected Amendment 5, a proposal to reduce and eventually eliminate the state individual income tax through the expansion of the sales and use tax.[38] There was no clearly defined plan as to how exactly the sales and use tax would be expanded. Voters had no way to know what the exact trade-off would be.

Florida voters will face a similar decision in November. Whether voters ultimately adopt or reject Amendment 3 will not necessarily be a reflection of whether they want property tax relief, but rather whether they think the long-term trade-offs of the proposal before them—and the many unknown factors associated with it—are worth it.

State legislators and governors across the country want to “fix” property tax burdens, but property tax bills reflect decisions made by locally elected officials. Commonly proposed fixes often make the underlying problems worse, as they commonly narrow tax bases through exemptions and assessment limitations, shifting burdens rather than reducing them.

Amendment 3 is not simply a tax cut. It represents a fundamental restructuring of local government finance. The primary beneficiaries of Amendment 3 would be homestead property owners, but those benefits would come with significant trade-offs. The cost of funding local government services would not disappear. Instead, burdens would shift to businesses, renters, new homebuyers, and other property owners through higher taxes, fees, and housing costs. Local governments would face increasing pressure to rely on less stable and more constrained revenue sources. Over time, those trade-offs could erode Florida’s fiscal stability and undermine the state’s future economic competitiveness.

Florida’s reputation as a nationally competitive, low-tax state depends not merely on keeping taxes low, but on maintaining a stable and sustainable revenue system capable of supporting future economic growth. Property tax reform should focus on achieving the best balance of affordability, predictability, and local fiscal stability. Amendment 3 fails to achieve that balance.

articles.title: International Tax Competitiveness Index 2026
articles.standfirst: While there are many factors that affect a country's economic performance, taxes play an important role. A well-structured tax code is easy for taxpayers to comply with and can promote economic development while raising sufficient revenue for a government’s priorities.
paragraphs: Note: Each year we review and improve the methodology of the Index. For that reason, prior editions are not comparable to the results in this 2026 edition. All data and methodological notes are accessible in our GitHub repository. Below is an abbreviated version of the 2026 Index. To access the full report, click the download button above.

The structure of a country’s tax code is a determining factor of its economic performance. A well-structured tax code is easy for taxpayers to comply with and can promote economic development while raising sufficient revenue for a government’s priorities. In contrast, poorly structured tax systems can be costly, distort economic decision-making, and harm domestic economies.

Many countries have recognized this and have reformed their tax codes. Over the past few decades, marginal tax rates on corporate and individual income have declined significantly across the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Now, most OECD nations raise a significant amount of revenue from broad-based taxes such as payroll taxes and value-added taxes (VAT).[1]

Not all recent changes in tax policy among OECD countries have improved the structure of tax systems; some had a negative impact. Though some countries, like Austria, have reduced their corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. rates by several percentage points, others, like France, the Slovak Republic, and Slovenia, have increased them. Corporate tax base improvements have occurred in Canada, Germany, Lithuania, the United Kingdom, and the United States, while the corporate tax base has been made less competitive in the Czech Republic and Slovenia. Germany and Finland are phasing out temporary improvements to their corporate tax bases that Lithuania, the United Kingdom, and the United States have made permanent and expanded.[2]

In recent years, tax policy has increasingly drifted away from its traditional roles of raising government revenue and encouraging investment into the toolbox of international tax and trade disputes, with import tariffs, digital service levies, and extraterritorial taxes deployed to exert economic pressure. In this environment, policymakers should refocus on neutral, internationally competitive tax policies that raise revenue with minimal harm to investment and economic growth. The variety of approaches to taxation among OECD countries creates a need to evaluate these systems relative to each other. For that purpose, we have developed the International Tax Competitiveness Index—a relative comparison of OECD countries’ tax systems with respect to competitiveness and neutrality.
The International Tax Competitiveness Index (ITCI) seeks to measure the extent to which a country’s tax system adheres to two important aspects of tax policy: competitiveness and neutrality.

A competitive tax code is one that keeps marginal effective tax rates low. In today’s globalized world, capital is highly mobile. Businesses can choose to invest in any number of countries throughout the world to find the highest rate of return. This means that businesses will look for countries with lower tax rates on investment to maximize their after-tax rate of return. If a country’s tax rate is too high, it will drive investment elsewhere, leading to slower economic growth. In addition, high marginal tax rates can impede domestic investment and lead to tax avoidance.

According to research from the OECD, corporate taxes are most harmful for economic growth, with personal income taxes and consumption taxes being less harmful. Taxes on immovable property have the smallest impact on growth.[3]

Separately, a neutral tax code is simply one that seeks to raise the most revenue with the fewest economic distortions. This means that it doesn’t favor consumption over saving, as happens with investment taxes and wealth taxes. It also means few or no targeted tax breaks for specific activities carried out by businesses or individuals.

As tax laws become more complex, they also become less neutral. If, in theory, the same taxes apply to all businesses and individuals, but the rules are such that large businesses or wealthy individuals can change their behavior to gain a tax advantage, this undermines the neutrality of a tax system.
A tax code that is competitive and neutral promotes sustainable economic growth and investment while raising sufficient revenue for government priorities.
There are many factors unrelated to taxes which affect a country’s economic performance. Nevertheless, taxes play an important role in the health of a country’s economy.

To measure whether a country’s tax system is neutral and competitive, the ITCI looks at more than 40 tax policy variables. These variables measure not only the level of tax rates, but also how taxes are structured. The Index looks at a country’s corporate taxes, individual income taxes, consumption taxes, property taxes, and the treatment of profits earned overseas. The ITCI gives a comprehensive overview of how developed countries’ tax codes compare, explains why certain tax codes stand out as good or bad models for reform, and provides important insight into how to think about tax policy.
Due to some data limitations, recent tax changes in some countries may not be reflected in this year’s version of the International Tax Competitiveness Index.

For the 13th year in a row, Estonia has the best tax code in the OECD. Its top score is driven by four positive features of its tax system. First, it has a 22 percent tax rate on corporate income that is only applied to distributed profits. Second, it has a flat 22 percent tax on individual income that does not apply to personal dividend income. Third, its property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. applies only to the value of land, rather than to the value of real property or capital. Finally, it has a territorial tax systemTerritorial taxation is a system that excludes foreign earnings from a country’s domestic tax base. This is common throughout the world and is the opposite of worldwide taxation, where foreign earnings are included in the domestic tax base. that exempts 100 percent of foreign profits earned by domestic corporations from domestic taxation, with few restrictions.

While Estonia’s tax system is the most competitive in the OECD, the other top countries’ tax systems receive high scores due to excellence in one or more of the major tax categories. Latvia, which recently adopted the Estonian system for corporate taxation, also has a relatively efficient system for taxing labor income. New Zealand has a relatively flat, low-rate individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source that also largely exempts capital gains (with a combined top rate of 39 percent), a broad-based VAT, and levies no taxes on inheritance, property transfers, assets, or financial transactions. Switzerland has a relatively low corporate tax rate (19.5 percent), a low, broad-based consumption taxA consumption tax is typically levied on the purchase of goods or services and is paid directly or indirectly by the consumer in the form of retail sales taxes, excise taxes, tariffs, value-added taxes (VAT), or income taxes where all savings are tax-deductible., and an individual income tax that partially exempts capital gains from taxation. Lithuania has a low corporate tax rate of 17 percent, allows businesses to fully expense the capital investment costs for machinery, equipment, and intangible rights, and levies a relatively flat and low-rate individual income tax. Luxembourg levies its broad-based VAT on 87 percent of final consumption, exempts long-term capital gains without substantial ownership from taxation, and has a competitive cross-border regime without withholdingWithholding is the income an employer takes out of an employee’s paycheck and remits to the federal, state, and/or local government. It is calculated based on the amount of income earned, the taxpayer’s filing status, the number of allowances claimed, and any additional amount the employee requests. taxes on interest or royalties.

France has the least competitive tax system in the OECD. It has the highest top corporate tax rate in the OECD, at 36.1 percent, including multiple surtaxes and distortive production taxes. It also applies multiple distortionary property taxes with separate levies on estates, bank assets, and financial transactions, in addition to a wealth tax on real estate. Its VAT covers about 50 percent of final consumption, and it has one of the highest VAT registration thresholds.

Colombia has the second-least competitive tax system in the OECD. It has a net wealth tax, a financial transaction tax, and a corporate income tax rate levied at 35 percent that does not generally exempt income earned abroad by subsidiaries. Colombia’s VAT covers less than 36 percent of final consumption, revealing both policy and enforcement gaps.

Countries that rank poorly on the ITCI often levy relatively high marginal tax rates on corporate income or have multiple layers of tax rules that contribute to complexity. Four of the five countries at the bottom of the rankings have higher-than-average combined corporate tax rates. Four out of the five countries have unusually narrow VAT bases, covering only between 35 and 50 percent of final consumption. They also tend to levy many distortive taxes on narrow bases, with four out of the five bottom five countries applying digital services taxes, financial transaction taxes, and inheritance taxes. Four out of five of the lowest-ranking countries also levy either some type of wealth tax or capital duties (or both). Ireland is not among them but ranks poorly on the ITCI despite its low corporate tax rate. This is due to high personal income and dividend taxes and a relatively narrow VAT base.

In 2025, Canada abolished its digital services tax, canceled the planned increase in the capital gains inclusion rate, and reinstated full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. for machinery and the accelerated investment incentive for buildings. In September 2026, after the cut-off date for the current Index edition, the Canadian government announced it would make full expensing for machinery and patent rights permanent and extend it to a larger share of assets, while introducing temporary full expensing for buildings used for manufacturing and processing until 2029. Canada’s rank stays constant at 15th.

Denmark added a new personal income tax bracket in 2026, increasing its top rate from 55.9 to 60.5 percent and raising the top rate threshold from around 1.2 to 5.3 times the average salary. Denmark’s rank fell from 29th to 31st.

In 2026, Finland phased out accelerated depreciationDepreciation is a measurement of the “useful life” of a business asset, such as machinery or a factory, to determine the multiyear period over which the cost of that asset can be deducted from taxable income. Instead of allowing businesses to deduct the cost of investments immediately (i.e., full expensing), depreciation requires deductions to be taken over time, reducing their value and disco for machinery and equipment, reducing the share of investment costs that businesses can recover by 10 percentage points in real terms. However, it also reduced its top rate on personal income from 57 to 50.4 percent. Finland kept its rank at 22nd.

Lithuania raised its corporate tax rate from 16 to 17 percent while substantially improving the competitiveness of its corporate tax base by introducing permanent full expensing for machinery, equipment, and intangible rights. Lithuania also broadened its VAT base. Lithuania ranks 5th, the same as last year.

Portugal has made several improvements to its personal and corporate tax regimes over the last years, reducing its tax rate on long-term capital gains from 28 to 19.6 percent and making its notional interest deduction more generous in 2025. Portugal continued to incrementally reduce its top corporate tax rate from 31.5 in 2024 to 30.5 percent in 2025, further down to 29.5 percent in 2026. Portugal’s rank is 33rd, the same as last year.

In 2025, the Slovak Republic increased its corporate rate from 21 to 24 percent, increased its VAT registration threshold, and introduced a financial transaction tax. In 2026, it raised its top personal income tax rate from 35 to 44.4 percent and raised the top rate threshold. The Slovak Republic’s rank continues to fall, from 9th to 12th.

In 2025, the US reinstated full expensing for plants and equipment and extended the policy to selected industrial buildings and structures. From 2026, the US is tightening its cross-border rules by abolishing the substance exclusion for income of US multinationals earned abroad. The US rank fell back again from 16th to 17th.

Each year, we review the Index’s data and methodology to improve how it measures both competitiveness and neutrality. This year, we have changed the way the Index treats corporate taxes, individual taxes, and cross-border rules.

We have applied each change to prior years to allow consistent comparison across years. Data for all years using the current methodology is accessible in the GitHub repository for the Index,[5] and a description of how the Index is calculated is provided in the Appendix of this report. Prior editions of the Index, however, are not comparable to the results in this 2026 edition due to these methodological changes.

The incentives and complexity subcategory now includes a new variable capturing the share of business tax revenue raised from turnover taxes, which burden investment by disallowing the deduction of input costs and cascading throughout the production process. The variable helps to better reflect the harmful practices of Hungary’s gross revenue retail tax and France’s production taxes.
The share of unallocable revenue is now expressed as a share of corporate tax revenue rather than as a share of GDP, matching the variable’s description.
