articles.title: Has Fiscal Policy Adjusted To A World Of Higher Interest Rates?
articles.standfirst: As all good economists know, fiscal sustainability comes down to the gap between the interest rate the government pays on its debt and the growth rate of the economy, r...
paragraphs: As all good economists know, fiscal sustainability comes down to the gap between the interest rate the government pays on its debt and the growth rate of the economy, r minus g. Think of this as a race. If r is lower than g, debt (the IOUs we’ve written in the past) will grow more slowly than the economy, exerting a downward force on debt as a share of GDP. In this world, government spending on schools, hospitals, defence and so on can exceed tax revenues indefinitely without the debt ratio rising—as long as the deficit isn’t too big. But when r is above g, the converse will be true, and the debt ratio will rise unless the government runs a primary surplus big enough to cover the gap.

The big change in the global financial system over the past few years has been the big increase in r. While the gap between r and g has worked in the government’s favour in the years since the global financial crisis, this has flipped recently with r exceeding g on new borrowing; importantly, the gap between r and g has widened further just this past year.

In this week’s blog, I look at what this means for the UK’s public finances and for our ability to keep the debt ratio stable over the medium term. My argument in a nutshell is this. The government’s plans already contain a £100 billion planned consolidation, roughly of the scale needed to stabilise debt at the interest rates prevailing in February. But much of it is back-loaded to around the next election, and is unlikely to be delivered. If the rise in rates since February persists, debt interest will be around £15 billion a year higher by the end of the decade than the OBR assumed, which means more tightening on top. This has the feel of a slow-motion car crash: each year, cheap debt issued when rates were low is refinanced at today’s rates.

The mood music ahead of the Budget later this month is that the Chancellor will instead allow borrowing to rise modestly relative to plan to cushion the effects of the Iran war. Some of that is justified—some limited energy cost relief for the most vulnerable households, for example. But borrowing to absorb a shock only makes sense if the shock is temporary. We can’t know for certain whether higher rates are here to stay, but there are good reasons to think they might be, and the costs of getting it wrong are skewed. That points to planning for rates staying high.

The 10-year gilt yield is now 5.3 per cent, its highest level since 2007 (Figure 1). The real yield, which strips out compensation for inflation, is 2.0 per cent, the highest since 2008. For most of the decade after the GFC, the real yield was negative, reaching minus 3 per cent in 2020 and 2021. That was when much of today’s debt stock was issued, and as it matures, it is refinanced at today’s rates.

Since the end of February, around the time of the OBR’s last forecast, the 10-year yield has risen by about a percentage point (Figure 2). At the short end, much of the rise reflects inflation compensation: 55 basis points of the 120-basis point rise at five years. At the long end, it’s almost all real: 60 of the 68 basis points at thirty years. This is just telling us that markets expect the energy shock to pass, but they are pricing in a more persistent increase in real rates.

The cleanest way to see this is via the 5-year rate 5-years ahead. This is the real rate financial markets are pricing for 2031-36. It’s useful because it looks through the near-term repricing of Bank Rate and inflation. Since February, it has risen by 75 basis points in the UK and almost 100 basis points in the US, taking both back to, or above, where they were before the financial crisis.

In all, real rates have risen by around 5 percentage points since the end of 2021. Most of that came in 2022 and 2023, after the first energy shock and the Liz Truss mini-Budget. There was a further lurch upwards of around 100 basis points from mid-2024, and yet another since February.

The benign reading of higher real rates is that they reflect stronger expected growth, in which case r minus g might not have moved much. There’s some support for this in the UK. GDP grew by 0.7 per cent in the three months to August, the eighth consecutive three-month rise, and was 1.8 per cent higher than a year earlier, comfortably above most estimates of trend growth. Last month, the ONS also revised up post-crisis productivity growth from 0.7 to 1.3 per cent a year. But that revision came from lower estimates of hours worked rather than higher output, so GDP is unchanged and the implications for future growth are unclear.

GDP growth so far this year is running close to our pre-war NIESR February forecast of 1.4 per cent, significantly stronger than the forecast we made once the war had begun. Is that telling us that the underlying growth capacity is stronger than we thought, perhaps because the AI capex boom is lifting growth everywhere? Or that the effects of the war have been smaller than feared, or have yet to be felt in full (inflation in the UK won’t peak until the new year).
The truth is, it’s too early to tell. The safer assumption for now is that g has barely moved, so the rise in r has widened the gap one for one.

On paper, the government’s plans already contain a large consolidation. The OBR’s March forecast, based on those plans, has the primary balance moving from a deficit of 1.5 per cent of GDP last year to a surplus of 1.5 per cent by 2030-31 (Figure 4). That is a tightening of 3 per cent of GDP, or around £100 billion per year by the end of the forecast. At the interest rates prevailing in February, this was enough to stabilise the debt ratio and then have debt falling, from 96.3 per cent to 95.1 per cent by 2030-31.

The key question is whether this path is credible. I doubt it. It has the classic shape of jam today, belt-tightening tomorrow, which Charlie Bean once called the Augustinian approach to fiscal policy. The timing makes it harder still. Around half of the tightening is scheduled to happen in 2028-29, and 2029-30, ahead of the next general election (which must happen by August 2029). Economists know this as the time-inconsistency problem, after Kydland and Prescott. We want to convince people that we’ll do something painful in future, whether going on a diet or saving more next year for retirement, but when the future arrives those plans no longer look so appealing and we renege. The problem is that the people we’re trying to convince understand that incentive and don’t believe us in the first place.

Figure 5 shows the problem in practice. It plots every OBR forecast of the primary balance since 2010 against what actually happened. Almost every forecast shows the primary balance rising into surplus within five years. The outturn has not been in surplus once over this period, the last being in 2001-02.
This time inconsistency may also help to explain why UK borrowing costs have stayed high relative to other countries’, even with a material consolidation pencilled in.

As we saw earlier, interest rates have moved a lot since the OBR’s last forecast. On our rough calculations, if they stay at today’s levels, debt interest will be £15 billion a year higher by 2030-31 than the OBR assumed in March. Will the Budget tighten policy to reflect this? It doesn’t appear so. The runway has instead been laid for a Budget with less “headroom” against the fiscal rules, which simply means more borrowing relative to plan.

Whether that is the right call depends on whether the rise in rates is temporary or permanent. The logic comes from Bob Hall’s famous 1978 paper on the consumption Euler equation (Hall shared this year’s Nobel prize with Michael Woodford). A household that smooths its consumption should respond only to news about its permanent income. Faced with a temporary hit, it borrows and keeps spending; faced with a permanent one, it cuts back. Robert Barro applied the same logic to government a year later: debt should absorb temporary shocks, while taxes and spending should adjust to permanent ones. Borrowing to help the most vulnerable through a temporary energy price spike passes this test. Borrowing to absorb a permanent rise in the cost of debt does not; it simply postpones the adjustment and makes it bigger.

So is the rise in rates permanent? We can’t know for sure. But the evidence in the first section points to a large persistent component. The rise at the long end of the gilt curve is almost entirely in real rates; the real rate markets expect in five to ten years’ time has risen by around 75 basis points and almost 100 in the US, which points to a global shift rather than something specific to the UK. Our recent Market Anatomy report sets out the evidence in more detail and finds that two-thirds of the move looks like a lasting rise in global real rates.

There are two ways to make decisions under this kind of uncertainty. The first is Bayesian: treat a share of the shock as permanent, in proportion to how persistent such shocks have been in the past, and update as the data come in. Real interest rates have historically been very persistent, and forward rates already embody markets’ best guess of the persistent component. On that approach, policy should respond to most of the move now.

The second is robust control: ask which outcome would be worst and set policy to avoid it. Here the costs of getting it wrong are lopsided. If the government tightens and rates fall back, it can loosen again later. If it borrows more and rates stay high, it risks a loss of confidence in the public finances that is hard to reverse, as France has found and as the UK learned in 2022. Robust control points to planning for rates staying high.

Both approaches point the same way. The rise in rates since February is not a reason to run down headroom; if anything, it is a reason to rebuild it. Borrowing more now also shifts the burden of adjustment onto younger and future taxpayers, who will inherit the higher debt interest bill.

articles.title: What Might the UK Budget Mean for the Devolved Governments?
articles.standfirst: John Healey’s first Budget as Chancellor will, understandably, be judged mainly on the UK government’s fiscal position: meeting the fiscal rules, who bears the burden of tax and spending changes,...
paragraphs: John Healey’s first Budget as Chancellor will, understandably, be judged mainly on the UK government’s fiscal position: meeting the fiscal rules, who bears the burden of tax and spending changes, and the reaction of increasingly captious gilt markets. But for a Chancellor who has pledged to “move power and money out of Westminster”, one question deserves more attention than it usually gets: how do Westminster’s funding decisions reach the nations that already have devolved budgets?

The answer is neither uniform nor straightforward. Spending, tax and benefit decisions reach the devolved budgets through different channels and to different degrees, so the net effect is rarely obvious from headline announcements. That matters more than usual this year, with all three devolved administrations facing a difficult 2027–28. What their finance ministers expect from the Budget on 28 October will depend as much on where changes are announced as on how large they are.

The devolved governments’ funding is mainly set at UK spending reviews. These fix departmental budgets for several years, and the Barnett formula turns those plans into a block grant for each administration. The grants are not recalculated from scratch at each Budget. Funding carries forward from the last fiscal year, and any change to UK spending flows through the same formula.

As a result, when a Chancellor changes spending, each nation gets roughly a population share of any increase or cut in services that are devolved to it, called a Barnett Consequential. What flows through depends on what is devolved. Health and schools are devolved in all three nations, policing and justice only in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and immigration and defence in none. As a result, UK government departments made up 39 per cent of identifiable public service expenditure in Wales in 2024-25, 30 per cent in Scotland and just 5 per cent in Northern Ireland.

Budget announcements are priced differently in each nation. The Barnett formula gives new funding as an equal amount per head, not as an equal percentage increase. Per-head spending in each nation started above England’s level, so the same cash amount translates to a smaller percentage increase. Over time, this ‘Barnett squeeze’ pulls funding per head towards English levels, which does not necessarily reflect each nation’s baseline needs or its urban–rural mix. To slow that erosion, Wales receives at least 105 per cent of its population share of new UK spending, and Northern Ireland currently receives 124 per cent.

On paper, the devolved governments enter this Budget in reasonable shape. Large real-terms expansions in the Autumn Budget 2024 and Spending Review 2025 settlements have fed through to the block grants, and in-year top-ups to English spending in 2026, such as the funding to clear local authorities’ SEND deficits, have produced large consequentials. But that expansion is front-loaded. Following the 2025 Spending Review, growth in UK day-to-day departmental spending slows from 2.4 per cent in real terms in 2025–26 to 1.0 per cent a year from 2027-28. The squeeze is sharper for the devolved governments, whose funding from the UK government is expected to fall by 0.7 per cent in real terms in the two years to 2028–29, according to the latest Treasury data.

One way to see what this means for the economy is the Hutchins Centre’s Fiscal Impact Measure (FIM), which NIESR has applied to track the direct contribution of fiscal policy forecasts to UK GDP growth. Because devolved governments control spending far more than taxes and benefits, I use only its government purchases component: the growth of real government consumption and investment relative to potential output1. When the two grow in line, the measure is neutral. Faster growth adds to demand, and slower growth subtracts from it.

The FIM shows that Scotland’s fiscal boost came earlier and is fading sooner than that for the United Kingdom as a whole. Government purchases added 0.58 percentage points to Scottish growth in 2024–25, against 0.17 for UK growth, helped by greater use of devolved borrowing powers and a rising share of government spending by the Scottish Government. The Scottish measure has since fallen below the UK average (0.27 against 0.49 percentage points in 2026–27). It is forecast to turn negative from 2028–29 and stay negative through 2030–31, even as the UK measure recovers. This reflects the tightening needed to absorb mounting pressures. An ageing population is increasing demand for health and social care, and Scotland’s more generous social security system costs around £0.8-1.1 billion a year more than its block grant adjustments provide. To accommodate this, the Scottish Government plans real-terms growth of around 2.4 per cent a year for health and social care, funded by cuts averaging 1.7 per cent across most other portfolios.

Wales faces a similar squeeze under a new government. Plaid Cymru won 43 of the 96 seats in May and leads a minority government that must negotiate its budget through the Senedd. Its first full budget, for 2027–28, faces funding that is effectively flat in real terms, with the core block grant set to fall. That leaves little room for commitments such as Plaid’s childcare expansion, costed at around £400 million a year once fully rolled out. With the draft Welsh budget due on 17 November, any consequentials announced on 28 October will feed almost directly into those choices.

Stormont’s difficulties are more immediate. It has yet to agree a budget for the current year, and departments have been limited to 95 per cent of last year’s funding since April. The Executive has so far refused to accept the UK government’s offer of £450 million in 2026–27 and £400 million in each of the following two years. Behind the dispute lies the question of need. The interim fiscal framework sets Northern Ireland’s relative need at 124 per cent of English spending per head, but Gerald Holtham’s 2025 review put it at 128 per cent, and the Treasury has agreed to consider a review if independent evidence points elsewhere. Executive ministers say parity with Scotland or Wales would require £1–3.5 billion a year in additional funding. That review, more than any one-off settlement, will decide whether Stormont’s funding keeps pace with its needs.

First, further top-ups to English spending. This year’s write-off of 90 per cent of English councils’ historic SEND deficits was worth around £5 billion. However, the OBR forecasts that councils will add a further £4.9 billion in 2027–28 alone, when the statutory override ends and councils must recognise them on their balance sheets. A second write-off is therefore possible, and it would again bring consequentials.

Second, how outstanding defence increases are paid for. The £15 billion Defence Investment Plan is funded mainly by cuts to other department spending, with £4.7 billion still to be found on Budget day. The devolved governments already expect to absorb a share of the announced savings, via the announced 1 per cent cut to UK departmental capital budgets. Of rumoured further cuts, those to carbon capture and hydrogen are mostly reserved and would not touch Scottish and Welsh block grants, but others such as cuts to the Boiler Upgrade Scheme will likely reduce Scottish and Northern Irish budgets. Where the remaining £4.7 billion cuts fall will decide how much devolved budgets shrink.

Third, the Chancellor’s promise to move money out of Westminster. The fiscal devolution roadmap due on Budget Day is expected to set out English mayors’ share of business rates from 2027, with a share of income tax to follow from 2028. All else being equal, replacing central grants with retained taxes would shrink the spending on which Barnett is based, so devolved administrations will be checking whether the Treasury adjusts their block grants to compensate.

Finally, some things are unlikely to change. The first is Northern Ireland’s settlement. The UK government has said its offer will not be improved, and the Northern Ireland Secretary has warned he will set a budget himself if the Executive does not. Even if a deal is confirmed on the day, it is unlikely to match what Northern Ireland ministers have asked for. The second is social security. With the recommendations from the Timms review of PIP yet to report, major reforms to disability benefits, which drive Scotland’s largest block grant adjustments, look unlikely before a later fiscal event. The third is tax. With the government’s commitment not to raise income tax, National Insurance or VAT still in place, large policy changes to the taxes behind Scotland’s and Wales’s block grant adjustments are unlikely.

Spending decisions are only one of the routes by which a Budget reaches the devolved governments. For those with significant devolved tax powers, Scotland above all, the forecast that comes with the Budget matters more. Each block grant is reduced by an adjustment reflecting the revenue, or the social security spending, that the UK government has given up through devolution. These adjustments rest on OBR forecasts that are revised at every fiscal event. They are reconciled against outturn years later, sometimes with large corrections.

For example, the reconciliation of Scottish income tax for 2024–25 will cut Scotland’s 2027–28 budget by £720.5 million. That is above the roughly £670 million the Scottish Government can borrow each year to cover forecast errors. Most of the cut (£512 million) comes from a larger block grant adjustment, as income tax receipts elsewhere in the United Kingdom outperformed the OBR’s forecast and the remainder (£209 million) comes from Scottish receipts falling short of the Scottish Fiscal Commission’s (SFC) forecast. In past reconciliations these forecast errors have largely offset each other, with an SFC estimated correlation of −0.86. However, this is the first time in the last five budgets that they have compounded.

A strong OBR forecast for UK income tax on 28 October would be good news for the Treasury, but it could signal a larger block grant adjustment, and a tighter budget, for Holyrood and, to a lesser extent, the Senedd. Devolved governments will have to absorb any forecast revisions into their plans while forming their own view of how plausible those forecasts are.

The headline figures on 28 October will be only a partial guide to what the Budget means for Holyrood, Cardiff Bay and Stormont. Each enters 2027–28 in a somewhat tighter position, as this year’s one-off funding falls away and UK spending growth slows. For Wales, the consequentials announced on the day will matter most, feeding straight into a draft budget three weeks later. For Scotland, the forecast revisions behind its tax adjustments may matter as much. And for Northern Ireland, the question remains whether there will be a settlement at all.
1 Forecast FIM is available at the UK-level through the OBR and at the Scottish level through the Scottish Fiscal Commission. Welsh and Northern Irish forecast data is not readily accessible.

articles.title: Is PIP reaching the right people?
articles.standfirst:
Afternoon all, It’s less than two weeks till the Budget and we’ve published our take on the key decisions – and constraints – facing Chancellor Healey. If you don’t have time for all 50 pages, we’ve got your primer in Something for the weekend, and a fresh podcast dropping next week. Budget enthusiasts should also … Continued
The post Is PIP reaching the right people? appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: It’s less than two weeks till the Budget and we’ve published our take on the key decisions – and constraints – facing Chancellor Healey. If you don’t have time for all 50 pages, we’ve got your primer in Something for the weekend, and a fresh podcast dropping next week. Budget enthusiasts should also sign up for our post-Budget event while tickets last.

This week the team also tackled a very difficult topic by rethinking Personal Independent Payment, and how the system could better meet its original aim of contributing towards the costs of disability to enable disabled people to live fuller lives. Chart of the week considers whether PIP is offering the right support to the right people.
Plus, we’ve got the lowdown on the IMF’s latest global forecasts, the impact of wealth taxes, and the connection between height and class.

An optimistic outlook. Rare is the IMF report that a British Chancellor might want to frame, but this week’s World Economic Outlook comes close. The Fund nudged its UK growth forecast this year up 0.5 percentage points to 1.3 per cent, the joint-largest upgrade in the G7. It also pencils in the biggest fall in borrowing of that gang, with the deficit shrinking to just 1.4 per cent of GDP by 2031. But as we pointed out in our response, the picture changes once you do a headcount. On GDP per capita, the measure that matters most for living standards, the UK is set to grow by just 0.7 per cent this year, a much measlier achievement. So, while the Government has some reason to be cheery, we’re not out of the woods yet.

Northern (f)lights? Speaking of which, John Healey has apparently rejected calls to equalise Capital Gains with Income Tax. Meanwhile, a new paper found that Norway’s wealth tax reform had some success. Between 2021-2024 the reforms doubled the top marginal tax rate on business wealth, increased dividend taxes by 6 percentage points, and closed loopholes in their exit-tax (the UK is internationally unusual in being silly enough not to have an exit tax at all). Despite headlines claiming the wealthy were fleeing to Switzerland, at most 100 people left, largely before that exit loop-hole was closed, and there was also no reduced inflow of startup founders or inventors. Their departure barely dented the revenue gain, as wealth tax receipts rose 71.5 per cent (down from 75 per cent growth if they’d stayed) with no hit to economic activity and investment. Something to come back to, perhaps, Chancellor?

Short changed. We all know someone who tries to add an extra few cm to their height – but have you ever considered that maybe they’re trying to manifest better living standards? Economic historians have long used height as a proxy for standards of living, and this Substack decided to see if this applied today (with our improved healthcare and living standards) using European survey data. The author finds a predicted height difference of 2 to 5 cm between the top and bottom of the social class and income distributions, particularly dependent on whether financial hardship was experienced in childhood. So, money can’t buy everything, but maybe it can still give a few extra cm.

Fairer firms. How do firms cope when the wage floor rises? A new piece takes us inside French firms to find out, exploiting a quirk of the 35-hour week reforms that raised the average cost of a minimum wage employee by 3.7 per cent. The main response was less about firing and more about reorganising: firms trained up their lowest paid staff, stripped out layers of management and held down pay further up the ladder. With that rejig, employment fell by only 0.9 per cent, while revenue per job rose by 1.1 per cent. The main lesson, though, is that businesses respond to wage floors not just by changing pay, but by reshaping their own internal hierarchies. If you want even more labour market fun, join us and Arin Dube next Thursday (22 October) for the UK launch of his new book, The Wage Standard.

It’s twelve sleeps till the Budget, and it looks like it won’t be the most exciting fiscal event since COVID which is, frankly, good news. But it still comes at a crucial time for public finances and living standards. So to help you contextualise the coming debates here are the key takeaways from our Budget preview.

We expect the OBR’s forecast (before new decisions) will be for borrowing to be about £10 billion a year higher than in Spring. The biggest driver is higher debt interest costs thanks to global bond market jitters. We reckon wiggle room against the fiscal rule to balance day-to-day spending with tax in 2029-30 will halve from £24 billion to £12 billion. The IFS forecast £20 billion with the difference due, I think, primarily to a higher wage forecast. Neither of us knows what the OBR will do, so this is a good reminder of how important that wage forecast will be. If we are right, I expect the Chancellor will raise some taxes in 29-30 to get him a bit closer to the £20 billion number, if not all the way.

But the other challenge is household budgets. We estimate a typical family is £2,900 worse off than they would have been if the cost of living crisis hadn’t materialised. With energy bills forecast to rise to nearly £2,000 a year in January and almost one-in-five households in the poorest half of the country already behind on priority bills, there is widespread expectation of greater support in this Budget.

How to balance these competing aims – medium term repair to the public finances and immediate cost of living support for vulnerable households – will be the central tension of this Budget. Decisions about the path of public spending, on the other hand, look set to remain unresolved.

We tackled the issue of PIP reform this week, so our chart digs into one of the most contentious questions in that debate – are some people receiving PIP who, on the system’s own terms, perhaps shouldn’t be? PIP is intended to help with the extra costs of disability, so in our recent analysis we asked recipients about their limitations, and the extra costs they faced. One-in-eight (12 per cent) report neither higher limitations nor higher costs (their demographic breakdown is on the left of the chart). There is a key age dimension too: almost half (44 per cent) of this group are under 35, compared with just a quarter (26 per cent) of the remaining caseload (right of the chart). The assessment doesn’t look to be doing a good job of identifying the right cohort, with 31 per cent of those without higher limitations or costs receiving a higher PIP award. On the other hand, quick fixes are not available: our research found that the scope to save money simply by excluding certain conditions is very limited. If we want a system that delivers better outcomes for disabled people, as well as being better targeted, it should also become more flexible to their needs, and more focused on their participation in society. Do read the full report for more interesting findings from our new survey of 2,500 PIP recipients, and for all the detail on our proposed changes to this vital area of the welfare state.

articles.title: Why Britain’s homes are becoming energy assets, not just places to live
articles.standfirst:
Recent energy crises have shown the degree to which Britain is exposed to global events. But advances in renewable energy technology, such as solar panels and home batteries, are transforming homes from passive energy consumers into active energy assets, with positive effects for household finances and the energy resilience of Britain, argues Erhan Kilincarslan. Enjoying … Continued
The post Why Britain’s homes are becoming energy assets, not just places to live first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: Recent energy crises have shown the degree to which Britain is exposed to global events. But advances in renewable energy technology, such as solar panels and home batteries, are transforming homes from passive energy consumers into active energy assets, with positive effects for household finances and the energy resilience of Britain, argues Erhan Kilincarslan.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

For most of the past century, British homes had a straightforward relationship with the energy system. They consumed electricity generated elsewhere, paid monthly bills and had little control over either the source or the price of their energy. That relationship is beginning to change.

Across the UK, a growing number of homeowners are installing rooftop solar panels, home batteries and smart energy technologies that allow them to generate, store and manage electricity themselves. In doing so, homes are evolving from passive consumers into active participants in Britain’s energy system.
The implications extend far beyond lower electricity bills. They could change the economics of home ownership itself.

The growing interest in household solar is no coincidence. The cost of photovoltaic (PV) systems has fallen substantially over the past decade as manufacturing has expanded and the technology has become more efficient. At the same time, government policies, including zero per cent VAT on eligible residential solar installations and the Smart Export Guarantee, which allows households to receive payments for surplus electricity exported to the grid, have strengthened the financial case for investing in rooftop solar.

Recent evidence suggests that demand remains exceptionally strong. Britain recorded a record 269,000 solar installations in 2025, the highest annual total on record, with rooftop systems accounting for more than 95 per cent of new installations. At the same time, interest in home battery systems has accelerated as households seek greater control over their energy costs and reduce their dependence on the grid.
The UK government is moving forward with plans to introduce low-cost plug-in solar panels that can be installed on balconies, terraces and other small outdoor spaces.

Technology is also expanding beyond traditional rooftop systems. The UK government is moving forward with plans to introduce low-cost plug-in solar panels that can be installed on balconies, terraces and other small outdoor spaces, potentially extending the benefits of solar generation to millions of renters and flat owners who have traditionally been excluded from the market. If widely adopted, these systems could broaden access to household renewable energy and accelerate the shift towards more decentralised electricity generation.

By lowering installation costs and reducing the need for home ownership, plug-in solar could broaden participation in Britain’s energy transition in much the same way that rooftop solar transformed owner-occupied housing over the past decade. Yet the growing popularity of household solar cannot be explained by falling costs alone.

The past few years have exposed how vulnerable British households remain to global energy markets. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine triggered Europe’s worst energy crisis in decades, sending wholesale gas prices to record levels and sharply increasing household energy bills across the UK. The episode served as a stark reminder that events taking place thousands of miles away can have immediate consequences for domestic finances.

More recently, renewed tensions in the Middle East have once again unsettled global oil and gas markets, highlighting the continued sensitivity of energy prices to geopolitical developments. Although Britain imports relatively little energy directly from the region, it remains exposed through interconnected international markets, where disruptions to global supply can feed through into higher wholesale prices and ultimately household energy bills.

For many homeowners, these repeated shocks have reinforced a simple lesson: generating at least some electricity at home offers not only environmental benefits but also a degree of protection against increasingly uncertain global energy markets.

This represents an important shift in thinking. Solar panels are increasingly viewed not simply as environmental investments but as financial assets capable of reducing long-term household expenditure and improving resilience against future price shocks. The transformation extends even further when battery storage enters the equation.

Rather than exporting surplus electricity during the day and buying it back in the evening, homeowners can increasingly store their own electricity for later use or combine battery systems with smart tariffs that charge when electricity is cheap and discharge when prices rise. The result is a home that no longer simply consumes electricity but increasingly generates, stores and manages its own energy.

Energy economists increasingly describe households equipped with rooftop solar and battery storage as “prosumers” because they both produce and consume electricity, reflecting a fundamental shift in the relationship between homes and the energy system. This transformation has wider implications for Britain’s electricity system.

Traditionally, electricity has been generated at large centralised power stations before being transmitted across the country through the national grid. As more households generate and store their own electricity, the energy system is becoming increasingly decentralised, with homes playing a more active role in balancing supply and demand. Millions of properties producing relatively small amounts of electricity can collectively become part of the country’s energy infrastructure, reducing pressure on the grid and improving system flexibility while supporting the wider integration of renewable energy.
As more households generate and store their own electricity, the energy system is becoming increasingly decentralised, with homes playing a more active role in balancing supply and demand.

This is not merely a theoretical possibility. In countries such as Germany and Australia, rooftop solar already accounts for a substantial share of electricity generation, demonstrating how decentralised energy production can complement conventional power generation. Britain appears to be moving steadily in the same direction as household solar and battery adoption continues to expand.

The housing market may eventually reflect this transition. Just as buyers routinely consider school catchment areas, broadband speeds or insulation standards, energy performance is becoming an increasingly important consideration for many households. Properties equipped with rooftop solar, battery storage and high energy efficiency ratings may become more attractive as buyers seek lower running costs and greater protection against future energy price volatility.

Of course, rooftop solar will not solve every challenge facing Britain’s energy system. Not every property is suitable, batteries remain expensive and large-scale investment in electricity networks, offshore wind and nuclear generation will remain essential.
But the cumulative impact of millions of household decisions should not be underestimated.

For decades, British homes have been viewed primarily as places to live and stores of wealth. Increasingly, they are becoming something else as well: energy assets capable of generating income, reducing costs and strengthening resilience against future energy shocks.

The next stage of Britain’s energy transition may depend not only on giant infrastructure projects but also on millions of small investments made by ordinary homeowners. If that trend continues, some of the country’s next generation of power stations may already be standing on suburban streets across Britain.
Enjoyed this post? Sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.
All articles posted on this blog give the views of the author(s), and not the position of LSE British Politics and Policy, nor of the London School of Economics and Political Science.

Erhan Kilincarslan is a Reader in Accounting and Finance at Huddersfield Business School. He obtained his PhD in Finance from Birkbeck, University of London. His research focuses on corporate finance, empirical finance, corporate governance, and corporate social responsibility, and spans applications of accounting and finance across sectors such as tourism, banking, REITs and green stocks.

articles.title: The California Billionaire Tax’s Ever-Shifting Goalposts
articles.standfirst: Wealth taxes have been a failure everywhere they’ve been tried, which may be why advocates for the California amendment are saying this is a new frontier. But the countries that have tried this gamble know the frontier well, and they’ve left it in the dust.
paragraphs: We were promised it was a modest idea. By passing a one-time taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities., targeted at just the highest earners in California, the state could fill some budget gaps for health care programs and schools.
But economists have been sounding the alarm that punitive measures like these are never as simple as they appear. And the very ones driving this tax hike are proving their point.

Take Gabriel Zucman, one of the key advocates of the ballot measure. He described the amendment in a September interview as “a one-time tax on billionaires.” And he assured readers in an op-ed for The New York Times that a tax like this wasn’t an attempt to “fix” all of California’s problems.
This is a preview of our full op-ed originally published in The Orange County Register.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Daniel Bunn is President and CEO of the Tax Foundation. Daniel has been with the organization since 2018 and, prior to becoming President, successfully built its Center for Global Tax Policy, expanding the Tax Foundation’s reach and impact around the world. Prior to joining the Tax Foundation, Daniel worked in the United States Senate at the Joint Economic Committee.

articles.title: Washington Voters Will Decide Whether to Keep or Reject an Income Tax on High Earners
articles.standfirst: Washington’s new income tax on high earners doesn’t take effect until 2028, but it is already generating a lot of activity. A measure on the ballot this November, Initiative 645, would reverse the legislature’s decision, preventing the new tax from taking effect.
paragraphs: Washington’s new income taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. on high earners doesn’t take effect until 2028, but it is already generating a lot of activity. A date has been set for oral arguments in a constitutional challenge to the new law. One state lawmaker recently proposed reducing the threshold to as low as $250,000. And a measure on the ballot this November, Initiative 645, would reverse the legislature’s decision, preventing the new tax from taking effect.

In 2024, the legislature overwhelmingly approved a filed ballot measure stipulating that “Neither the state nor any county, city, or other local jurisdiction in the state of Washington may tax any individual person on any form of personal income,” rather than letting it go to voters. This was largely a procedural move: amending language adopted by ballot measure requires a two-thirds legislative supermajority for the first two years. Had voters approved it in November 2024, lawmakers would not have been able to consider an income tax until the 2027 session. Taking it off the ballot and passing it themselves in early 2024 started the clock sooner, allowing lawmakers to come back during the 2026 session (rather than waiting until the 2027 session) and do what the measure prohibited: adopt an income tax.

In another procedural move, Washington lawmakers added an emergency clause to the high-earner income tax, asserting that the new tax—which doesn’t go into effect until 2028, with a tax filing date in 2029—was “necessary for the support of the state government and its existing public institutions.” This shielded the measure from a provision in Washington law that ordinarily lets voters review tax changes through a referendum. With that avenue blocked, opponents of the income tax instead filed their own initiative to repeal the tax, which was successfully placed on the ballot.

In Washington, which had no income taxation until recently, and where the constitution has previously been interpreted as largely prohibiting income taxation (hence the pending litigation), some high earners in Seattle could face the highest combined state and local top rate in the country—18.037 percent (split across employer and employee)—under the tax, combining the new 9.9 percent tax with the 5 percent Seattle Social Housing Tax, 2.557 percent Seattle JumpStart Tax, and 0.58 percent WA Cares tax.

The tax, imposed on individuals or couples with incomes above $1 million, will largely fall on small business owners and highly compensated tech workers. Very few people earn salaries over $1 million. In most instances, incomes at that level flow through three channels: capital gains and dividend income, pass-through businessA pass-through business is a sole proprietorship, partnership, or S corporation that is not subject to the corporate income tax; instead, this business reports its income on the individual income tax returns of the owners and is taxed at individual income tax rates. income, and restricted stock unit (RSU) vesting, where years’ worth of granted shares can vest all at once, particularly when a company goes public. Someone could work at a startup for five years, and then when it goes public, all five years of accumulated stock vests at once, yielding income above $1 million even though their average income over the period is well below that.

The tax also affects pass-through businesses. According to the US Small Business Administration, Washington’s 672,472 small businesses (most of which are pass-throughs) employ 1.4 million people, representing 48.4 percent of all Washington employees. A 9.9 percent tax on small business owners imposes one of the nation’s highest taxes on their income in a state that already imposes a high-rate gross receipts taxGross receipts taxes are applied to a company’s gross sales, without deductions for a firm’s business expenses, like compensation, costs of goods sold, and overhead costs. Unlike a sales tax, a gross receipts tax is assessed on businesses and applies to transactions at every stage of the production process, leading to tax pyramiding. (the Business & Occupation Tax) and subjects an unusually high share of their business inputs to the sales taxA sales tax is levied on retail sales of goods and services and, ideally, should apply to all final consumption with few exemptions. Many governments exempt goods like groceries; base broadening, such as including groceries, could keep rates lower. A sales tax should exempt business-to-business transactions which, when taxed, cause tax pyramiding. .

Washington’s existing tax code is heavily skewed toward business taxes, in part because it forgoes a broad-based individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source, but, unlike other states without one, Washington doesn’t have a low-tax, limited-government ethos. This forces businesses to shoulder a disproportionate share of the tax burden. By imposing a high-rate income tax only on high earners, Washington creates the worst of both worlds for its small business owners, limiting their ability to grow and undercutting job creation.

Those with RSUs vesting aren’t the only ones who could find themselves unexpectedly subject to the tax. Someone selling a business they built up for many years, or generating significant capital gains from selling a home, could also find themselves subject to the tax in a given year.

The tax also features an unusual design. Its charitable deduction is capped at $50,000. Joint filers’ income is taxed above $1 million the same as single filers; two single earners with $600,000 each would not face any tax liability, while those two taxpayers would as joint filers. And it doesn’t include any safe harbor for those who unexpectedly become subject to the tax when their income suddenly exceeds the threshold. Under federal law and in other states, underpayment penalties are not imposed if the taxpayer pays at least 90 percent of their current year’s tax liability or 100 (or 110) percent of the prior year’s tax liability throughout the year through withholdingWithholding is the income an employer takes out of an employee’s paycheck and remits to the federal, state, and/or local government. It is calculated based on the amount of income earned, the taxpayer’s filing status, the number of allowances claimed, and any additional amount the employee requests. or quarterly estimated payments. Washington’s new tax has no such safe harbor, meaning someone who did not anticipate becoming a filer or misjudged their liability could be hit with penalties.

Repealing the new tax by ballot measure is an uphill battle, made harder by ballot language warning that repeal would require cuts to education funding, even though the tax is not even in place yet. (A 2022 law allows the attorney general to supply a fiscal impact statement to ballot measures, but critics of the statement attached to this measure point out that it speaks of decreasing funding even though the tax in question does not yet exist and no budget has been adopted incorporating those future revenues.) But especially as lawmakers start discussing ways to expand the tax to more taxpayers before it even takes effect, many voters may be inclined to do what voters in many previous Washington elections have done: reject an income tax.

Jared Walczak is a Senior Fellow at the Tax Foundation, where he spent five years as Vice President of State Projects, and president of Walczak Policy Consulting.

articles.title: Raising Revenue: Taxing the Wealthy?
articles.standfirst: The case of wealth taxes Wealth in the United Kingdom has grown far faster than incomes over recent decades, yet the tax system still heavily taxes income over wealth. Income...
paragraphs: The United Kingdom faces record borrowing costs, and while public debt sits at 95 per cent of GDP and spending is set to rise, the Chancellor needs to raise revenue. After pledging not to tax working people, the focus will likely turn to taxing the wealthy.

Wealth in the United Kingdom has grown far faster than incomes over recent decades, yet the tax system still heavily taxes income over wealth. Income taxes are targeted because they are easy to measure and taxed at source; however, a wealth tax, defined as an annual levy on an individual’s worth, is difficult to measure. While such a tax can help redistribute wealth and reduce inequalities, in practice, valuing total assets such as homes, shares, pensions and businesses can prove very difficult. As such, pure annual wealth taxes are rare, found in only a handful of OECD countries such as Norway and Switzerland.

They also have economic implications; the Mirrlees Review notes that a 1 per cent annual wealth tax lowers the reward for saving, yet charges investors earning exceptional returns no more than those with the same wealth earning ordinary ones. The United Kingdom therefore has no annual net wealth tax; instead, it targets assets predominantly held by the wealthy, including capital gains tax (CGT), inheritance tax (IHT), stamp duty land tax (SDLT), council tax and, from 2028, a “mansion tax”.

Ahead of the 28 October Budget, Chancellor John Healey faces a difficult backdrop. Public sector net debt stands at 94 per cent of GDP, and borrowing is already £8.1bn above forecast. Debt interest now costs around £110bn a year, more than the defence budget, as 10-year gilt yields hit their highest level in nearly two decades. With public finances under pressure, the Chancellor must bring down borrowing while raising defence spending, supporting welfare and easing rising household energy bills. With little room to borrow more, the Budget will need to raise revenues.

Two taxes dominate speculation: a rise in CGT and a lower threshold for the new mansion tax. Both promise money from the wealthy without breaking the manifesto pledge not to raise taxes on working people, namely income tax, National Insurance and VAT, which together make up 60 per cent of tax revenues.

CGT affects less than one per cent of the population and contributes around 1.3 per cent of total receipts, yet it is the lever politicians often reach for first, with policy swinging between taxing gains like income and lower flat rates. Raising rates or aligning them with income tax at up to 45 per cent looks like a clear way to make wealth pay its share. But unlike income, gains are highly elastic as investors can choose when to sell and when to hold. If investors anticipate a rate rise, they can rush to sell assets at the lower rate, as was seen in the run-up to the 2024 Budget, which triggered an 82 per cent increase in realised gains (which then rose a smaller-than-expected 24%), leading to a one-off record of £24.2bn in receipts. In the longer run, the behaviour can flip, as investors “lock-in” and hold assets for longer than intended or productive, reducing the flow of revenue. Higher rates can also push highly mobile investors and business owners to relocate to countries with more favourable tax rates, removing the tax base entirely. The true impact on revenue is unclear, but HMRC estimates show that by 2028-29 an extra percentage point on the higher rate would have minimal impact, while a 10-percentage point rise would reduce receipts by around £3.6bn a year.

Property taxes, however, are inelastic. Since they are in fixed supply, the charge cannot be avoided by selling or moving abroad. Hence, the mansion tax, an annual surcharge on homes worth over £2m, is more predictable and efficient than CGT, but few homes are liable, and it is expected to raise just £430m a year. Lowering the threshold to £1.5m would roughly double the number of homes liable but would still do little to cover proposed additional spending and bring down borrowing.

While this sits with the wealthy, those who are asset-rich and cash poor, or highly leveraged, may feel impacted disproportionately, particularly in London, where liable homes are concentrated after decades of house-price growth.

These adverse impacts will be compounded as the surcharge sits on top of an outdated council tax, and they do not stop with owners, as landlords may pass the cost on to renters. Perception is a risk too, as the mansion tax announcements showed; tax-related backlash can reach far beyond those paying, so the Chancellor must weigh revenue against fallout.

Rather than tweaking rates, the Chancellor could reform how wealth is taxed. The Mirrlees Review, offers a better route to a “progressive, neutral” system, where similar activities are taxed alike. Given many people hold money in assets rather than income because gains are taxed less, taxing gains at income tax rates, but only above a risk-free return such as gilt yields, would remove that incentive without discouraging investment. Also, ending CGT’s exemption at death would ease lock-in and ensure gains passed on at death are taxed.

Reforming property taxation may offer a stronger case, given the current system’s inefficiencies. Despite decades of rising house prices and a shortage of homes, council tax in England still rests on 1991 valuations, so lower-income households pay a larger share of their income than wealthier ones. Stamp duty, meanwhile, penalises buyers upfront and discourages moving. Replacing both with a single tax on current property values, or a land value tax, could raise revenue more efficiently, falling hardest on the most valuable homes and drawing on an inelastic base. While this would take time to implement and raise little additional revenue at first, it is economically efficient and, as research suggests, land tax comes with a growth boost after shifting taxes from labour and capital onto land. As a NIESR blog by Mark Cliffe suggests, to prelude this, new high-value council tax bands from 2028 could fund a temporary stamp duty holiday for downsizers, incentivising better use of under-occupied homes. Further still,NIESR’s modelling suggests that if a large sum is needed quickly, a rise in income tax would do the least damage to GDP, even though that would break the manifesto pledge and fall on workers rather than wealth.

Overall, wealth should be taxed to reduce inequality, but tweaking rates will do little to reduce borrowing materially. Although harder to implement and slower to pay off, reforming the base, would raise more and distort less, offering a fairer and more lasting way to make the wealthy pay their share.

articles.title: Spain’s Transformation After a Decade of Fiscal Competition
articles.standfirst: The 2026 Regional Tax Competitiveness Index for Spain highlights a growing divergence between regions that have embraced tax reform and those whose tax systems have remained largely unchanged.
paragraphs: Over the past decade, Spain’s autonomous communities have increasingly used their taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. powers to make their tax systems more attractive for both entrepreneurs and residents. Now in its 10th edition, the Regional Tax Competitiveness Index (RTCI) highlights a growing divergence between regions that have embraced tax reform and those whose tax systems have remained largely unchanged. By 2026, some territories had transformed themselves from laggards into leaders, while others fell behind as their neighbors modernized their tax systems.
The most remarkable success stories over the period are Extremadura and Andalusia.
No region improved more between 2017 and 2026 than Extremadura. Over the decade, it climbed 11 positions, moving from 19th to 8th place and increasing its overall score by 1.43 points.

This remarkable transformation was the result of a sustained reform agenda. The regional government progressively reduced the burden of key taxes, beginning with the introduction of a 99 percent inheritance taxAn inheritance tax is levied upon the value of inherited assets received by a beneficiary after a decedent’s death. Not to be confused with estate taxes, which are paid by the decedent’s estate based on the size of the total estate before assets are distributed, inheritance taxes are paid by the recipient or heir based on the value of the bequest received. rebate for close relatives. The reform effort accelerated in 2023 with the approval of a full wealth taxA wealth tax is imposed on an individual’s net wealth, or the market value of their total owned assets minus liabilities. A wealth tax can be narrowly or widely defined, and depending on the definition of wealth, the base for a wealth tax can vary. exemption, placing Extremadura among the most competitive regions in this area. Income tax rates were also reduced, particularly for lower-income earners, while further changes introduced in 2026 extended inheritance tax relief to nephews and nieces in specific circumstances. Together, these reforms fundamentally changed the region’s fiscal position and allowed it to become one of Spain’s strongest improvers over the last decade.

Andalusia experienced the second-largest improvement in Spain, rising from 16th position in 2017 to 7th place in 2026. Its score increased by 1.13 points, reflecting a broad-based strategy aimed at enhancing tax competitiveness.

The region pursued a series of reforms across several tax categories. Successive reductions in personal income tax rates were combined with the indexation of tax bracketsA tax bracket is the range of incomes taxed at given rates, which typically differ depending on filing status. In a progressive individual or corporate income tax system, rates rise as income increases. There are seven federal individual income tax brackets; the federal corporate income tax system is flat. and allowances to mitigate the effects of inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin. At the same time, Andalusia significantly reduced inheritance taxation by introducing a 99 percent rebate and establishing a €1 million exemption for close relatives. Wealth taxation was also reformed through a rebate mechanism linked to the national solidarity tax. In addition, the regional government permanently reduced property transfer taxes and stamp duties. These changes transformed Andalusia from one of Spain’s least competitive fiscal jurisdictions into one of the top-performing regions.

Murcia also made substantial progress during the period, climbing five positions to reach 9th place in 2026. Its improvement was driven by reforms that reduced the burden of inheritance taxation, lowered personal income tax rates, and eased wealth taxation.

The Valencian Community followed a different path. After losing ground because of tax increases introduced in 2021 and 2022, the region began reversing course in recent years. In 2026, it regained two positions thanks to a package of reforms that included lower income tax rates, a higher wealth tax exemptionA tax exemption excludes certain income, revenue, or even taxpayers from tax altogether. For example, nonprofits that fulfill certain requirements are granted tax-exempt status by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), preventing them from having to pay income tax. threshold, reductions in transfer and stamp duties, and broader inheritance tax relief. These measures suggest a renewed focus on improving fiscal competitiveness after a period of deterioration.

Castilla-La Mancha recorded the largest decline in the ranking, dropping from 8th in 2017 to 16th in 2026. As neighboring regions modernized their tax systems and reduced tax burdens, the region gradually lost competitiveness, illustrating how inaction can be as consequential as adopting higher taxes.

Asturias also lost considerable ground, falling from 13th to 18th position. Although the region introduced some reforms in 2025 and 2026, these changes arrived relatively late and were not sufficient to offset years of limited policy action. As a result, Asturias continues to rank among the weakest performers, particularly in inheritance taxation, where it remains one of the least competitive jurisdictions in Spain.

Navarre’s position also weakened over the decade, falling five places to 12th position in 2026. While recent reforms improved the treatment of lower-income taxpayers within the personal income tax system, earlier decisions relating to inheritance and wealth taxation reduced the region’s overall competitiveness. Navarre continues to rank last in the wealth tax component of the index, which significantly weighs on its overall performance.

Catalonia remains the least competitive tax jurisdiction in Spain, occupying 19th place in 2026 with a score of 4.45. Several factors explain this outcome. The region maintains relatively high marginal income tax rates, imposes one of the heaviest wealth tax burdens in the country, and applies high rates to property transfers. In addition, Catalonia levies 11 regional own taxes, approximately twice as many as most other autonomous communities. Although some reforms have been introduced over the years, they have not been sufficient to reverse the effects of previous tax increases or to significantly improve the region’s standing.

The top of the ranking continues to be dominated by Madrid and the three Basque provinces. Madrid remains the clear leader, supported by a long-term strategy based on low taxation and administrative simplicity. The region has eliminated all regional own taxes, applies a full rebate to the wealth tax linked to the national solidarity tax, maintains a highly competitive inheritance tax system, and has repeatedly reduced personal income tax rates while adjusting tax brackets for inflation.

Madrid’s leadership is particularly evident when comparing its score with those of other top-performing jurisdictions. In 2026, Madrid achieved a score of 7.12, enjoying a lead of 0.35 points over Biscay, 0.38 points over Álava and 0.52 points over Guipúzcoa. The difference becomes even more striking when compared with Catalonia, as Madrid outperforms the region by 2.67 points, underlining the substantial divergence that has emerged between Spain’s most and least competitive tax systems.

One of the most striking features of the 2026 RTCI is the high degree of concentration among Spain’s regions. The most competitive group below Madrid and the Basque provinces is found between 5th and 10th place, where score differences are exceptionally small. The Canary Islands ranks 5th with 6.38 points, followed by La Rioja (6.36), Andalusia (6.31), Extremadura (6.26), Murcia (6.19), and Cantabria (6.18). The difference between 5th and 10th place is just 0.20 points, illustrating how closely matched these regions have become. In such a condensed group, even relatively modest tax reforms could result in significant changes in the ranking from one year to the next.

A clear break appears immediately after this cluster. While only 0.20 points separate the regions between 5th and 10th place, the gap between Cantabria in 10th and the Balearic Islands in 11th widens to 0.21 points. This marks the boundary between the upper-middle group and the rest of the ranking. The regions from the Balearic Islands in 11th place to Castilla-La Mancha in 16th place are separated by 0.36 points in total. This spread reflects a high degree of convergence among these regions and suggests that they operate with broadly similar levels of tax competitiveness.

The picture changes below Castilla-La Mancha. Despite ranking 16th, it remains clearly ahead of the bottom-performing regions, with a gap of around 0.60 points, underscoring the divide between the middle-lower tier and the least competitive territories.

Taken together, the 2026 results reveal an increasingly segmented landscape. At the top, Madrid and the Basque provinces maintain a clear advantage over the rest of Spain. Beneath them lies a highly competitive upper-middle tier stretching from the Canary Islands in 5th place to Cantabria in 10th. A second, equally concentrated group extends from the Balearic Islands through Navarre, Castile and Leon, Valencia Community, Galicia, and Castilla-La Mancha in 16th place. Finally, a lower-performing group, including Aragon, Asturias, and Catalonia, remains significantly behind the national average, creating a visible divide between the mainstream of Spain’s regional tax systems and the jurisdictions at the bottom of the RTCI.

The period from 2017 to 2026 shows that tax policy matters. Regions that consistently reduced tax burdens, simplified their systems, and improved inheritance and wealth tax treatment moved sharply upward in the rankings. Higher-ranked regions tend to offer tax systems that are more neutral, predictable, and investment-friendly, making them better positioned to attract economic activity, retain talent, and support long-term growth. Extremadura and Andalusia are the clearest examples of successful reform strategies, while Castilla-La Mancha, Asturias, and Catalonia illustrate the costs of stagnation or heavier taxation.

By 2026, Spain’s fiscal landscape is characterized by four distinct groups: a leading quartet headed by Madrid and the Basque provinces, a densely packed upper-middle tier stretching from the Canary Islands to Cantabria, a lower-middle tier formed by six regions, and a group of lagging regions still burdened by less competitive tax systems. The next round of reforms will likely determine whether these gaps continue to widen or begin to narrow in the years ahead.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Cristina Enache writes on the economics of tax policy and is the author of the Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index. She was formerly the Director of Research at Civismo, an economic research organization based in Spain. She also served as head of research at Institución Futuro, a regional think tank based in Navarra in northern Spain. She is also currently Secretary-General at the World Taxpayers Associations and General Manager of the Spanish Taxpayers Union, which she joined in 2016.
